A run-level review model override can select such a target because a pinned routing chain bypasses the free-only filter.
findings.suggestion: Carry the finder’s local status into the call and omit checkout or explicitly exclude that call from worker eligibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel has a local finder and the run pins review to a Claude or Codex subscription model. With review workers enabled for the repository, the finder creates a worker job instead of running locally.

output.summary: Reviewed worker review dispatch, execution, result validation, and restart handling. The focused tests could not run because the checkout is missing the entities package.

findings.title: Local panel finders can be dispatched to workers
findings.detail: The shared review call supplies checkout metadata to every production panel finder, but the executor has no indication that a finder is marked local. A free target using a Claude or Codex CLI without backend metadata passes worker eligibility. The request explicitly requires local finders to stay local.
findings.suggestion: Pass an explicit local-finder flag through the call seam, or omit checkout metadata for local finders, and test a free CLI target without backend metadata.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel roster contains a local finder routed to a configured free Claude CLI provider, and review workers are enabled for the repository. The finder creates a worker job instead of running locally.

output.summary: Reviewed the generator, eval preparation and report formats. The targeted test could not run because the checkout lacks the 'entities' dependency. The default dataset is also absent from this checkout.

findings.title: The documented generator cannot start without a dataset file
findings.detail: The default path points to evals/implement/cases.json, but neither that file nor its parent directory exists in this commit. The unconditional read fails before any PR is inspected, so the documented command cannot generate a case in a fresh checkout. The tests create their own envelope and therefore do not exercise the default path.
findings.suggestion: Provide the existing dataset at the runner's default path, or support initializing the required version-1 envelope when it is absent.
findings.failure_scenario: Run the documented generator in a fresh checkout: reading evals/implement/cases.json fails with ENOENT and no case is generated.

findings.title: The CLI never retrieves available production complexity
findings.detail: The production metadata parser can use an injected run lookup, but the only documented CLI entry point never supplies one. Consequently every generated case defaults to medium even when the report identifies a locally stored run with a known triage complexity. This misses the explicit requirement to use production complexity when it can be found and can misclassify cases.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only run-record lookup, retaining the documented unknown fallback when the record cannot be found.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR's report identifies a persisted run whose triage complexity is small; running the documented command records medium instead.

output.summary: Reviewed the generator, eval-runner integration, report parsing, and tests. The targeted test could not start because this checkout lacks the entities dependency. The default dataset is also absent from the reviewed tree.

findings.title: The documented command cannot open its default dataset
findings.detail: The generator unconditionally reads evals/implement/cases.json, but neither that file nor the evals directory exists in the reviewed tree. A fresh checkout therefore fails before inspecting any PR or printing the validation table.
findings.suggestion: Provide the existing implement dataset at the default path, or establish a compatible way to initialize or locate it before reading cases.
findings.failure_scenario: Running the documented command in a fresh checkout fails with ENOENT for evals/implement/cases.json.

findings.title: Generated cases can be rejected by the runner's contamination check
findings.detail: The generator validates tests in ordinary worktrees but never enables snapshot mode or checks the runner's history restrictions. For a PR whose base history contains evals/implement, it can accept and publish a case that the runner refuses during preparation because its pinned history contains eval labels.
findings.suggestion: Validate generated cases against the runner's contamination rules and use snapshot mode where appropriate, or exclude cases that cannot be run.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged factory PR based on a revision after the implement dataset was added has tests that fail at base and pass at head. Generation accepts it, but an implement eval fails preparation with 'pinned history contains eval labels'.

findings.title: The CLI never looks up production triage complexity
findings.detail: Although the generator supports an injected lookupRun function, the only documented CLI invocation does not provide one. Consequently every case generated by the command records medium, even when its production run and complexity are available locally. This misses the requested production complexity and can change the implement prompt and budget selection.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only production run lookup and use the recorded complexity when available.
findings.failure_scenario: A factory PR has a run footer identifying a stored run with small complexity. The documented command generates a medium case and notes that lookup was not configured.

output.summary: Reviewed the generator, eval preparation changes, and factory report format. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout lacks the entities dependency: `bun test test/implement-replay-cases.test.ts test/evals-implement-runner.test.ts` reported `Cannot find package 'entities'` before running any tests.

findings.title: Generated cases cannot be prepared for the target repository
findings.detail: Every generated case enables snapshot mode, which removes `evals/`. The generator then requires all baseline checks to pass in that snapshot. Limitless's own test suite reads `evals/`, so its baseline test gate fails and preparation excludes the PR before hidden-test validation. This prevents the generator from producing cases from the factory's own merged Limitless PRs, the stated purpose of the request.
findings.suggestion: Provide a replay preparation strategy that both avoids exposing the solution and permits the target repository's baseline checks to run.
findings.failure_scenario: Generate a case from a merged Limitless PR whose base has the repository's normal test gate: the snapshot removes `evals/`, the baseline test gate fails, and the case is excluded.

findings.title: CLI never looks up production triage complexity
findings.detail: The generator supports an injected run lookup, but the actual CLI supplies no `lookupRun`. Consequently, even when the report identifies a run whose record is available locally, every generated case receives the default medium complexity instead of its production triage complexity.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only run-record lookup and retain the documented fallback only when the record or complexity is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR has a report footer identifying a locally stored run with complexity `small`; invoking the documented CLI writes `medium` and says lookup was not configured.

findings.title: Validation retains setup modifications that grading discards
findings.detail: Validation injects and runs hidden tests immediately after setup, while actual grading runs gates and then resets and cleans the checkout before injecting hidden files. A setup command that changes a tracked source file can therefore make the reference pass validation using content that will not be present when a candidate is graded.
findings.suggestion: Match the grading checkout's reset and clean behavior before injecting the hidden files during validation.
findings.failure_scenario: A base-configured setup command rewrites a tracked module to provide an export needed by the hidden test. Head validation passes with that rewrite, but grading resets it before the hidden test and the same implementation fails.

output.summary: Reviewed the generator, replay preparation, grading path, and production metadata extraction. Targeted tests could not start because this checkout lacks the installed `entities` dependency: `bun test test/implement-replay-cases.test.ts test/evals-implement-runner.test.ts` reported `Cannot find package 'entities'` and ran no tests.

findings.title: The command fails before generating a case in this checkout
findings.detail: The default dataset file is read unconditionally, but neither the base commit nor this change contains an `evals/` directory. The documented CLI provides no way to supply another case file, so a fresh checkout cannot run the generator or add a case to the runner's default dataset.
findings.suggestion: Provide the default dataset through the supported repository setup, or initialize an appropriate dataset when it is absent while preserving existing cases when present.
findings.failure_scenario: Running the documented command from a fresh checkout fails with ENOENT for `evals/implement/cases.json` before querying the PR.

findings.title: Validation retains setup files that grading deletes
findings.detail: Validation injects hidden tests immediately after setup, while `gradeImplement` resets and runs `git clean -fdq` before injecting them. Untracked, non-ignored files created by setup therefore exist during validation but disappear during actual grading. A case can be accepted with a passing head even though the same hidden tests fail for a correct implementation.
findings.suggestion: Apply the same reset and clean sequence used by grading before running the hidden command in validation.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command creates an untracked `ready` file and the hidden test reads it. Head validation passes, but grading removes `ready` and the hidden test fails.

findings.title: The CLI never looks up production complexity
findings.detail: Although `replayProduction` supports an injected run lookup, the actual CLI supplies only `cache`. Consequently every generated case receives the default medium complexity, even when the production run and its triage complexity are available locally. This misses the explicitly requested production complexity and can misclassify the generated dataset.
findings.suggestion: Connect the CLI to a read-only production run lookup and retain the default only when the record or complexity is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged PR's report names a locally recorded high-complexity run; invoking the documented generator saves the case as medium and notes that lookup was not configured.

output.summary: Reviewed snapshot creation, gate execution, reuse, and verification evidence. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout's installed dependencies are incomplete or incompatible: `bun test test/agent-full-suite-gate.test.ts test/agent-test.test.ts test/gate-evidence.test.ts` reported a missing `entities` package and missing Zod methods. Those environment errors are not treated as findings.

findings.title: Timed-out factory executions are never reused
findings.detail: The record is written only when `completed(result)` is true, and that predicate rejects timeouts and interrupted exits. Consequently, a full suite that times out in the implement session is run again in the gates stage even when the tree, configuration, and environment are identical. The request explicitly requires the recorded failure, retries, and classification to carry over.
findings.suggestion: Apply the normal gate timeout retry and classification policy to the session execution, then persist and reuse its completed failure outcome as well as passing outcomes.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer requests the full suite on the final tree; the configured test check reaches its timeout. The session receives a failure, but no record is stored, so the gates stage runs the full suite again on the same tree.

findings.title: Record can attest to a tree the gate no longer checked
findings.detail: Unlike the gates stage, the session gate does not check whether its checkout's HEAD changed during setup or the test command before recording the result under the original snapshot tree. A successful check after such a change can later be reused and accepted as evidence for the original tree.
findings.suggestion: Verify the snapshot checkout still points to the synthetic commit after execution, and refuse to record its result if HEAD changed.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured setup or test command checks out another commit and passes there; the final round retains the original snapshot tree, and its gate stage reuses that passing result.

output.summary: Reviewed the snapshot, execution, reuse, and evidence paths. The targeted command `bun test test/agent-full-suite-gate.test.ts test/agent-test.test.ts test/gate-evidence.test.ts` could not start: the installed Zod lacks `overwrite` and `prefault`, and the `entities` package is missing.

findings.title: Interrupted and timed-out gate failures are never reused
findings.detail: The record is saved only when `completed(result)` is true, which excludes timeouts, confinement failures, and signal-style exit codes. A subsequent gates stage therefore runs the test check again for the same tree instead of carrying over the factory gate failure and its classification. The request explicitly requires failures and their classifications to carry over unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Persist and validate these factory gate results as failures, and reuse their original classification without turning an incomplete or unreadable record into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer requests the full suite, the factory test gate times out, and the implementer makes no further changes. The round gates stage runs the full suite again instead of reusing the timeout failure.

findings.title: LAN executor configuration disables local-session gate requests even for local repositories
findings.detail: The handler is disabled whenever the configured executor has kind `lan`. However, the LAN executor runs gates locally for repositories outside its configured worker repository list. Thus a local implement session for such a repository receives a factory-gate-unavailable error even though its normal gate execution is local. This violates the requested local implement-session behavior.
findings.suggestion: Decide whether the repository's gate execution is local rather than rejecting the entire LAN executor by kind, and use a local executor for eligible snapshot gates.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon uses the LAN gate executor for selected repositories, but the current repository is not in that list. Its implementer runs `bun test` in gate mode; the wrapper fails instead of running the local factory gate.

output.summary: Reviewed lease ownership, restart, release transitions, scheduling, and worktree cleanup. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` could not start because the checkout is missing the `entities` package; it reported 0 tests run and one module-resolution error.

findings.title: Targeted retries cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. A running targeted retry has a different purpose, so the resumed stage cancels its job and repeats earlier gate work instead of attaching to it. The same applies to the other retry purposes.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage progress to resume the recorded retry and accept its matching purpose.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts during a long `regression-retry-targeted` check. On resume, the handle fails the purpose allowlist, the executor stops the check, and the run starts gate work again.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release leaves the old executor running
findings.detail: Release changes are detected solely through a setting written by the new daemon. The previous release does not write that setting, so rolling back to it leaves the newer release SHA in the database. The newer executor continues renewing and running its jobs, while the older daemon cannot understand the new in-place handle or coordinate with that executor.
findings.suggestion: Detect the active daemon release using a durable source that the previous release already updates, and stop jobs when it changes.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy starts an in-place gate and then rolls back to the previous release. The previous daemon never updates `executor.daemonRelease`, so the newer executor does not detect the rollback and its gate can continue alongside recovery by the older daemon.

findings.title: A live PID is treated as a fresh executor heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability checks only process identity; the executor never records a heartbeat. If its process remains alive but stops making progress, new jobs are sent to it and cancellation waits indefinitely for `stopped` because `waitStopped` considers the owner alive. Lease expiry therefore cannot reliably lead to local fallback.
findings.suggestion: Record and check executor heartbeat freshness, and provide a bounded failure path when an owner cannot confirm process cleanup.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor becomes stuck while its process remains alive during a gate. The lease expires, but `waitStopped` keeps polling the live PID forever, so the run never falls back or completes.

findings.title: One executor serializes all jobs before slot scheduling
findings.detail: The polling loop awaits each entire gate before leasing the next job. Consequently one executor can use only one gate slot even when the configured capacity is larger, and a low-priority job waiting for a slot prevents later high-priority jobs from entering the slot queue. This defeats the requested per-job slot priority and can cause queued jobs to time out and fall back unnecessarily.
findings.suggestion: Allow independently managed leased jobs to enter the shared slot scheduler, while preserving one active job per worktree.
findings.failure_scenario: With two available gate slots, one long in-place suite runs and a second independent suite remains queued until pickup expiry instead of using the free slot.

output.summary: Reviewed the executor, lease, restart, release and fallback paths. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` could not start because the checkout is missing the `entities` package; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: A rollback to the previous release does not stop its successor's executor
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change solely through `executor.daemonRelease`. The previous release does not write that setting, so after rollback it retains the newer SHA. The newer executor continues renewing and running its jobs while the old daemon resumes without understanding the in-place handle. This can repeat a gate and allow both processes to operate in the same worktree.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator release identity that the previous-release rollback path invalidates, and ensure the old executor stops before the resumed daemon starts work in its worktree.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release executor is running a long gate when deployment rolls back to the base release. The old daemon never changes `executor.daemonRelease`, so the executor keeps running while the old daemon restarts the gate.

findings.title: Running targeted retries cannot reattach after a restart
findings.detail: Resume accepts only baseline, initial and rebase purposes. A surviving targeted or regression retry is therefore cancelled when the restarted stage calls `resumeGateExecution` for its initial gate, and the stage starts its checks again. The request explicitly includes targeted retries in the restart coverage.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage progress and inputs to resume the matching retry without replaying the initial gate.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts during a long `regression-retry-targeted` job. On resume, the initial-gate path treats that handle as a mismatch, cancels it and reruns the stage.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local fallback repositories
findings.detail: When `gates.executor` is `lan`, the factory always constructs the LAN executor, even if `[executor] enabled` is true. Its local fallback for repositories outside `workers.repos` runs directly in the daemon, so those local gates still die and restart with the daemon despite the enabled executor.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local fallback through the in-place executor when it is enabled, while keeping LAN jobs separate.
findings.failure_scenario: LAN gates are configured for one repository, an in-place executor is enabled, and a run for another repository starts a local gate. A daemon restart discards that gate instead of reattaching.

output.summary: Reviewed the identity provider, its callers, configuration validation, and merge observation. The focused test could not run because the checkout is missing the entities dependency: bun test test/github-app.test.ts reported “Cannot find package 'entities'”.

findings.title: Key validation accepts modes other than 0600 and does not establish readability
findings.detail: The startup check accepts any mode with owner-read and no group or world bits, including 0400 and 0700, despite the explicit requirement that the key have mode 0600. It also checks only metadata, so a file owned by another user can pass this check even when the daemon cannot read it; failure is deferred until a GitHub operation.
findings.suggestion: Require the specified mode and verify at startup that the configured key can be read by the daemon, with a clear error when it cannot.
findings.failure_scenario: A key file with mode 0700 passes startup even though the requested validation requires mode 0600. A mode-0600 file owned by another user can also pass stat validation but fail when the first App token is requested.

output.summary: Reviewed identity selection, configuration validation, GitHub calls, and approval handling. The targeted command `bun test test/github-app.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing the `entities` package; it exited before executing tests.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory remains readable by agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts an arbitrary absolute key path, but the read policy only adds the config directory to its protected paths. A key placed in a checkout or another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate, despite the requirement that the App key never reach either.
findings.suggestion: Include the resolved key path in the confinement deny policy and reject configurations where that protection cannot be enforced, including paths inside an allowed checkout or scratch directory.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator sets `private_key_path` to a mode-0600 PEM file inside the repository checkout. Startup accepts it, and a tool-enabled agent or gate reads the key from its allowed checkout.

findings.title: Startup does not verify that the key is readable by the daemon
findings.detail: The mode check verifies the file owner's read bit but neither verifies ownership nor attempts a read. A mode-0600 file owned by another user passes validation even when the daemon cannot read it; the daemon starts and only fails when a configured repository first needs a token.
findings.suggestion: Verify that the key is actually readable during configuration loading and report a clear startup error when it is not.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured PEM is a regular 0600 file owned by a different user. `statSync` succeeds, startup accepts it, and the first App-backed GitHub operation fails to sign its JWT.

findings.title: Manual landing still merges as the owner
findings.detail: The manual landing script invokes this helper to perform the merge, but its `gh` calls use `sh` directly and never configure or consult the new identity provider. An App-configured repository therefore still gets an owner-authored merge through this supported landing path, and an App token exchange failure cannot fail that operation closed.
findings.suggestion: Load the configured identity in the manual landing path and route its repository-scoped GitHub calls through the same provider.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator runs `scripts/land-pr.sh` for a repository listed in `[github.app].repos`; the helper executes `gh pr merge` using the owner's login instead of the App.

output.summary: Reviewed identity selection, GitHub callers, polling, approval handling, and configuration validation. findings.title: Reject unusable App keys during startup
findings.detail: Startup validates the key with `statSync`, which follows symlinks and does not verify ownership or actually open the file. The identity provider later refuses symlinks and files owned by another user. Consequently, configurations that startup accepts can leave every GitHub operation for an App repository failing only when first attempted. The request explicitly requires startup to refuse an invalid key. The same check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite the stated 0600 requirement.
findings.suggestion: Use a shared key validation routine at startup and signing time that checks the opened file's type, owner, permissions and readability, and rejects symlinks consistently.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure `private_key_path` as a symlink to a 0600 regular key. Configuration loads and the daemon starts, but the first App token exchange fails with `symlink refused`, preventing GitHub operations for the configured repository.

output.summary: Reviewed identity selection, GitHub call paths, configuration, and secret handling. The targeted test command could not run because dependencies including entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk are missing from the checkout.

findings.title: Invalid private keys can pass startup validation
findings.detail: Startup checks permission bits with statSync but does not check the file owner, rejects neither symlinks nor modes such as 0400, and does not open the file to establish readability. The identity provider performs some stricter checks only on the first GitHub operation, so the daemon can start successfully with a key it cannot use. This misses the explicit requirement to refuse an invalid key at startup.
findings.suggestion: Validate the opened key at startup using the same regular-file, ownership, mode and readability checks used by the identity provider, and require the specified 0600 mode.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured key path is a symlink to a 0600 key, or a 0600 file owned by another user. Configuration loads and startup succeeds; the first App operation then fails with a symlink or ownership error.

output.summary: Reviewed Claude stream parsing, worker fallback, coordinator routing, and release compatibility. The targeted test command could not run because dependencies including entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime are missing.

findings.title: Older workers do not report the new authentication classification
findings.detail: The coordinator relies exclusively on failureClass, but a worker running the previous release parses the same Claude rejection as an ordinary error and sends no failureClass. During a rolling deployment, or when resuming a completed job produced by an older worker, the new coordinator accepts that error as the round result and proceeds to gates and review. This preserves the failure the change is intended to prevent.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-compatible way to recognize or safely reject authentication failures from older worker reports, and test a previous-release worker result against the new coordinator.
findings.failure_scenario: A new coordinator receives a completed implement job from an older worker whose Claude login expired. The report has status error and no failureClass, so it is returned instead of running locally.

findings.title: A 401 after agent work is treated as a failure before the session ran
findings.detail: The classification applies to any error result with API status 401, regardless of whether earlier turns executed tools or edited files. On a worker, the coordinator adopts the worker's published changes and then runs the same round locally; on the coordinator it falls back to another candidate. A token expiring during a multi-turn session can therefore repeat work and side effects after the first agent already ran.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish authentication rejection before any model work from a failure after work has begun, and handle the latter without automatically replaying the round.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude completes a turn that edits files or invokes a tool, then its token expires and a later API request returns 401. The result is classified as authentication and the round is dispatched again.

output.summary: Traced authentication failures through Claude parsing, worker publication, and coordinator routing. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout has missing or incompatible dependencies: entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime are missing, and the installed Zod lacks z.json(). The added fixture triggers the protected-path warning but does not itself block the change.

findings.title: Authentication failure after a session starts can repeat completed work
findings.detail: The new classification treats every structured authentication failure as a failure to start a session. A Claude session can instead authenticate, make edits or perform other tool actions, and then receive a 401 on a later model request. The worker publishes its changes before returning the result, and this path adopts that commit before running the same round locally. The local implementer then repeats the task without being told what the worker already did. The coordinator path likewise falls back to another candidate with the first candidate's edits still present.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish authentication rejection before session work from a failure after the session has started, and preserve the existing interrupted-session handling for the latter.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker implementer edits a file or runs a side-effecting tool, then its OAuth token expires before the next Claude API request. Its changes are published and adopted, after which the coordinator starts the round locally and can repeat the work or side effect.

output.summary: Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, queue eligibility, persistence, and integration startup. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks the `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` dependency; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are disabled outside configured queue repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue has trusted accounts and only processes repositories in its queue list. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in other repositories receive none of the requested lifecycle labels or comments, even when the GitHub App covers them.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and apply it to linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: The issue queue is disabled, or a repository is absent from githubQueue.repos, and a user starts a run with `Closes #7`; no lifecycle label or comment is posted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current status, and a pending checkpoint is created only when polling observes that status. If a run enters needs_human or failed and is resolved before the next poll, the event and its reason disappear without a comment. The same snapshot approach can skip the corresponding label transition. A second needs_human episode also cannot produce a comment because the first episode permanently marks the shared effect done.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events and their publication-safe payloads when transitions occur, with distinct checkpoints for repeated episodes, then reconcile those durable events.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or reason comment.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy failure re-approval
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority-label event, even when that label is no longer on the issue. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so removing the later label does not revoke re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure label.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:1 from before failure. A trusted account applies priority:5 after failure and then removes it; the issue remains eligible using the stale priority:1 label.

output.summary: Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, queue eligibility, checkpoints, and integration wiring. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout is missing the entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk dependencies.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to repositories in the issue queue
findings.detail: The reconciler skips every repository outside githubQueue.repos and is only started when the queue is enabled. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in other configured repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover linked issues for all supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured repository has GitHub integration but is not listed in githubQueue.repos; a user starts a run with Closes #123, and no lifecycle label or comment is posted.

findings.title: Transitions completed between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: The reconciler creates needs_human, failed, and cancelled events only from the current status. No pending effect is recorded when the transition occurs, so a status that changes again before the next poll disappears from history. The label reconciliation likewise applies only the current desired label. This violates the required durable side effects across restarts.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events and their intended effects durably at the state transition, then reconcile the recorded events independently of current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next poll, or while the daemon is restarting. The needs-you label and reason comment are never posted.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority application in the timeline, even if that label was subsequently removed. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure, so the currently effective approval need not postdate the failure.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose latest application occurred after the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:5 from before failure. A trusted user briefly applies and removes priority:1 after failure. The queue considers the issue eligible using the removed priority:1 event and the old priority:5 label.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a CLI-linked issue to be picked again
findings.detail: Reconciliation logs a failed label write and continues to queue admission. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only finds runs with an issue sourceRef, while CLI and MCP runs may link an issue through their prompt. Thus neither the failed label nor the local latest-run reapproval check protects that issue during a write failure.
findings.suggestion: Include prompt-linked runs in the existing latest-run admission evidence, so a failed GitHub write cannot bypass re-approval.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #123 fails, and GitHub rejects the failed-label write. The same poll sees the issue's old priority label and starts a queue run without new approval.

output.summary: Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, queue admission, persistence, and publication handling. The targeted issue-queue test could not run because the local @modelcontextprotocol/sdk dependency is missing.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments always contain only a link to the UI. The request requires the reason to be included when it passes publication checks; the fixed UI message is the fallback when it does not.
findings.suggestion: Build the comment from the recorded reason, redact and check it, and use the fixed message only if publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe, actionable error such as a gate failure. The issue receives only “failed: see the UI,” so watchers cannot see the reason.

findings.title: A publication check failure permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When checking a comment throws, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed fallback. The same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check. It also prevents retry if loading the private-string configuration fails temporarily.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a checked fixed fallback when the text is blocked; leave transient checking failures pending for retry.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the run link or another comment field. The check rejects the body and the issue never receives either the intended comment or the required fallback.

findings.title: Polling current state loses intermediate lifecycle events
findings.detail: Events are created only from the status visible during reconciliation, and each event type has one permanent key per run. A needs-human state entered and exited between polls is never recorded; a later needs-human episode also cannot produce another comment after the first effect is done. No durable checkpoint is written at the state transition.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur and reconcile those records independently of the run's current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next issue-queue poll, or the daemon restarts during that interval. No needs-you update or reason comment is ever recorded.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler runs only when the issue queue is enabled and filters every linked issue to githubQueue.repos. The request covers manual, MCP, label, and comment starts as well as queue starts; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue pickup.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and apply it to linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts a run with “Closes #123” in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle labels or comments are posted even though the run is linked to the issue.

output.summary: Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, queue eligibility, persistence, and notifier integration. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; it reported 0 tests run and one module-resolution error.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle processing is gated on the repository being listed in githubQueue and on the queue having trusted accounts. The request requires updates for issue-linked runs from every start path, including manual, MCP, label, and comment triggers. Those runs can target repositories that are not enabled for issue queue admission, so they receive no lifecycle labels or polling comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for issue-linked runs independently of whether their repository is enabled for queue admission.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #123` in a configured repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos; the run starts and fails without adding either lifecycle label or posting the required comments.

findings.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies are fixed text and never include the run's reason. The request explicitly requires a comment with the reason for needs_human and failed runs, with redaction and private-string screening before publication.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after redaction and publication checks, falling back to fixed text when it cannot safely be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails because its gates failed; the issue receives only `failed: see ...` and readers cannot see the failure reason in the required comment.

findings.title: Blocked public text suppresses the comment instead of posting a fallback
findings.detail: When the private-string check rejects a comment body, the effect is marked done without posting anything. The same happens if a pending body fails its check during delivery. The request requires a fixed safe message in this case, so the event is permanently lost.
findings.suggestion: Prepare and validate a fixed fallback body and leave its effect pending for delivery when the original text is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL contains a private string, so checkBody rejects the started comment; the effect is recorded done and no comment is ever posted.

findings.title: Polling current status loses transitions between polls
findings.detail: Events are created only from the current run snapshot, and each event type has a single effect key. A needs_human state that is resolved before the next poll is never recorded; a later needs_human episode is also suppressed if an earlier episode was already recorded. The durable effect table therefore cannot deliver every required transition across polling or restarts.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when run transitions occur, with an identifier for each episode, and have polling deliver those records.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next issue queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or comment.

findings.title: A failed label write permits approval before the failure label
findings.detail: When the latest run failed but the failed label is not currently present, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority application after finishedAt. If lifecycle label delivery failed or is still pending, that approval can precede the required failure-label application, yet the issue can be picked immediately.
findings.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence of the failure-label application followed by a trusted priority application, including while the label write is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, its in-progress label is removed, and adding limitless:failed fails. A trusted user reapplies a priority label before the next successful lifecycle write; the queue accepts it and starts another run even though no approval followed the failure label.

output.summary: Traced audit and delivery paths, including worker publication and restart behavior. Focused tests could not start because the checkout is missing the entities dependency.

findings.title: In-flight old workers can publish an ungranted workflow after deployment
findings.detail: The publication guard runs in the worker, but a worker already executing an edit job from the previous release continues across a coordinator restart and retains its lease. The resumed coordinator accepts that job because resume reconciliation does not check the worker's release or require the new workflow guard. The old worker can then push its commit directly before the coordinator audits it. Release matching prevents new leases to old workers, but does not retire an already leased job.
findings.suggestion: Retire or refuse pre-upgrade publication jobs before they can push, and require evidence that a resumed publishing worker supports the workflow guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A build edit is leased to an old worker, the daemon deploys this release while the edit is running, and the edit adds .github/workflows/ci.yml without an allowance. The old worker pushes the branch after the restart, allowing the workflow to run before the new coordinator can block delivery.

output.summary: Reviewed audit, delivery, worker publication and verify-change paths. Focused tests could not run because the checkout is missing the entities package.

findings.title: An in-flight old worker can still push an ungranted workflow after deploy
findings.detail: The new publication guard runs inside the worker, but an agent job leased before the deploy can continue using the previous release, which has no such guard. The coordinator's resume check accepts the persisted job without requiring evidence that the worker supports workflow blocking. That worker pushes its commit before the coordinator adopts it or runs the new delivery checks, so those checks cannot prevent the push.
findings.suggestion: Retire or safely drain pre-upgrade publication jobs, or require a worker capability that guarantees the workflow check before permitting publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker on the previous release is editing a GitHub run when the daemon deploys and restarts. Its edit adds .github/workflows/ci.yml without an allowance; the old worker commits and pushes it while the new coordinator resumes the job.

output.summary: Reviewed the rejection checkpoint, rollback, scheduler recovery, and restart tests. The targeted test could not run because the checkout is missing the entities package.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents interrupted rollback from resuming
findings.detail: The rejection is saved with status needs_human before rollback starts. On daemon restart, the scheduler requeues only running and waiting_input runs, so it never invokes rollbackRejectedMerge for this terminal run. The new restart tests call executeRun directly, bypassing the scheduler and concealing this failure. A reset or clean failure has the same effect because the catch path returns needs_human without arranging another attempt.
findings.suggestion: Keep the run eligible for scheduler recovery until rollback is complete, while persisting the rejection before rollback, and test restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after the rejection checkpoint is saved but before git reset completes. The run remains needs_human with the merged checkout and pending rollback state; starting the scheduler does not finish the rollback.

output.summary: Reviewed the rejection checkpoint and scheduler restart path. The focused test could not run because the checkout is missing the `entities` package.

findings.title: Keep interrupted rollback eligible for scheduler recovery
findings.detail: The rejection checkpoint sets the run to `needs_human` before rollback starts. On daemon restart, `Scheduler.start()` only requeues interrupted `running` and `waiting_input` runs, so it never calls the new rollback recovery path for this terminal run. The new tests call `executeRun` directly after reopening the store and therefore bypass the scheduler behavior that determines whether production resumes it.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while keeping the run recoverable until rollback completes, or explicitly teach scheduler startup to recover terminal runs with unfinished rejection rollback. Exercise the restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon after the rejection checkpoint is saved but before `reset --hard`, or after reset but before cleanup and state save. The run remains `needs_human`, but its checkout and persisted merge state are never rolled back or cleared.

output.summary: Reviewed the polling, webhook, boundary and run-creation paths. The targeted issue-queue test could not run because the checkout lacks the @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js dependency.

findings.title: An empty first poll causes the first later command to be discarded
findings.detail: When the first successful poll has no open issues, there is no timestamp and no boundary is stored. The first later poll containing an issue establishes the boundary from that issue and skips all its comments. A valid command posted after enablement is therefore never run, even if it remains among the last 20 comments. This violates the requested first-successful-poll boundary and command delivery behavior.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues, and add a test covering a command posted after an empty initial poll.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue on a repository with no open issues, allow its first poll to succeed, then open an issue and post a trusted /limitless command before the next poll.

findings.title: Marker substring rejects valid owner requests
findings.detail: The factory-comment filter rejects any command containing `<!-- limitless-` anywhere in its body. A trusted, unedited command can legitimately ask about or quote one of these markers; it meets the specified command definition but is silently skipped on every poll. The shared webhook builder accepts the same request.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments without treating an arbitrary substring inside the request as proof of authorship.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless Fix handling of <!-- limitless-lifecycle:... -->` after the boundary.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue poll, webhook routing, comment transaction, and enable boundary. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not load because the checkout is missing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; no tests ran.

findings.title: An empty repository loses its first command
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues leaves the boundary unset. The next poll that sees an issue establishes the boundary from that issue and skips all its comments, even though they were created after the queue was enabled. The new test explicitly asserts this loss.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue polls an empty repository successfully. A trusted user then opens an issue and posts `/limitless fix it` before the next poll. That poll sets the boundary to the comment timestamp and the command never runs.

findings.title: The boundary can admit commands written before enablement
findings.detail: The newest timestamp among currently open issues can be much older than the first poll. A closed issue is absent from that response, so a pre-enable command on it can be newer than the stored boundary and will be treated as new when the issue is reopened. This violates the requirement that commands created before enablement never run.
findings.suggestion: Use a GitHub-derived enable timestamp that represents the first successful poll, including when the open-issue data is stale.
findings.failure_scenario: At enablement the only open issue was last updated in January. A trusted command was posted on a closed issue in February, before enablement in March. When that issue is reopened in April, its February comment is newer than the January boundary and starts a run.

findings.title: A marker substring silently discards valid user commands
findings.detail: The factory-authorship check rejects any comment containing `<!-- limitless-` anywhere in its body. A trusted user's unedited command can legitimately quote or request changes to such a marker; it meets the specified command conditions but is skipped on every poll.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments without rejecting arbitrary marker text inside a user's request.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless fix handling of <!-- limitless-lifecycle:... -->` after enablement. The poll skips it indefinitely and records no outcome.

output.summary: Reviewed the evidence checkpoint, classification, promotion and resume paths. The targeted classifier and persistence tests passed, but the pipeline and worker tests could not load because the environment lacked the `entities` package.

findings.title: Replay completed in-place jobs across a release change
findings.detail: Resume accepts an in-place handle only if the executor's `canResume` returns true. The production in-place executor requires the job request's `releaseSha` to equal the current daemon's release SHA even when the job is already done and has a stored result. A deploy changes that SHA, so resume cancels and clears the completed handle without replaying its result, then executes a new job. If the daemon stopped after the job stored a failure but before the observation checkpoint, that failure is lost.
findings.suggestion: Allow a completed in-place job's stored result to replay independently of the compatibility checks needed to resume a running job, and test a real engine restart with a changed release SHA.
findings.failure_scenario: An in-place gates job stores a failing result; the daemon is restarted for a deploy before the evidence insert; the new daemon has a different build SHA, rejects the stored handle, and a passing replacement execution leaves no observation of the failure.

output.summary: Reviewed the evidence, attribution, finalization, and restart paths. The targeted classifier and database tests passed. Integration and worker tests could not load because the checkout lacks the entities dependency.

findings.title: A replayed timeout is recorded as a retry instead of a stage rerun
findings.detail: The earlier-stage check takes precedence over the timeout-rerun evidence. Reattaching a durable execution creates a new stage row, so its existing observation appears to come from an earlier stage even though the same execution was replayed. If the timed-out check then passes on the stage's timeout rerun, its history is finalized as retry_passed instead of the required rerun_passed. The targeted command `bun -e 'import { observationHistory } from "./src/gates/failure-class.ts"; const c = { verdict: "pass", result: { ok: true, firstAttempt: { timedOut: true } } }; console.log(observationHistory(c, true));'` outputs `retry_passed`.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a replayed execution from a genuinely new execution and prioritize explicit timeout-rerun evidence when deriving its history.
findings.failure_scenario: A durable LAN or in-place execution times out, its observation is inserted, and the daemon restarts before the handle is cleared. The resumed stage reattaches that result and its timeout rerun passes.

findings.title: Inspection failure skips executor installation rollback
findings.detail: If launchctl inspection fails after reconcileExecutor has enabled the replacement executor, this catch immediately rethrows instead of restoring the old plist and disabling the replacement. The new plist remains enabled, so launchd can load it on a subsequent login even though installation failed. This violates the requirement that a failed replacement restore the old plist and leave the executor unloaded and disabled.
findings.suggestion: Attempt the journaled executor restoration on inspection errors as well, using the recovery command path; if shutdown cannot be confirmed, retain the journal and report the recovery commands.
findings.failure_scenario: During executor replacement, launchctl enable succeeds but the following launchctl print times out or returns an unrecognized error. Service install exits with the replacement plist still present and enabled.

output.summary: Reviewed executor installation, deploy, rollback, recovery, and release following. Targeted tests could not run: the checkout’s dependencies lack the expected Zod API and the entities package.

findings.title: Inspection failure bypasses executor replacement restoration
findings.detail: A ServiceInspectionError is rethrown after the old plist has been removed and the replacement written. The install journal remains in the replacing phase, but the failed install does not restore the old plist or confirm that the replacement is disabled. For a fresh install, enable can also have succeeded before inspection fails, leaving the new plist enabled for a later login. This violates the requirement that a failed executor replacement restore the old plist and leave the executor unloaded and disabled.
findings.suggestion: Route inspection failures through executor restoration and shutdown using the recovery command path, preserving the journal and reporting any unconfirmed shutdown.
findings.failure_scenario: During executor installation, launchctl enable succeeds but the subsequent launchctl print times out or returns an unexpected error. Installation exits immediately with the new plist still present and the label enabled; on replacement, the old plist has not been restored.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue, configuration and store changes. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` is missing from the checkout.

findings.title: Lowercased queue requests can create a duplicate repository registration
findings.detail: The queue now passes a lowercased repository slug to run creation. Repository resolution uses case-sensitive `getRepoBySlug` lookups, so an existing registration with uppercase characters is not found. Resolution instead calls GitHub and creates a second registration with default settings. Queue runs can consequently use a different merge policy and repository identity from existing runs; if GitHub resolution fails, admission fails altogether.
findings.suggestion: Use canonical keys for queue comparisons while resolving run requests to the existing case-insensitive repository registration, preserving its stored settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository is already registered as `Owner/Repo`, and the queue is configured for that repository. An approved issue produces a request for `owner/repo`; `resolveRepo` misses the existing row and creates a separate repository row.

findings.title: Every poll performs an ownership query for every historical run
findings.detail: Seeding observations loads all runs across all repositories, then `decision` calls `linkedIssues`, which executes a recursive ownership query for each run. This adds synchronous database work proportional to the entire run history on every queue poll, including runs unrelated to configured repositories, and grows as history accumulates. It risks reintroducing daemon stalls in the path this issue follows up on.
findings.suggestion: Seed the needed observations with a batched ownership lookup or limit the seed to relevant runs without issuing a query per historical run.
findings.failure_scenario: A long-lived installation with thousands of historical runs polls one configured repository: each poll synchronously loads all those runs and executes thousands of recursive queries before contacting GitHub.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue, configuration, and repository-resolution paths. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; Bun reported 0 passing tests and one module-resolution error.

findings.title: Preserve the registered repository when canonicalizing queue keys
findings.detail: Lowercasing the configured repository also changes the repository passed to run creation. Repository registration and resolveRepo use case-sensitive slug lookups, so an existing registration such as `Owner/Repo` is not found when the queue requests `owner/repo`. The queue then performs a new GitHub repository lookup and creates a second registration, instead of using the existing repository and its persisted identity. If that lookup fails, queue admission fails even though the repository was already registered.
findings.suggestion: Deduplicate using lowercase comparison keys while preserving a usable configured or registered slug for run creation, or make repository resolution reuse an existing case-insensitive GitHub registration.
findings.failure_scenario: A deployment has `Owner/Repo` in github.queue.repos and an existing `Owner/Repo` registration. After upgrade, an approved issue is submitted as `owner/repo`; resolveRepo misses the existing row and either creates a duplicate repository row or fails its extra remote lookup.

findings.title: Avoid an ownership query for every historical run on every poll
findings.detail: Seeding observations loads every run and calls linkedIssues for each one. That function executes a recursive ownership query even for ordinary runs, so each queue poll now issues one database query per historical run and parses every historical prompt. The work grows with the entire database even when only one repository or a few issues are queued, reintroducing synchronous daemon stalls as history grows.
findings.suggestion: Seed the relevant observations with a batched ownership lookup or restrict the seed to runs that can affect configured repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: An installation with a large accumulated run history and one configured queue repository performs thousands of synchronous SQLite queries and scans all historical prompts at the start of every poll.

findings.title: Classify the observed tip before marking a replayed release lost
findings.detail: Every `moved` result is treated as a superseding claim, but the claim client also returns `moved` when the newly observed tip contains a malformed record or a non-superseding record. In those cases recovery clears the release intent and marks confirmed ownership lost, even though the requested recovery table requires malformed records to remain pending and only qualifying generations or holders to supersede ownership. The final status and checkpoint can consequently be discarded.
findings.suggestion: Classify `result.tip` using the same record and generation checks as the initial recovery read; preserve the intent and return `pending` when the tip is malformed or does not establish supersession.
findings.failure_scenario: Recovery reads the confirmed tip and starts replaying a release. Before its compare-and-swap, the ref moves to a commit with a malformed claim record. The client returns `moved`, and recovery clears the journal and marks the lease lost instead of keeping the release pending.

output.summary: Reviewed lease storage, recovery, and the claim client. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout has no local node_modules and the resolved Zod lacks prefault.

findings.title: Classify the new tip before settling a moved replay
findings.detail: Every moved result from a replay marks confirmed ownership lost and clears the intent, without inspecting the returned tip. ClaimClient can return moved with a malformed record or with a valid record that does not meet the supersession conditions. The requested recovery table requires malformed tips to retain the intent for retry, and only identifies specified generation or holder changes as superseding ownership. Clearing the journal can permanently lose the final release and checkpoint pointer.
findings.suggestion: Classify result.tip using the same rules as the initial read; retain the intent when the new tip is malformed or cannot establish supersession.
findings.failure_scenario: Recovery reads the confirmed tip and starts replaying a release. Before updateRefs, another writer moves the ref to a commit with a malformed claim record. The compare-and-swap fails, ClaimClient returns moved with that malformed tip, and recovery clears the release intent and marks the confirmed lease lost instead of leaving it pending.

output.summary: Reviewed land and post-merge observation, classification, and restart paths. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout lacks the entities dependency.

findings.title: Recover slow-regression observations from the earlier stage
findings.detail: The lookup requires the observation's stage_id to equal the current stage ID. A resumed gates stage gets a new stage ID, while reattaching to the completed primary execution attempts to insert the same observation and leaves the original row in place. The selector therefore cannot mark that row as slow, so a passing re-check is classified flaky instead of load.
findings.suggestion: Identify the primary observation by its durable execution identity across resumed stages, rather than filtering it by the newly created stage ID.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after recording a failed, slow post-merge primary execution but before the slow-regression selector runs. On resume, the same execution is reattached and its re-check passes; the observation retains slow_regression=0 and is finalized as flaky.

findings.title: Preserve the failed re-check in confirmation history
findings.detail: When coordinator confirmation exists, observationHistory returns only the confirmation outcome. A prior failed slow-regression re-check is discarded from the observation's history, so downstream consumers cannot distinguish the requested combined history from a failure confirmed directly on the coordinator.
findings.suggestion: Persist both retry and confirmation outcomes in the observation evidence and classify using the combined history.
findings.failure_scenario: A slow worker regression fails its re-check and then passes coordinator confirmation. The stored row contains slow_regression=1 and confirmed_passed, but no retry_failed evidence.

output.summary: Reviewed the land and post-merge observation paths.
