findings.suggestion: Keep the key in a location excluded from agent and gate reads, and reject configured paths that are exposed to those processes.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator configures an absolute private_key_path pointing to a 0600 PEM file in a repository checkout. A tool-enabled agent or gate command reads the PEM directly.

findings.title: Key validation does not establish ownership or readability
findings.detail: The startup check only inspects the file type and permission bits. A 0600 file owned by another user, or a file denied by an ACL, passes validation even though the daemon cannot read it. Startup succeeds and configured GitHub operations fail later, contrary to the explicit startup validation requirement. The same mask also accepts modes such as 0700 despite the requested 0600 mode.
findings.suggestion: Validate the effective owner and readability at startup, and enforce the intended allowed modes.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured path names a regular 0600 file owned by another user that the daemon can stat but cannot read. The daemon starts, then every App-scoped operation fails when signing.

output.summary: Reviewed the identity provider, configuration, GitHub callers, polling, approval handling, and documentation. Targeted tests could not run because dependencies including entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk were unavailable in the checkout.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents and gates
findings.detail: The configuration accepts an absolute key path anywhere, but the confinement read policy denies the config directory and known credential paths, not the configured private key. A key placed in a repository checkout remains readable by the agent and gate commands running there, despite the requirement that neither receives the key.
findings.suggestion: Include the resolved key path in every relevant confinement read-deny policy, or reject paths that cannot be protected from agents and gates.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator configures an owner-only key file inside a repository checkout using its absolute path. A tool-enabled agent or a gate reads that file and obtains the App private key.

findings.title: Key validation does not verify ownership or actual readability
findings.detail: The startup check inspects permission bits but does not check the file owner or attempt to open the file. A regular file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes validation even though the daemon cannot read it; startup succeeds and the first App operation fails later. The check also accepts owner-executable modes such as 0700 despite the requested mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Validate ownership and actual readability at startup, and enforce the requested permission mode.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key is a mode-0600 file owned by another account in a searchable directory. Configuration loads successfully, but every GitHub call for an App repository fails when it tries to read the key.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed identity, configuration, GitHub call, polling, approval and documentation paths. Targeted tests could not run because checkout dependencies were missing: `entities` and `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`.

findings.title: Validate the key using the same rules at startup and signing
findings.detail: Configuration loading follows symlinks and checks only the target's mode bits. The signing path later rejects symlinks and files owned by another user. Consequently, startup can accept an App configuration that cannot authenticate any listed repository, contrary to the requirement to refuse an invalid key at startup. The mode check also accepts owner-executable modes such as 0700 although the request specifies 0600.
findings.suggestion: Apply the signing path's no-follow, ownership, regular-file and readability checks during configuration loading, and enforce the requested mode consistently.
findings.failure_scenario: Set `private_key_path` to a symlink to a mode-0600 key. The daemon starts successfully, but the first GitHub operation for a listed repository fails with `symlink refused`; subsequent operations continue to fail until configuration is corrected and the daemon restarted.

output.summary: Reviewed the identity provider, its GitHub call paths, configuration, doctor, polling, and merge handling. The targeted test command could not run because checkout dependencies were missing: Bun reported that it could not find 'entities' and '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js'.

findings.title: Validate the actual key access requirements at startup
findings.detail: Startup checks permission bits through statSync, which follows symlinks, but does not check file ownership or open the file. It also accepts modes such as 0700. The signing path later refuses symlinks and wrong ownership, so a configuration can pass startup and then fail every App-authenticated GitHub operation. This misses the explicit requirement to refuse an invalid key at startup.
findings.suggestion: Use a shared key validation routine at startup and signing time that checks the opened file's ownership, type, readability, and permitted mode, including the intended symlink policy.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key path is a symlink to an owner-readable 0600 regular file. The daemon starts successfully, but the first GitHub operation fails with 'symlink refused' instead of rejecting the configuration at startup.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed harness, routing, worker protocol, and LAN execution paths. The targeted test command could not run because the checkout resolved missing or incompatible dependencies: entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime were missing, and the resolved Zod lacked z.json().

findings.title: New worker reports are rejected by the previous coordinator
findings.detail: The previous release validates agent reports with a strict object schema. A new worker includes failureClass in an authentication-failure report, so an older coordinator rejects the result instead of recording it. The worker then reports a failed job, causing worker retry or failure handling rather than the requested local fallback. This can occur during a rolling deployment or after coordinator rollback.
findings.suggestion: Negotiate the report capability or use a representation accepted by the previous coordinator, and test a new worker against the previous report schema.
findings.failure_scenario: A newly deployed worker encounters an expired Claude token while its coordinator is still on the previous release; its result contains failureClass and the coordinator's strict schema rejects it.

findings.title: Old workers still turn authentication failures into completed rounds
findings.detail: The fallback depends exclusively on failureClass, which workers running the previous release never send. Their Claude harness returns the original task-level error, so a new coordinator accepts it and proceeds to commit and gates. Deploying the coordinator before its workers therefore leaves the reported failure mode active during version skew.
findings.suggestion: Add a version or capability check that routes jobs locally when a worker cannot classify authentication failures, and cover an old-worker report in a compatibility test.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator is upgraded while a LAN worker remains on the previous release and has an expired Claude token; the worker returns status error without failureClass, and the coordinator counts the unchanged implementation round.

findings.title: Authentication after partial work adopts the worker commit before rerunning
findings.detail: The parser classifies any final structured 401 as authentication failure, including one after earlier successful model turns. The worker publishes its changes before reporting the result, and this path adopts that commit before checking failureClass and starting the local session. The local implementer can repeat work or act on a partial implementation, even though the fallback treats the worker session as if it never ran.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a rejection before any successful session work from a later authentication failure, and preserve or explicitly handle partial work before deciding to rerun.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker edits files during a session, then its token expires on a later API request. It publishes the partial changes, the coordinator adopts them, and a local implementer receives the original round prompt and runs again on those changes.

output.summary: Reviewed the parser, routing, worker fallback, protocol, and changed tests. Targeted tests could not load because this checkout has missing or mismatched dependencies, including entities, sandbox-runtime, and Zod.

findings.title: Older workers still turn authentication failures into completed rounds
findings.detail: The coordinator recognizes a worker authentication failure only through the new optional failureClass field. A worker running the previous release does not populate that field: it reports the same Claude rejection as a task-level error, which this condition returns as the round result. The engine then commits or records no changes and proceeds to gates, verification, and review. This preserves the original failure during a rolling upgrade or after a coordinator upgrade before workers are updated.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-compatible way to identify the structured authentication failure from older worker reports, or prevent incompatible workers from receiving these jobs until they support the classification.
findings.failure_scenario: A new coordinator dispatches an implement job to a previous-release worker whose Claude OAuth token has expired. The worker returns status error without failureClass; the coordinator accepts it as the implementation result and consumes the round on unchanged code.

output.summary: Reviewed the lifecycle reconciliation, queue eligibility, persistence, notifier, and report changes. The targeted issue-queue test could not run because the checkout is missing @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js.

findings.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments solely from the current run status. If a run enters needs_human and is resolved before the next poll, no event or pending checkpoint is created, so the comment is permanently lost. The same loss occurs if an earlier comment write fails and breaks the loop before the current status's comment is checkpointed.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe payload durably at the state transition, then reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human, the owner resolves it before the next queue poll, and the issue never receives the required needs-you comment.

findings.title: Allow separate needs-human episodes to produce separate updates
findings.detail: The comment checkpoint is keyed only by run and event name and remains done for the lifetime of the run. A run that resumes from needs_human and later needs the owner again updates its label but never posts the new reason. This also loses the second notification across a restart.
findings.suggestion: Give each lifecycle transition or status episode its own durable effect identity.
findings.failure_scenario: A run asks for owner input, resumes after resolution, and later enters needs_human for a different reason; only the first reason is posted.

findings.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside configured queue repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle updates are restricted to repositories in githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. The request requires updates for every start path, including CLI, MCP, label, and comment triggers; those runs can target a repository without enabling automatic issue selection there.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and apply it to issue-linked runs in eligible repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a CLI run with Closes #7 in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; the run receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

findings.title: Preserve a failed run's pending label transition when a newer run exists
findings.detail: Only the latest linked run is allowed to reconcile labels. If the failed-label write fails and a newer run is created before the next poll, the older run's failed label is never retried. This drops a recorded lifecycle side effect and can erase the GitHub evidence that a failure requires re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Durably record transitions and complete or explicitly reconcile pending effects in order before transferring label ownership to a newer run.
findings.failure_scenario: A manual issue-linked run fails, the failed-label API call fails, and another run for the issue starts before the next poll; the failed label is never applied.

output.summary: Reviewed the lifecycle reconciliation, queue eligibility, persistence, notifier, and PR report changes. The focused test command could not start because dependencies including entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk were missing from the checkout.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue is configured with trusted accounts and only processes repositories listed in that queue. The request requires lifecycle updates for issue-linked runs from every start path, including repositories where the issue queue is not enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover every repository with an issue-linked run.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a CLI or webhook run for an issue in a configured repository that is absent from githubQueue.repos. The issue receives no lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human, failed, and cancelled events only from the current run status. It records a pending effect only after observing that status, so a transition that begins and ends between polls is never recorded or retried. The single comment key also suppresses a later needs-human episode after the first one was posted.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events when transitions occur, with an identity for each occurrence, and reconcile those durable events independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next poll. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever published; a subsequent needs-human episode can likewise be suppressed by the first episode's completed checkpoint.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a CLI-linked issue to be picked again
findings.detail: A failed lifecycle write is caught and queue admission continues. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only finds issue source references, so it does not protect runs linked through a CLI or MCP prompt containing Closes #n. Until the failed label is successfully written, neither the label rule nor the latest-run rule prevents re-picking that issue.
findings.suggestion: Apply the existing re-approval admission check to the latest linked run from every supported start path, independently of whether the GitHub label write succeeded.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for an approved issue fails, and GitHub rejects or times out the failed-label write. In the same poll, the issue retains its old priority label and can be queued again without a new approval.

findings.title: Any issue comment can impersonate a completed lifecycle write
findings.detail: Recovery accepts the marker in any comment body without checking its author. Issue comments are untrusted input, and the marker format and run ID are observable. A matching comment causes the pending effect to be marked done even if the factory never posted its own comment.
findings.suggestion: Verify that a matching marker belongs to the factory's authenticated identity before treating the effect as complete.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails or the daemon restarts with the effect pending. Another issue participant posts the predictable marker before the next poll; reconciliation marks the effect done and never posts the required factory comment.

output.summary: Reviewed the lifecycle reconciler, queue admission, persistence, reporting, and notifier changes. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the local dependency `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` is missing; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs for repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, despite the request covering every start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle polling for issue-linked runs independently of queue admission configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with `Closes #7` in a configured repository that is not in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or lifecycle comment is posted.

findings.title: Needs-human and failure comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both events always use fixed text and never include the run's reason. The requested fallback applies when publication checks block the reason, but this implementation discards it even when it is safe to publish.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize and check the reason before including it, using fixed fallback text when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a safe error such as `tests failed`; the issue comment only says to see the UI and does not explain the failure.

findings.title: A blocked comment is recorded as delivered instead of posting the fallback
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment body, the effect is marked done and no comment is posted. The request explicitly requires a fixed message when publication is blocked. The same suppression occurs if the body becomes blocked before delivery.
findings.suggestion: Construct and validate a fixed fallback message and record the effect as pending for delivery.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or run ID matches a private string; the start or failure comment is permanently suppressed rather than replaced with a safe message.

findings.title: Polling snapshots lose transitions and repeated needs-human events
findings.detail: Comments are created only from the current run status and keyed once per status for the lifetime of the run. A needs-human state resolved between polls is never recorded, and a later needs-human episode is suppressed by the first episode's completed effect. There is no durable checkpoint at the state transition itself.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each episode, and let the poller deliver them.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and is resumed before the next poll, or enters needs_human a second time after being resumed; the corresponding issue comment is never posted.

findings.title: Failed label write can leave an issue eligible for immediate re-pick
findings.detail: The reconciler removes in-progress before adding failed, then proceeds to queue admission even if adding failed fails. The admission lookup only considers issue-sourced runs, so a failed CLI or MCP run linked by `Closes #n` supplies no latest-run guard. The issue can be picked using its existing priority approval before the failure label is ever applied.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission blocked until the failure label is durably applied, including for all issue-linked start paths, while retaining a single admission check.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run linked to an approved issue fails; GitHub accepts removal of in-progress but rejects adding failed. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

output.summary: Reviewed the lifecycle reconciler, queue admission, persistence, notifier, and report changes. The focused command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the checkout is missing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs for repositories listed in `githubQueue.repos` with trusted accounts configured. The request covers issue-linked runs from every start path, including CLI, MCP, labels, and comments; those runs receive no lifecycle labels or comments when their repository is not in the issue queue.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of issue-queue admission and include issue-linked runs in all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository uses `limitless run` with `Closes #42` but does not enable the issue queue. The run starts and fails without either lifecycle label or comment.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments contain only fixed text and a UI link. The requested lifecycle updates explicitly require a comment with the reason; this implementation never reads `run.error` or another reason for either event.
findings.suggestion: Include the sanitized and checked reason in these comments, with the specified fixed fallback when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human because a gate failed. The issue says only “needs you: see …”, so its watchers cannot see why intervention is needed.

findings.title: Blocked comment text is marked complete without posting the fallback
findings.detail: When the publication check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done and no comment is sent. The same happens if a pending body is rejected on retry. The request requires a fixed message without the blocked text, not suppression of the lifecycle update.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a checked fixed fallback body when the original body cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string occurs in the UI URL or run ID. The publication check rejects the start or failure comment and the checkpoint permanently prevents any replacement comment.

findings.title: Polling snapshots can lose lifecycle transitions
findings.detail: Events are created only from the run's current status at observation time. A needs_human state that is resolved or resumed before the next poll, including while the daemon is stopped for a deploy, leaves no durable comment checkpoint and is never reported. The effect key also allows only one needs_human comment per run, so subsequent needs-human episodes are suppressed.
findings.suggestion: Record each relevant transition durably when state changes and reconcile those recorded events by episode.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human, the daemon restarts, and the owner resumes it before the lifecycle poll observes that status. No needs-you comment is ever posted; a later needs-human episode can likewise be lost after the first one was recorded.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a manually started issue to be picked again
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, queue admission still proceeds in the same poll. The local latest-run check only finds issue source references, so a CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` does not protect the issue during this gap.
findings.suggestion: Keep the issue ineligible until the failed label is durably applied, and make the existing claim and latest-run checks cover all supported issue links.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #42` fails. Deleting in-progress succeeds, adding failed gets a transient GitHub error, and the queue observes the still-approved issue with neither status label and starts another run without re-approval.

output.summary: Reviewed the audit, delivery paths, worker publication, and compatibility with the base release. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout is missing the entities dependency.

findings.title: Older workers can push ungranted workflow changes
findings.detail: The coordinator still delegates publication to workers without requiring a worker version that implements the new workflow check. A worker running the previous release ignores the new allowance field and pushes its commit before reporting it to the coordinator. The coordinator's later audit or delivery check cannot undo a workflow triggered by that push.
findings.suggestion: Require a worker capability or protocol version that guarantees the workflow publication check before delegating a publishing job, and refuse or route jobs elsewhere when the worker lacks it.
findings.failure_scenario: After the coordinator is upgraded while a remote worker remains on the previous release, an ungranted build job assigned to that worker adds .github/workflows/ci.yml. The old worker pushes the commit directly, allowing the workflow to run before the coordinator can audit it.

output.summary: Reviewed the audit, delivery, worker publication, and verify-change paths. Focused tests could not start because the checkout is missing the entities dependency. An in-flight worker can bypass the new publication guard during a coordinator upgrade.

findings.title: In-flight old workers can push ungranted workflows after an upgrade
findings.detail: The new publication check exists only in the worker executable. A coordinator deploy reattaches to existing implement jobs, so a job already running on the previous release continues executing the old publication code and can push its commit before the upgraded coordinator audits it. Release-SHA matching prevents new leases to outdated workers but does not stop an already leased job.
findings.suggestion: Prevent pre-upgrade publishing jobs from continuing across this security change, or require a coordinator-authorized publication protocol that old workers cannot satisfy before they obtain push credentials.
findings.failure_scenario: An implement job is running on a worker when the coordinator deploys this release. The old worker adds .github/workflows/ci.yml to an ungranted run and pushes the candidate branch after the restart; the workflow can execute before the coordinator receives and audits the result.

output.summary: The rejection is persisted before rollback, but the scheduler cannot resume the rollback after a restart because the run is already terminal. The targeted command `bun test test/pipeline-delivery-restart.test.ts` could not run: Bun reported `Cannot find package 'entities'` before executing any tests.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents interrupted rollback from resuming
findings.detail: The rejection checkpoint writes `needs_human` before rollback begins. On daemon restart, `Scheduler.start()` only requeues runs in `running` or `waiting_input`, so it never calls the new rollback resume path for this run. A shutdown or Git error during rollback has the same result: the catch returns `needs_human` without arranging another attempt. The new tests call `executeRun` directly after reopening the store, bypassing scheduler recovery and therefore missing this failure.
findings.suggestion: Keep the run recoverable until rollback completes, or explicitly have scheduler startup recover terminal runs with an unfinished rejection checkpoint. Test the restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon after the rejection is saved but before `reset --hard` completes. The run remains `needs_human`, but its checkout and recorded head still point to the rejected merge and rollback never runs.

output.summary: Reviewed the delivery state transitions, scheduler recovery, and restart tests. The targeted command `bun test test/pipeline-delivery-restart.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing the `entities` package. The restart tests call the engine directly and do not exercise scheduler recovery.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents the scheduler from resuming rollback
findings.detail: The rejection checkpoint sets the run to `needs_human` before rollback starts. On daemon restart, Scheduler.start only requeues runs in `running` or `waiting_input`, so it never calls the new rollback recovery path for this terminal run. The new tests bypass the scheduler by calling executeRun directly, masking this failure.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while the run remains recoverable, and set the terminal status after rollback; alternatively, explicitly recover terminal runs with an unfinished rejection checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon after the rejection is saved but before reset or clean completes. The run remains needs_human with the merged checkout or partially cleaned state, and its running stage is not recovered.

findings.title: A failed rejection save is treated as a durable terminal outcome
findings.detail: The rejection is assigned to in-memory state before updateRun persists it. If that write throws, this catch branch sees the in-memory rejection and returns needs_human without updating the database or requeueing the run. The scheduler considers execution finished while the stored run can remain running with no rejection checkpoint.
findings.suggestion: Only take the rejection-specific interruption path after confirming the checkpoint was persisted, and propagate or handle persistence failures so the scheduler records a recoverable outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: SQLite rejects the rejection checkpoint write, for example because of a transient storage error. executeRun returns needs_human, but the persisted run remains running and has no durable rejection; a later restart can repeat the merge and gates.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue poll, webhook routing, persistence, migration, and tests. The targeted issue-queue test could not run because the checkout lacks the @modelcontextprotocol/sdk dependency.

findings.title: An empty first poll causes the first later command to be discarded
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues leaves the enable boundary unset. The next poll containing an issue establishes the boundary from that issue and skips all its comments, including commands created after the original successful poll. The added test explicitly accepts this behavior, but the request requires the first successful poll to establish the boundary and later commands to run.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary even when there are no open issues, and test a command posted after an empty successful poll.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue on an empty repository, let its first poll succeed, then create an issue and post a trusted /limitless command before the next poll. That command never starts a run.

findings.title: Marker substring suppresses otherwise valid commands
findings.detail: The factory-origin check rejects any comment containing `<!-- limitless-` anywhere in its body. A trusted user's unedited request can legitimately contain that text, yet it is silently skipped on every poll. The request defines a command by its prefix, author, edit state and boundary; it does not exclude requests containing this substring.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments without rejecting arbitrary content in a trusted user's request.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless Fix rendering of <!-- limitless-status -->` after the boundary. The command is never processed or recorded.

findings.title: Rollback permits a webhook command to run again after re-upgrade
findings.detail: The processed-comment record exists only when the new release handles a command. After a rollback, the previous release handles queue comment webhooks directly without writing this table. On re-upgrade the existing boundary remains, so the poll sees the same post-boundary comment as unprocessed and can start another run after the first claim has finished.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible way to identify commands handled by the previous release before replaying post-boundary comments.
findings.failure_scenario: Establish the boundary, roll back, receive an owner comment webhook and complete its run, then upgrade again while the comment remains among the last 20. The queue starts a second run for that comment.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue, webhook, persistence, migration, documentation, and tests against the requested invariants. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; it failed during module loading, before executing tests.

findings.title: The enable boundary can precede commands already present on closed issues
findings.detail: The boundary is the newest timestamp among open issues, which can be much older than the first poll. A command already present on a closed issue is absent from that response. If that issue is later reopened, the old command can be newer than the stored boundary and will start a run, even though it predates enablement.
findings.suggestion: Establish the boundary using GitHub-time evidence that covers the enablement instant and includes commands on issues that may later reopen.
findings.failure_scenario: The newest open issue was updated Monday; a trusted user commented on a closed issue Tuesday; the queue is enabled Wednesday; that issue reopens Thursday. Tuesday's command passes the Monday boundary and runs.

findings.title: An empty first poll causes later commands to be discarded
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues stores no boundary. The first later poll containing an issue instead establishes the boundary from that response and skips all its commands. The added test explicitly expects this behavior, but it loses commands posted after the first successful poll.
findings.suggestion: Persist a GitHub-time enable boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue starts with no open issues. A user subsequently opens an issue and posts a command before the next poll. That poll treats the new command as part of initialization, and it never runs.

findings.title: A marker anywhere in a trusted request silently suppresses the command
findings.detail: The command predicate excludes any body containing `<!-- limitless-`, even when a trusted human authored the comment. The request defines commands by their prefix, author, edit status, and boundary; it does not exclude request text containing this substring. A legitimate request to change or investigate such a marker is silently skipped forever.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments from reliable author identity rather than excluding arbitrary request content.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless Fix parsing of <!-- limitless-example -->` after enablement. The poll never creates or records a run for it.

output.summary: Reviewed the evidence checkpoint, replay, attribution, classification, promotion and terminal paths. The focused classifier and persistence tests passed, but the pipeline and worker tests could not run because the checkout lacks the entities package.

findings.title: In-place observations ignore the injected load source
findings.detail: For an in-place handle, the observation reads load_per_core from the job. The separate in-place executor constructs its own WorkerStore with the default host load source, so EngineDeps.loadSource is never used for these executions. This violates the requested injectable load capture and makes in-place evidence inconsistent with local and LAN-fallback evidence.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for in-place completion to capture the configured load source, including across replay, and exercise the real in-place executor path with an injected value.
findings.failure_scenario: An engine is configured with loadSource returning 3.25 and an in-place gate fails. Its observation contains the executor process's host load instead of 3.25.

output.summary: Reviewed execution, replay, classification, persistence, attribution, and terminal handling. Targeted classifier and store tests passed, including the migration check. The pipeline and worker tests could not run because the local checkout is missing the entities package.

findings.title: Injected load source does not reach the in-place executor
findings.detail: In-place observations read the load stored by the separate in-place executor's WorkerStore. That executor constructs its own WorkerStore with the default hostLoadPerCore source, so EngineDeps.loadSource is never used for actual in-place jobs. The integration test supplies the source to its fake WorkerStore, which masks this difference.
findings.suggestion: Arrange for in-place completions to capture the injected coordinator load source while retaining the captured value across replay, and exercise the actual in-place execution path.
findings.failure_scenario: An engine configured with loadSource returning 8 runs a failed gate through the real in-place executor. Its observation contains the host's measured load instead of 8.

findings.title: Redacted names can collapse distinct failed checks into one observation
findings.detail: The unique key uses the normalized name, and insertion ignores conflicts. Two distinct check names that normalize to the same value therefore share a key and the second failure is silently discarded. Terminal formatting or registered credentials in names can produce such a collision.
findings.suggestion: Preserve a privacy-safe identity that distinguishes distinct original names, and use it when enforcing execution identity.
findings.failure_scenario: Two failed checks have names that differ only by ANSI formatting; redaction normalizes them to the same name, and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING drops the second row.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed service, deploy, executor, documentation, and test paths. Targeted tests could not start because the installed dependencies are incomplete or mismatched: Zod lacks prefault, and the entities package is missing.

findings.title: Restore the previous executor plist when inspection fails during replacement
findings.detail: A ServiceInspectionError bypasses the replacement catch block's restoration. At this point the old plist has already been removed and the replacement written; reconcileExecutor may also have enabled the replacement before its print call fails. The install exits with the old plist unrestored and the replacement potentially enabled, contrary to the requirement that a failed executor replacement restore the old plist unloaded and disabled. A later recovery may repair it, but it does not satisfy the failed install's required outcome and launchd can load the enabled replacement in the meantime.
findings.suggestion: Attempt the executor journal's fail-closed restoration for inspection failures as well, retaining the journal and reporting recovery commands if shutdown cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing executor is being replaced. Launchctl enable succeeds, then launchctl print returns an unknown result such as a timeout. ServiceInspectionError escapes immediately after the old plist has been replaced, without restoring it or disabling the newly enabled label.

output.summary: Reviewed the executor lifecycle, deploy rollback, installation recovery, release following, and changed tests. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout’s dependencies are incomplete or incompatible: zod lacks prefault and entities is missing.

findings.title: Treat a timed-out disable as an unconfirmed shutdown
findings.detail: shutdownExecutor checks only the disable command’s exit code. The subprocess wrapper can report timedOut: true with exitCode: 0, so this path can declare shutdown confirmed even though the disable operation timed out. Rollback can then restore a different checkout with no confirmed persistent disable, and recovery can clear the intent after the same false confirmation. The enable and bootstrap calls likewise ignore timedOut.
findings.suggestion: Treat timedOut as failure for executor launchctl mutations, including disable, enable, bootstrap, and bootout, and retain the intent when shutdown cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: launchctl disable reaches its timeout and subsequently exits zero; shutdownExecutor returns successfully, allowing rollback to check out the previous release even though disable was not confirmed.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue, store, configuration and test changes. The targeted queue suite could not start because the checkout is missing @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. Canonicalizing configured names introduces a compatibility problem with repositories registered under mixed-case slugs.

findings.title: Lowercasing configured names bypasses existing repository registrations
findings.detail: The queue now passes a lowercase slug to run creation, but resolveRepo and getRepoBySlug look up registered slugs case-sensitively. A repository registered by an earlier release as Owner/Repo is therefore not found when the queue requests owner/repo. The factory invokes gh to register a second repository with default settings instead of using the existing registration; if that lookup fails, queue admission fails. Existing runs and the new run also belong to different repository records.
findings.suggestion: Resolve GitHub repository registrations case-insensitively before creating a new registration, while retaining canonical keys for queue comparisons.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing installation has a registered Owner/Repo and configures that repository in the issue queue. After upgrading, an approved issue is admitted with owner/repo; resolution misses the existing record and either creates a duplicate with default repository settings or fails the remote lookup.

output.summary: Reviewed the queue, configuration, store and test changes, including snapshot invalidation and review-round linkage. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`.

findings.title: Lowercasing the run request bypasses existing repository registrations
findings.detail: The canonicalized key is also passed as the repository in queue-created run requests. Repository resolution uses a case-sensitive `getRepoBySlug`, so it does not find an existing mixed-case registration. It instead queries GitHub and creates a separate lowercase registration, losing the existing registration's local path, default branch and merge policy. If GitHub lookup fails, admission fails entirely.
findings.suggestion: Use lowercase only for queue identity keys, and resolve run requests to the existing repository registration case-insensitively, preserving its configured settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue configured for `Owner/Repo` has an existing repository registered as `Owner/Repo`. After upgrade, an eligible issue is submitted as `owner/repo`; resolution misses the existing row and either creates a second GitHub repository registration or fails during the remote lookup.

output.summary: Reviewed the lease storage, recovery paths, migration, and replaced fake. The focused tests could not start because the installed Zod lacks `prefault`; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: A malformed tip during release replay clears the journal
findings.detail: Every `moved` result is treated as proof that ownership was superseded, but `ClaimClient.write` also returns `moved` when its follow-up read finds a malformed record. This marks confirmed ownership lost and clears the release intent, even though the required recovery classification says a malformed tip must leave the intent and confirmed history unchanged for a later retry.
findings.suggestion: Classify the moved tip using the same recovery rules before settling the intent; retain the journal when its record is malformed or otherwise cannot establish supersession.
findings.failure_scenario: Recovery reads the confirmed tip and starts replaying a release. Before the compare-and-swap arrives, the ref moves to a commit with a malformed claim record. The write returns `moved`, and recovery clears the final-status intent instead of returning `pending`.

output.summary: Reviewed the lease storage, recovery paths, migration, and extracted fake. The targeted tests could not start because the installed Zod version is 3.25.76 while the project requires ^4.6.5; both failed during module loading with “floors.prefault is not a function.”

findings.title: Classify the moved tip before discarding a release intent
findings.detail: Every moved result from a replay is treated as supersession. ClaimClient.write also returns moved when the new tip is malformed or contains the same generation and holder with different fields. Neither establishes that ownership was superseded. This clears the journal and marks confirmed ownership lost, so the final status and checkpoint can no longer be replayed. A malformed tip observed before the replay correctly remains pending, making the result depend on when the same change arrives.
findings.suggestion: Classify result.tip using the same rules as the initial recovery read; retain the intent for malformed or otherwise unclassifiable records, and mark lost only when the supersession conditions hold.
findings.failure_scenario: Recovery reads the confirmed tip and begins replaying a release. Before updateRefs, the ref moves to a malformed commit. The compare-and-swap fails, write returns moved, and recovery clears the release intent and marks the confirmed lease lost instead of retaining it for a later retry.

output.summary: Reviewed the observation, classification, land, and post-merge paths, including retry and restart behavior. The targeted test command could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency; Bun reported that it could not find the package. The findings below are based on tracing the code.

findings.title: Post-merge completion applies one execution's result to other executions
findings.detail: Finalization matches rebase observations by round and SHA but ignores their execution handle and stage. If a post-merge execution is interrupted after recording a failure and a later execution on the same SHA completes, both rows are finalized using the later comparison. The interrupted execution can therefore acquire the later execution's retry or confirmation history and class, even though its own outcome was never determined.
findings.suggestion: Carry the primary execution identity into completion and finalize only its observations; leave interrupted executions for terminal-state finalization.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restart follows a recorded worker failure before the post-merge result checkpoint. A replacement execution on the same commit fails and its coordinator confirmation passes. Both observation rows are finalized as confirmed-passed, although only the replacement execution was confirmed.

findings.title: A resumed slow re-check can lose its slow-regression flag
findings.detail: The selector only updates observations from the current stage ID, but every resumed stage gets a new ID. When a completed primary GitHub Actions execution is replayed from the checkpoint after a restart during its re-check, its existing observation belongs to the earlier stage and no new observation is inserted. The selector therefore leaves slow_regression unset, so a passing re-check is classified as flaky rather than load.
findings.suggestion: Find the observation by the durable primary execution identity rather than the current stage ID, including when replaying a completed execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A slow post-merge failure is recorded, the daemon restarts while its re-check is running, and the primary result is replayed before the re-check passes. The observation remains slow_regression=0 and finalizes as flaky instead of load.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed observation, classification, land and post-merge paths. The targeted test command could not start because the checkout is missing the entities dependency; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Preserve the slow-regression flag when a gate resumes in a new stage
findings.detail: The handle lookup filters observations by the current stage ID. A restarted gates stage receives a new stage ID, while reattaching a durable LAN execution reuses its existing handle. The observation insert then conflicts with the existing row and leaves its original stage ID intact. The selector consequently finds no handle to update, so a passing slow-regression re-check is finalized as flaky instead of load.
findings.suggestion: Associate the selector with the primary execution identity across stage restarts, rather than requiring the observation's stage ID to match the newly created stage. Add a restart test that interrupts after observation insertion but before the slow-regression selector runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts after a slow post-merge LAN gate failure has been observed but before its re-check. The resumed stage reattaches the same job, its re-check passes, and the observation remains slow_regression=0 and is classified flaky.

output.summary: Reviewed the lease manager, its tests, and the surrounding claim, clock, and intent APIs. The targeted command `bun test test/leases.test.ts` could not run: module loading failed with `TypeError: floors.prefault is not a function`, consistent with an incompatible installed Zod dependency.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits leases recovered after restart
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes performed by this manager. Confirmed held rows already in SQLite, including acquisitions confirmed by startup recovery or by a later intent reconciliation, never enter that map. Starting a new manager therefore leaves those leases without automatic renewal.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive the renewal set from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, while retaining generation-bound handle checks.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts with a confirmed held lease, starts the manager, and the run remains active. No renewal is attempted on subsequent ticks, so the lease expires.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile a pending acquisition
findings.detail: The cross-run guard returns `refused` before reconciling an existing intent. The request requires every operation to reconcile first and return `wait` while an intent remains unresolved. It also prevents the new run from immediately progressing when reconciliation would drop a never-confirmed acquisition.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row's intent before applying the cross-run ownership guard, then inspect the resulting confirmed state.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A's first acquisition has an unconfirmed outcome and leaves an intent. Run B requests the same ref after A ends; even if GitHub now shows that A's write did not occur, B is refused without a reconciliation read.

findings.title: Mutation tests explicitly accept the broken unconditional write
findings.detail: The concurrency helper expects two winners when the unconditional-ref-write mutant is enabled, so both mutant cases pass when the safety invariant fails. The request explicitly requires the concurrent-create and takeover tests to fail under that mutant.
findings.suggestion: Assert the one-winner invariant independently of fake mode and run those tests against the mutant as a separate expected-failure check.
findings.failure_scenario: The fake is configured to bypass the ref compare-and-swap. Both managers acquire the same generation, but the mutant test expects two winners and passes.

output.summary: Reviewed the lease manager, intent recovery, time checks, and tests. The targeted command `bun test test/leases.test.ts` could not load the suite: the installed Zod reports `TypeError: floors.prefault is not a function`. No behavioral test results were available from that run.

findings.title: Release intent replay bypasses the lease time guard
findings.detail: The manager delegates reconciliation to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a pending release with `client.write` without a `beforeSend` predicate or a fresh GitHub-time sample. This path runs both at startup and on later operations or ticks, so a release can be sent after its generation has expired.
findings.suggestion: Make release replay use the same fresh-time decision and send-time revalidation as an ordinary release, including re-decision when the send is aborted.
findings.failure_scenario: A release is journaled, the daemon stops before its ref update, and restarts more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery sends the old generation's release without checking whether it is still renewable.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits confirmed leases restored after restart
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied through this manager instance. Confirmed held rows already in SQLite at construction, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never populate that map. Starting the manager therefore does not renew those active leases.
findings.suggestion: Reconstruct loop handles from confirmed held rows, including rows confirmed by reconciliation, while retaining generation checks under the mutex.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts with a confirmed held lease and starts the manager with `active` returning true. No renewal is attempted on subsequent ticks, so the lease expires despite remaining active.

findings.title: A different run is refused before a pending intent is reconciled
findings.detail: The cross-run check returns `refused` whenever the existing row has an intent, before reconciliation can determine whether that intent was dropped or released. This violates the required reconciliation-first behavior and reports a live refusal even when an unresolved acquisition should return `wait` or can be forgotten.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the existing row first, return `wait` while it remains pending, and then re-read the row before deciding whether the other run can acquire.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent and ends. Run B tries to acquire the same ref while GitHub is readable and still shows the ref absent. The manager returns `refused` without dropping A's intent or allowing B to proceed.

findings.title: Concurrency tests explicitly accept the unconditional-write mutant
findings.detail: The race helper expects two winners when the unconditional-ref-write mutant is enabled, and both mutant cases are registered as passing tests. The request explicitly requires the concurrent-create and takeover tests to fail under that mutant, so these tests do not provide the requested mutation check.
findings.suggestion: Assert the single-winner invariant independently of implementation mode and run those assertions against the mutant as a separate expected-failure mutation check.
findings.failure_scenario: The fake's ref update is changed to unconditional writes. Both managers acquire the same generation, yet the mutant test cases pass because two winners are their expected result.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed prompt, schemas, verification, preview, persistence, and resume paths. Focused tests could not start because the checkout is missing the entities dependency.

findings.title: Treating the absence of a warning as successful browser setup
findings.detail: The engine records the browser as available whenever a preview exists and the invocation has no browser_unavailable event. That event reports failures while constructing the MCP configuration; it does not establish that the MCP server started or that Chromium was usable. If either fails afterward, a verifier can correctly report an environmental block, but the engine converts it to unclear and sends the run through implementation feedback instead of bounded environment-block handling. The persisted context repeats that decision after restart.
findings.suggestion: Record and require a positive, same-invocation browser setup result before converting blocked rows. Preserve environment-block handling when setup cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: The preview starts and browserMcp constructs a configuration, but the MCP server fails to launch or Chromium cannot start. The verifier reports a marked browser check blocked; no browser_unavailable configuration warning was emitted, so the engine records available and converts the row to unclear.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed prompts, schemas, verdict normalization, preview setup and resume paths. Focused tests could not start because the checkout resolves a missing `entities` package and an incompatible Zod version.

findings.title: Treating absence of a warning as successful browser setup misclassifies startup failures
findings.detail: The engine labels the browser available whenever a preview exists and the invocation emitted no `browser_unavailable` warning. That warning is emitted when the harness cannot construct the MCP configuration, but constructing it does not start the MCP server or Chromium. If either fails after the CLI launches it, the verifier can correctly report the browser as blocked without an engine warning; this code converts the result to `unclear` and sends it through an implementation feedback round instead of the bounded environment-block path. The request requires positive same-attempt evidence of successful browser setup before converting the verdict.
findings.suggestion: Record an engine-owned successful browser setup outcome for the invocation and convert blocked rows only when that outcome is present; treat absent or failed setup as unavailable or unknown.
findings.failure_scenario: A preview is ready and browserMcp returns a configuration, but the MCP server or Chromium fails to launch. The verifier reports a marked browser check as blocked; the engine records `available` and converts it to `unclear`.

output.summary: Reviewed the changed lifecycle, storage, dispatch, documentation, and tests. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not run because `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js` is missing from the environment.

findings.title: A superseded set can never be published when the run waits again
findings.detail: Superseding an unsent question effect records it as done, and observation refuses to create any effect whose key already exists. If the run later returns to waiting with the same unanswered IDs, it has no GitHub question comment and will never get one. A daemon restart can produce this transition: the engine first writes `running` while resuming, then returns to `waiting_input`. The new tests explicitly retain the done checkpoint in this situation even when the POST was never accepted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish an unpublished superseded effect from a successfully published or deliberately suppressed set, and allow a fresh eligible waiting episode to publish it after uncertain delivery has been resolved.
findings.failure_scenario: A question POST has not been accepted, the daemon restarts, and lifecycle reconciliation sees the run temporarily running before the engine resumes waiting on the same unanswered question. The effect is closed and no later poll publishes the question.

findings.title: Inspection failure closes an uncertain POST without recovery
findings.detail: The stored body is re-inspected before marker recovery, and any inspection failure immediately marks the effect done even when its page indicates a POST was issued and its outcome is uncertain. This violates the requirement to recover an uncertain POST by marker before closing its checkpoint. For example, a transient failure reading the private-strings configuration after restart permanently discards the recovery record.

findings.title: Superseded sets can never be published when they become current again
findings.detail: A stale unsent question effect is marked done, and observation refuses to create another effect with the same question IDs. If the run returns to waiting with those unanswered questions, or the issue link is restored, the current set is never published. The new tests explicitly preserve this behavior even when the earlier POST was not accepted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish superseded, never-published effects from completed publications and allow a fresh publication when that set becomes eligible again, while retaining uncertain-POST recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: A question POST fails before acceptance, the run briefly leaves waiting_input, and then returns to waiting_input with the same unanswered question. Recovery closes the effect as done and subsequent polls never publish the question.

findings.title: Inspection failure closes an uncertain POST without recovering it
findings.detail: The stored body is re-inspected before checking the checkpointed marker. If inspection now fails, the code marks the effect done without searching GitHub, even when page indicates that a POST was issued and its outcome is unknown. This violates the requirement to recover an uncertain POST before closing its checkpoint and loses the accepted comment's identity.
findings.suggestion: Recover an issued POST using the independently generated marker and checkpointed author before deciding whether a body can be sent again; suppress only a prospective POST when inspection fails.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but the response is lost; before the next poll, the private-string configuration becomes unreadable or gains a string in the stored body. The checkpoint is closed without fetching the accepted comment.

findings.title: Publication failures log raw command and server error text
findings.detail: The catch passes the exception to logFailure, which only redacts registered credentials. The real subprocess wrapper includes the complete command and stderr or stdout in its exception; GitHub error output can contain configured private strings or other withheld content. This also contradicts the explicit requirement that publication diagnostics use fixed codes rather than exception output.
findings.suggestion: Log a fixed publication failure code without the exception or command output.
findings.failure_scenario: A lifecycle comment POST or recovery request fails with a GitHub error response containing a configured private string. The error is written to lifecycle diagnostics without private-string inspection or redaction.

findings.title: Excluded native providers make smoke deployment fail
findings.detail: When every catalog model for Claude or Codex is excluded, cheapestModel throws. The smoke runner records each native check as a failure, so reportChecks returns a nonzero exit code and deploy --smoke fails. Backend checks already treat a provider whose models are all excluded as skipped.
findings.suggestion: Skip native provider checks with the exclusion reason when that provider has no eligible model, while still failing genuine checks of eligible models.
findings.failure_scenario: An installation configures exclude_origins = ["US"] and deploys with --smoke. All built-in Claude and Codex models have US origins, so their smoke checks fail even if eligible models from other providers are available.

findings.title: Verifier exhaustion can hide the exclusion reason
findings.detail: Exclusion reasons are reported only when the filtered verifier list is empty. If it contains a model that raised the finding, pickVerifier rejects that model and throws its own error without mentioning the excluded alternatives. The invocation therefore fails without the origin exclusion reason required when exclusions leave no candidate.
findings.suggestion: Include the collected exclusion reasons when verifier selection fails after filtering, including when the remaining targets cannot independently verify the finding.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel verifier list contains an allowed model that raised the finding and a CN-origin alternative, with CN excluded. The only independent verifier is excluded, but the run reports only that the allowed model raised the candidate.

findings.title: Excluded native providers make the deployment smoke gate fail
findings.detail: When every catalog model for a native provider is excluded, the native smoke checks call `modelsByPrice`, which throws an origin-exclusion error. The smoke runner records that as a failed check, so `limitless deploy --smoke` rolls back even if other eligible providers remain. Backend checks already treat the same condition as a skip.
findings.suggestion: Skip native provider checks when all of that provider's models are excluded, while retaining the exclusion reason in the report.
findings.failure_scenario: With `exclude_origins = ["US"]`, the native Claude and Codex models are excluded; their smoke checks fail instead of skipping, preventing a smoke-gated deploy.

findings.title: Verifier exhaustion can omit the required exclusion reason
findings.detail: The verifier selection discards excluded targets before calling `pickVerifier`, but reports their reasons only when the filtered list is empty. If the remaining eligible verifiers all raised the finding being checked, `pickVerifier` fails with a message about those verifiers and never reports that the alternative was origin-excluded. The request requires an invocation with no candidate due to exclusions to fail with the exclusion reason.
findings.suggestion: Include the collected exclusion reasons when verifier selection fails after filtering.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel verifier list contains an excluded independent model and an eligible model that raised the finding. The eligible model cannot verify its own finding, and the failure names only that model instead of the excluded alternative and its reason.

The added native smoke test checks the reason but does not assert the resulting failure status.
findings.suggestion: Skip native-provider smoke checks with the exclusion reason when that provider has no eligible model, as the backend checks already do.

findings.title: A declined answer bypasses the required no-candidate failure
findings.detail: When an allowed model returns a decline marked as a last-resort answer, the next routing attempt returns that answer before examining or reporting origin exclusions. If the remaining candidates are excluded, the invocation succeeds with the declined answer instead of failing with the exclusion reason, contrary to the requested behavior.
findings.suggestion: Inspect the final routing decision for origin exclusions before returning a last-resort answer, and fail with the required reason when exclusions leave no candidate.
findings.failure_scenario: An allowed review model returns a last-resort decline, and the only remaining fallback is a CN-origin model excluded by configuration. The invocation returns the declined answer rather than failing with the origin exclusion reason.

findings.detail: The new reviewableText check requires strict UTF-8 and rejects several control bytes. Git's text classification does not impose those restrictions, so executable text can still be reported as binary and require an allowance. The request explicitly limits the mode condition to INERT_MEDIA_PATH and requires other text files to be reviewed normally.
findings.suggestion: Apply the mode-based allowance condition only to paths matching INERT_MEDIA_PATH, leaving the existing binary classification to handle other paths.

findings.title: Executable text in a non-UTF-8 encoding still requires a binary allowance
findings.detail: The new mode check uses strict UTF-8 decoding to decide whether a file is text. Git can produce a normal text diff for files in other encodings, but an executable file containing such text is still reported as binary. This leaves part of the explicitly requested behavior unresolved. A targeted fixture containing a Latin-1 comment produced `3  0  tool.sh` from `git diff --numstat`, while `diffSince` returned `["tool.sh"]` in `binaryPaths`.
findings.suggestion: Apply the requested mode restriction to inert-media paths and use the existing Git text classification for other paths.
findings.failure_scenario: An executable shell script contains a Latin-1 comment such as `# café` and is added or edited. Git displays its lines as text, but the audit blocks it unless the request grants `Allow: binary`.

Consequently, the requested exemption does not apply to every text script: an executable script encoded in a legacy single-byte encoding, or containing an escape byte, is still reported as binary solely because of its mode. The request explicitly limits the mode condition to inert-media paths and requires executable text to be reviewed like other text.
findings.suggestion: Apply the mode-based allowance condition only to paths matching `INERT_MEDIA_PATH`, leaving the existing binary classification to handle other paths.

findings.detail: The poller saves the new PR snapshot before it requeues draft deferrals. If the daemon stops between those operations, the next poll sees the saved head as unchanged and does not call `recheckDraftConflictTriggers` while the PR remains a draft. The skipped trigger can then remain deferred indefinitely despite the requested head-change recheck.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land conflict trigger
findings.detail: When any saved PR snapshot exists, the land trigger is evaluated against it without refreshing the PR. If the snapshot predates the approved head, `startConflictTrigger` marks the trigger skipped as `PR head moved`. The blocked land entry is not retried, and a later poll does not reconsider skipped triggers.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation before consuming a land trigger, or leave the trigger pending until an observation for its head is available.
findings.failure_scenario: A PR advances to a new head and is approved before the next poll. Landing detects a conflict at that head, but the stored poller snapshot still names the previous head, so no conflict round starts.

findings.title: Conflict rounds are indistinguishable to a rolled-back release
findings.detail: The new kind is stored in the existing review-round table and the run uses the existing `review-round` source kind. The previous release ignores the new column and treats a queued or resumed conflict round as an ordinary review round. Its preparation refuses a conflicting base rather than resolving it, so rollback can fail work that the newer release had queued.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible representation or a release transition that prevents the previous release from processing conflict rounds as ordinary review rounds.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy creates a conflict round, then rolls back while that run is queued or before preparation completes. The previous daemon resumes it as a review round and fails on the merge conflict.

findings.title: A comment failure leaves a delivered resolution without its required PR comment
findings.detail: The push and delivered record are committed before reading or posting the comment. An ordinary GitHub error in either subsequent call fails the run after the branch has changed; the failed run is terminal and there is no durable retry for the missing comment. The marker only prevents duplicates when delivery is retried, not when the run has failed.
findings.suggestion: Persist comment publication as a resumable delivery step and retry it independently after an uncertain or failed GitHub request.
findings.failure_scenario: The push succeeds, then `gh pr view --json comments` or `gh pr comment` fails temporarily. The entry says the conflict was resolved, but the PR never gets the required resolution comment.

findings.title: A conflict observed during another round is permanently discarded
findings.detail: A trigger encountered while any review or conflict round is active is marked skipped. The poller emits pr.conflicting only on entry into the conflicting state, so it will not recreate the trigger when the active round ends while the PR remains conflicting. The same permanent discard occurs at the daily cap, even after the cap window expires.
findings.suggestion: Keep temporarily ineligible triggers pending and reconsider them when the active round ends or the cap expires, while retaining the one-in-flight and daily limits.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is running when the base advances and the poller observes CONFLICTING. The review round later fails without pushing; subsequent polls still report CONFLICTING, but no conflict round starts.

findings.title: A saved PR snapshot prevents a fresh lookup for land triggers
findings.detail: When any saved snapshot exists, the land trigger is immediately decided against that snapshot, even if it predates the land queue's approved head. findings.suggestion: Store conflict rounds where the previous release's review-round queries cannot count them, or ship a compatible reader before writing these rows.

findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue finds a conflict at B. Processing compares B with saved A and permanently skips the trigger.

findings.title: Starting a round trusts an old snapshot over the supplied observation
findings.detail: When a saved snapshot exists, the eligibility checks use it instead of the observation passed to `startConflictTrigger`. In particular, the startup recovery path can launch a round based on a PR's former open, non-draft state without checking its current state. The later delivery check prevents a draft push, but the prohibited round and its model work have already started.
findings.suggestion: Decide eligibility from a fresh observation and fail closed when draft or head identity cannot be verified.
findings.failure_scenario: A trigger is persisted while a PR is open, the daemon stops, and the PR is converted to draft before restart. Startup consumes the trigger using the previously saved non-draft snapshot and starts a conflict round.

findings.title: The PR comment does not summarize the resolution
findings.detail: The comment contains the merged base SHA, a list of conflicted paths, and the resulting SHA, but no description of how the conflicts were resolved. A path list does not let the PR reader understand the resolution, which the request explicitly requires.
findings.suggestion: Produce and publish a concise summary of the actual resolution, with the same redaction and publication checks.

output.summary: Reviewed the trigger, persistence, merge, and delivery paths. The targeted command `bun test test/conflict-rounds.test.ts` could not load the tests: this checkout has no local node_modules and resolved an incompatible Zod version, producing `TypeError: z.number().overwrite is not a function`.

findings.title: A stale poller snapshot can permanently discard a land trigger
findings.detail: A land trigger is immediately consumed using any saved GitHub snapshot, even if that snapshot predates the head approved by the land entry. `startConflictTrigger` marks a head mismatch as skipped, so a later poll of the current head cannot recover the trigger. The land entry remains blocked without the requested conflict round.
findings.suggestion: Refresh the PR observation when the saved snapshot does not match the trigger, and retain the trigger until a current observation can decide it.
findings.failure_scenario: The poller last observed head A, the PR advances to B and B is approved before the next poll, and the land queue finds a conflict at B. Processing compares B with saved A and permanently skips the trigger.

findings.title: Starting a round trusts an old snapshot over the supplied observation
findings.detail: When a saved snapshot exists, the eligibility checks use it instead of the observation passed to `startConflictTrigger`. In particular, the startup recovery path can launch a round based on a PR's former open, non-draft state without checking its current state. The later delivery check prevents a draft push, but the prohibited round and its model work have already started.
findings.suggestion: Decide eligibility from a fresh observation and fail closed when draft or head identity cannot be verified.
findings.failure_scenario: A trigger is persisted while a PR is open, the daemon stops, and the PR is converted to draft before restart. Startup consumes the trigger using the previously saved non-draft snapshot and starts a conflict round.
