Reviewed the executor integration, persistence, retries, and landing checks. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-executor.test.ts` could not run: the installed Zod lacks `z.number().overwrite`, causing an import error before tests execute. That dependency/environment failure is not attributed to this change.

Reviewed executor routing, retry and restart handling, cancellation, and event delivery. The targeted executor test could not run because the installed Zod is 3.25.76 while the repository requires Zod 4; it failed during module loading before any tests ran.

findings.title: Restarting during a retry removes the build output that retry needs
findings.detail: On resume, the gates stage cleans the checkout before recovering the saved initial result and attaching to the retry. `checkoutCommitted` removes ignored files and dependencies, but the saved initial result prevents its setup from running again. The local retry therefore runs in a different environment from its first attempt and can report a false regression. The prepare path similarly discards changes before recovering a saved baseline retry.
findings.suggestion: For local executions, restore the setup and initial-attempt environment before replaying a retry after restart, or rerun the complete local gate sequence while preserving the recorded attempt semantics.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command installs dependencies or builds an ignored artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts after the regression retry handle is saved. Resume cleans the dependencies or artifact, then replays only the selected check, which fails because its setup output is missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: The shared execution path awaits only `execution.result` and never iterates `execution.events`. Local execution happens to invoke the supplied hooks directly, but an executor implementing the exposed interface has no hooks and cannot deliver check or status events to the pipeline or landing log. This leaves the requested shared executor seam unable to preserve gate events for another implementation.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream in the shared execution path and translate its events into the existing pipeline and landing callbacks, avoiding duplicate local events.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields check events and returns a successful GateRun. The stage completes, but no check events are recorded and landing's gate log contains no check output.

findings.title: Restarting a retry reuses results after deleting its prerequisites
findings.detail: The persisted initial result skips the initial gate execution on resume, but the resumed gates stage first calls checkoutCommitted, which removes ignored files and dependencies. The retry request has an empty setup and therefore runs without the build output or dependencies produced by the initial attempt. Prepare similarly discards changes before resuming a baseline retry. This changes retry results and can turn a transient failure into a blocking failure or an incorrect baseline.
findings.suggestion: Restore the retry's required workspace state on resume, or rerun the initial local execution and setup before retrying when that state cannot be preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate setup installs dependencies, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts while its regression retry is pending. On resume checkoutCommitted removes the dependencies, the cached initial result suppresses setup, and the retry fails because its executable is missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: executeGate awaits only execution.result and never reads execution.events. Consequently an injected executor's check events never reach the pipeline gate events or landing log; only the local implementation's separate direct hooks happen to preserve those outputs. A targeted probe using `bun -e` to return one check event from an injected executor printed `hook calls: 0`. The shared executor path therefore does not deliver the event behavior required by the seam.
findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream while awaiting the result and forward events through the existing reporting hooks, without duplicating local events.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor emits a check result through its events iterable while its result is pending; the run's gate event feed and landing check log omit that result.

Reviewed executor lifecycle, retries, resume paths, cancellation, and landing checks. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-executor.test.ts test/gates.test.ts` could not run: both files failed during module loading because the installed Zod lacks `z.number().overwrite`; this was not attributed to the diff.

findings.title: Resumed retries reuse results after their build outputs have been discarded
findings.detail: The completed initial gate result is reused on resume, but the prepare and gates resume paths clean the worktree before reaching the retry. A local retry therefore runs without the files produced by the initial setup or checks, even though retries previously ran before cleanup specifically to retain those outputs. This can turn a passing retry into a failure or otherwise change its result.
findings.suggestion: For local executions, restore the prerequisite work before replaying a retry, or arrange checkpointing and cleanup so the retry sees the same build outputs as its initial attempt.
findings.failure_scenario: A baseline setup generates an ignored build artifact, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts during its retry. Prepare discards the artifact, reuses the stored initial result, and reattaches the local retry without rerunning setup.

findings.title: Landing executions have no persisted handle for restart
findings.detail: Landing calls executeGate without a stored handle or persistence callback, so its handle is discarded. After a daemon restart the landing checks start a new execution instead of attaching to the one already started. This leaves the shared executor path unable to provide the requested restart semantics for landing and can duplicate work for an executor whose jobs survive the daemon.
findings.suggestion: Persist the landing execution handle with the landing state before attaching, and restore it when the checks resume.
findings.failure_scenario: A non-local executor starts a long landing gate suite and the daemon restarts while it is running; the resumed queue starts a second suite while the original continues.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed
findings.detail: executeGate awaits only the result and never iterates execution.events. Local executions happen to call the supplied hooks directly, but an injected or future executor can report progress and check results only through its event stream. Those events never reach the pipeline or landing log, and an executor that requires its event stream to be drained may not complete.
findings.suggestion: Consume the event stream alongside the result and translate its events into the existing gate hooks, with appropriate cancellation and error handling.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor emits check results through Execution.events while running a landing suite; the suite completes but the landing log contains none of those check outputs.

findings.title: Resuming a retry reuses results after deleting their build output
findings.detail: On a gates-stage restart, the engine calls `checkoutCommitted`, which removes ignored and untracked build output, before this cached initial result is returned. If a regression retry was pending, the resumed local executor then runs only the selected checks with no setup. Those checks no longer see the workspace produced by the initial gate run, despite the retry depending on it. This can turn a flaky check into a blocking failure or otherwise change the verdict after a routine daemon restart. Prepare-stage cleanup can similarly remove untracked output before a baseline retry resumes.
findings.suggestion: Restore the workspace needed by a local retry, for example by replaying the initial local gate execution after restart before rerunning its retry, while preserving the durable executor behavior for remote work.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command installs dependencies or creates build output, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts after the retry handle is saved. On resume, checkout cleanup removes that output; the attached local retry has an empty setup list and fails because its dependencies are missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed by daemon callers
findings.detail: `executeGate` attaches and awaits only `execution.result`; it never reads `execution.events`. Local execution happens to invoke the supplied hooks directly, but an executor implementing the advertised interface can report progress and check results only through its event stream. Its events therefore never reach pipeline gate events or the landing log, and an implementation whose event producer applies backpressure can stall. This leaves the shared executor seam incomplete for the executor implementations it is intended to support.
findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream concurrently with the result and route its events through the existing pipeline and landing reporting hooks, with appropriate cancellation and error handling.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields check events while its result is pending. The gate stage and landing log receive none of those events; if the producer waits for a consumer, the gate never completes.

findings.title: Resuming a retry reuses results after deleting their build output
findings.detail: On a gates-stage restart, the engine calls `checkoutCommitted`, which removes ignored and untracked build output, before this cached initial result is returned. If a regression retry was pending, the resumed local executor then runs only the selected checks with no setup. Those checks no longer see the workspace produced by the initial gate run, despite the retry depending on it. This can turn a flaky check into a blocking failure or otherwise change the verdict after a routine daemon restart. Prepare-stage cleanup can similarly remove untracked output before a baseline retry resumes.
findings.suggestion: Restore the workspace needed by a local retry, for example by replaying the initial local gate execution after restart before rerunning its retry, while preserving the durable executor behavior for remote work.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup command installs dependencies or creates build output, a check fails transiently, and the daemon restarts after the retry handle is saved. On resume, checkout cleanup removes that output; the attached local retry has an empty setup list and fails because its dependencies are missing.

findings.title: Executor events are never consumed by daemon callers
findings.detail: `executeGate` attaches and awaits only `execution.result`; it never reads `execution.events`. Local execution happens to invoke the supplied hooks directly, but an executor implementing the advertised interface can report progress and check results only through its event stream. Its events therefore never reach pipeline gate events or the landing log, and an implementation whose event producer applies backpressure can stall. This leaves the shared executor seam incomplete for the executor implementations it is intended to support.
findings.suggestion: Consume the execution event stream concurrently with the result and route its events through the existing pipeline and landing reporting hooks, with appropriate cancellation and error handling.
findings.failure_scenario: An injected executor yields check events while its result is pending. The gate stage and landing log receive none of those events; if the producer waits for a consumer, the gate never completes.

findings.title: Gate allowance exposes Cargo registry credentials
findings.detail: The gate profile allows reads throughout the real Cargo home, but the denied credential list does not include Cargo's credentials files. Cargo commonly stores registry tokens in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml or ~/.cargo/credentials. A candidate gate command can read those files by absolute path despite CARGO_HOME being redirected to scratch, and can send the tokens over the network. The overlap check and runtime probes do not detect this because those files are absent from the deny list.
findings.suggestion: Allow only the Cargo toolchain paths gates need, while explicitly denying Cargo credential files; ensure the overlap handling supports those specific denies and add a real read probe.
findings.failure_scenario: The owner has authenticated to a Cargo registry, leaving a token in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml, and a malicious dependency or gate script reads that file during a factory run.

findings.title: Cargo home allowance exposes registry credentials to gate commands
findings.detail: The gate policy allows reads throughout the Cargo home, but the denied credential list does not include Cargo's credentials files. A gate command can therefore read ~/.cargo/credentials or ~/.cargo/credentials.toml by absolute path and exfiltrate registry tokens. Changing CARGO_HOME to scratch for the command does not prevent that absolute-path read. This violates the requirement that credential stores fall outside the gate allowlist.
findings.suggestion: Deny Cargo credential files explicitly while allowing the toolchain files gates need, and add a real Seatbelt probe for both supported credential filenames.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine has a Cargo registry token in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml and a candidate test reads that file during a gate.

findings.title: Gate allowlist exposes Cargo registry credentials
findings.detail: The gate profile allows reads of the entire Cargo home, while the credential deny list does not include Cargo's credential files. A gate can therefore read `~/.cargo/credentials` or `~/.cargo/credentials.toml` by absolute path and send registry tokens over the unrestricted network. Setting the gate's `CARGO_HOME` to scratch does not prevent an absolute-path read.
findings.suggestion: Deny Cargo credential files explicitly after granting the toolchain home, or narrow the readable Cargo paths so credential files remain inaccessible. Add a real gate probe for both credential filenames.
findings.failure_scenario: An installation has a Cargo registry token in the default Cargo home and a dependency install script or candidate test reads that file during a gate.

findings.title: HOME override leaves the account's actual home unprotected
findings.detail: `homedir()` follows the process's `HOME` environment variable. If the daemon starts with HOME pointing elsewhere, both the gate home deny and the editor credential list protect that alternate directory instead of the account home that tools such as SSH obtain from the password database. The account's actual SSH keys and other listed stores remain readable. The local check `HOME=/example/alternate bun -e 'console.log(require("node:os").homedir())'` printed `/example/alternate`.
findings.suggestion: Resolve and protect the account home independently of an overridable HOME, and fail closed if it cannot be established. Include a test with HOME different from the account home.
findings.failure_scenario: The factory is launched with a custom HOME while the account's password-database home still contains `.ssh` or another listed credential store; an editor or gate reads the actual path.

findings.title: Gate allowlist exposes Cargo registry credentials
findings.detail: The gate profile allows reads throughout the real Cargo home, but the credential deny list does not include Cargo's credentials files. Consequently, untrusted gate code can read registry tokens from ~/.cargo/credentials or ~/.cargo/credentials.toml by absolute path and send them over the network. Redirecting CARGO_HOME to scratch does not prevent absolute-path reads. This violates the request that every credential store fall outside the gate allowlist.
findings.suggestion: Keep the toolchain files gates need readable while explicitly denying Cargo credential files, and add a real Seatbelt probe using stand-in credentials under the allowed Cargo home.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner has a crates.io or private registry token in ~/.cargo/credentials.toml, and a malicious dependency or candidate test reads that file during a gate and exfiltrates its contents.

When a daemon restarts while one of those executions is pending, the stage starts over and discards its stored handle instead of attaching to the work already started. This violates the requested executor durability contract and can duplicate work for an executor whose work survives the daemon.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough preceding stage state to resume each retry at its pending handle, then attach to it without starting another execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restarts after a regression retry has started but before its result arrives; on resume the stored retry handle is discarded and another execution is started.

findings.title: Handle is cleared before the gate result is durably recorded
findings.detail: The `gate-result` save clears the handle inside `runGateExecution`, before its caller stores the baseline or gate comparison. A restart after that save but before the enclosing stage checkpoint has neither the handle nor the result, so it starts the same gate work again. The window includes subsequent comparison, retry and artifact work, not just the duration of a single write.
findings.suggestion: Checkpoint the result and clear its handle atomically with the state needed to resume the enclosing stage.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after an initial gate execution returns and `gate-result` is saved, but before the gates stage persists its comparison; the resumed stage starts a new execution instead of attaching or reusing the completed result.

findings.title: Reopened historical run state is no longer sanitized
findings.detail: Removing the constructor's `redactGateData` call leaves legacy gate output and commands containing registered credentials in `ctx.state`. Subsequent checkpoints can persist that unsanitized state again, and code consuming the reopened state can use the raw values. The changed gate-feedback test explicitly stops checking that the reopened state is redacted.
findings.suggestion: Restore sanitization of historical gate data on load while preserving any execution identity needed for attachment, and retain a test that checks the reopened state.
findings.failure_scenario: A run created by an older release has a registered credential in a persisted gate result or command. After deployment and restart, loading that run leaves the credential in its in-memory state and a later save writes it back unredacted.

findings.title: Resume discards handles for in-flight retries
findings.detail: The resume guard only accepts baseline, initial and rebase handles. After a restart during a baseline retry, regression retry or timeout rerun, the pipeline discards the persisted handle and starts the earlier gate execution again. It never attaches to the retry that was already started. The added restart test explicitly expects this replay. This violates the requested restart contract and can repeat work or leave a non-local execution running without observation.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough intermediate gate state to resume each retry purpose and attach to its stored handle without starting it again.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts after a regression-retry handle is saved but before its result is received. On resume, the initial gate starts again and the stored retry handle is discarded instead of being attached.

findings.title: Pending retry executions are discarded on restart
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A restart during a baseline retry, regression retry, or timeout rerun instead clears the stored handle and starts the earlier execution again. The new restart test explicitly expects this behavior, but the request requires a restart between start and result to attach without starting work again. An executor whose work survives daemon restarts can consequently leave the original execution running and duplicate gate work.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough preceding attempt state to resume each retry and attach its stored handle without restarting the earlier execution.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a regression retry is running on an executor whose work survives restarts; the resumed stage discards that retry handle and starts a new initial gate run.

findings.title: The handle is cleared before the result is durably recorded
findings.detail: After an execution completes, this checkpoint removes its handle before the caller records the baseline or gate comparison. A daemon restart after this save but before the caller's subsequent state checkpoint has neither the result nor the handle, so it starts the execution again instead of reattaching. This applies even to the initial executions that the resume logic otherwise supports.
findings.suggestion: Keep the handle until the corresponding result and stage progress are durably checkpointed together, or persist the result with the handle before clearing it.
findings.failure_scenario: A daemon restart occurs after the gate-result save and before the baseline or comparison is saved; resume starts a second execution for the same stage.

findings.title: Retry handles are discarded on restart instead of reattached
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial and rebase handles qualify for reattachment. If the daemon restarts during a baseline retry, regression retry or timeout rerun, the resumed stage starts its initial execution again and clears the stored retry handle. An executor whose work survives a restart is therefore started again instead of being reattached, contrary to the requested durability contract. The new restart test explicitly expects this behavior for retries.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough attempt context to resume each retry and attach its stored handle without starting another execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression retry is running when the daemon restarts; its persisted handle is discarded and a new initial gate execution starts while the original retry may still be running.

findings.title: The handle is cleared before the result is durably recorded
findings.detail: The gate-result checkpoint removes the execution handle before the caller stores the resulting baseline or gate comparison. A restart after that save but before the caller's subsequent state save leaves neither the handle nor the result in run state, so the stage starts the work again. The same clearing also occurs when attach throws, losing the identity needed to retry attachment.
findings.suggestion: Keep the handle until the result and stage progress are durably checkpointed together, and retain it when attachment fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate execution completes, gate-result is saved, and the daemon restarts before the stage saves its comparison; on resume a new execution starts instead of attaching to the completed one.

findings.title: Gate profile exposes manifest-named files outside its allowlist
findings.detail: The ancestor exceptions grant file-read access to four filenames in every ancestor of every allowed path. Since the home directory is normally an ancestor of the checkout or toolchain, a gate can read `~/package.json`, `~/bunfig.toml`, `~/tsconfig.json`, and `~/jsconfig.json` despite the home-wide deny. The same exception applies to intermediate factory-data directories. These files can contain private configuration or tokens, and the request explicitly requires files directly under home to remain denied.
findings.suggestion: Avoid granting ancestor file contents outside the approved roots; if toolchain discovery requires an exception, constrain it to a trusted location that does not expose arbitrary home or factory files.
findings.failure_scenario: An untrusted gate runs `cat ~/package.json` when that file exists; the literal allow overrides the home deny and returns its contents.

findings.title: Gate profile permits reads of files directly under home
findings.detail: ancestorReadPolicy grants file-read access to package.json, bunfig.toml, tsconfig.json, and jsconfig.json in every ancestor of an allowed path. When a checkout is under the home directory, those literal grants follow and override the home-wide deny in the Seatbelt profile. This violates the requested boundary that files directly under home fall outside the gate allowlist. A focused check of ancestorReadPolicy returned all four paths under /Users/example.

The report filter can expose a line quoted from a multiline holdout test. Targeted MCP tests could not start because the checkout lacks the MCP SDK dependency.

findings.title: Line-by-line filtering can expose excerpts of a hidden scenario
findings.detail: The new filter evaluates each report line independently. The catalogue generally contains complete scenario phrases and selected literals, not every partial quotation. If a report contains both a complete hidden phrase and a shorter excerpt without a distinctive literal, the complete phrase is withheld but the excerpt remains visible. Previously, a match caused the whole report to be withheld. This violates the requirement that report lines quoting holdout text stay hidden.
findings.suggestion: Ensure partial quotations of holdout prose are withheld, or conservatively withhold the report when a matching holdout quotation makes the remaining prose unsafe to expose. Add a regression test containing both a full phrase and an excerpt.
findings.failure_scenario: A hidden scenario says “Walk along the shoreline at twilight.” A report contains that full sentence on one line and “Walk along the shoreline” on another. The first line matches the catalogue, while the second can be returned to the reviewer and subsequently shared with the implementer.

findings.title: Partial quotations of multiline holdout tests remain visible
findings.detail: The catalogue records a multiline holdout field as a complete phrase and harvests selected syntax-shaped literals, but it does not record each test line. A report quoting only a generic line from that field can therefore pass both the multiline and single-line filters. This violates the explicit requirement that any report line quoting hidden test text stay withheld. The underlying matching limitation predates this diff, but the requested behavior remains undelivered.
findings.suggestion: Protect individual lines or other quotable fragments of multiline holdout material, and add a regression test that puts only one such line in a report.
findings.failure_scenario: A holdout step contains `return true;\nexpect(x).toBe(1)` and a report outside the holdout section contains `Quoted test: return true;`. The complete multiline phrase is absent from the report, and `return true;` yields no independently harvested literal, so the quotation is returned.

findings.detail: If the immediate post-merge lookup fails or returns no merge metadata, this update emits run.merged with null fields. The test for delayed observations confirms the columns but leaves the original feed item unchanged, so the reported disagreement persists.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the merge feed entry receives the confirmed metadata when a later observation supplies it, while preserving the intended one-event behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub returns an incomplete or unavailable observation immediately after a successful merge, then the poller observes mergedBy and mergedAt. The run has the values but its run.merged feed item still contains nulls.

findings.title: Do not overwrite a cancellation after the metadata lookup
findings.detail: The new awaited lookup opens a window in which cancel() marks the entry cancelled and aborts its signal. The lookup rejection is swallowed, after which landed() unconditionally changes the entry to landed and emits a land.landed event. This overwrites the newer queue state.
findings.suggestion: Re-read the entry after the lookup and make the terminal queue transition conditional on its still being in the expected state.
findings.failure_scenario: A user cancels a merging entry while the post-merge GitHub lookup is pending; the aborted lookup returns through catch and the cancelled entry is subsequently marked landed.

findings.title: A failed metadata lookup permanently records an incomplete merge event
findings.detail: If the post-merge lookup fails or returns an observation without merge metadata, landed() immediately marks both runs merged with null fields. findings.suggestion: Make merge metadata recovery durable and ensure the merge feed item reflects the recovered fields without emitting duplicate merge events.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts the merge, but the subsequent PR lookup times out or briefly returns an OPEN snapshot. The parent run's run.merged event contains null mergedBy and mergedAt even after a later observation supplies both values.

findings.title: Cancellation during the new lookup is overwritten as landed
findings.detail: The new post-merge lookup catches every rejection, including an abort from cancel(), and then calls landed() unconditionally. cancel() has already written the cancelled state, but landed() calls finish() without rechecking it, replacing cancellation with landed and emitting a land.landed feed item.
findings.suggestion: After the lookup, recheck the abort signal and current land-entry state before making terminal writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A user cancels an active land while the post-merge PR lookup is pending. The lookup rejects on abort, its rejection is converted to null, and the cancelled entry is changed to landed.

findings.title: MCP approvals still default to reviewer human

Reviewed the merge, MCP review and change-view, and CLI authentication paths. The targeted command passed 62 notifier tests, but the MCP, CLI and land-queue test files could not load because the MCP SDK was unavailable in the sandbox. Found merge recovery, cancellation and change-view accuracy defects.

findings.title: A failed post-merge lookup permanently records an incomplete merge event
findings.detail: If the lookup after a successful merge fails or returns an observation without merge metadata, landed() immediately marks both runs merged with null fields. That transition writes the run.merged feed item. Later reconciliation can fill the run fields from a saved snapshot, but it does not repair the already-written feed item; with polling disabled, it also never fetches missing metadata for an already-merged run. The original incorrect feed information therefore persists after a transient GitHub failure.
findings.suggestion: Preserve a durable pending metadata state and complete the merge record and feed with a confirmed observation, including when polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts the merge, but the subsequent PR lookup times out. The parent run's run.merged feed item retains mergedBy and mergedAt as null even if a later poll supplies both values.

findings.title: A push in progress can be reported as the current head
findings.detail: The final consistency check treats an in-progress push as superseded, but passes the currently recorded SHA to the error formatter. During the push that SHA can still be the old head, so the response labels the head the caller just read as the current head instead of identifying the new one.
findings.suggestion: Only label a SHA as the current head when it is confirmed after the push; otherwise report that the head is changing.
findings.failure_scenario: A push starts while Git reads are in progress, before the new SHA is recorded. The response says the old SHA is the current head and asks the caller to restart.

findings.title: A failed metadata lookup leaves the merge feed permanently incomplete
findings.detail: After a successful merge, a failed or stale GitHub lookup is converted to null and landed() immediately sets merged=true. That transition emits run.merged with null metadata. Later reconciliation only updates the run fields from a saved snapshot; it does not correct the already emitted feed event, and it never fetches missing metadata itself. This leaves the exact feed discrepancy described in the request, even if a later poll supplies the fields.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the merge event receives confirmed metadata, or provide a durable correction path for both the run and its feed event when the lookup is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds but the subsequent gh pr view times out or still reports OPEN. The parent run emits run.merged with null mergedBy and mergedAt; a later merged snapshot cannot repair that event.

findings.title: Cancellation during the new lookup is overwritten by landed
findings.detail: The new awaited lookup catches abort errors and unconditionally calls landed(). If cancel() runs while the lookup is in flight, it aborts the signal and records cancelled, but this continuation changes the entry to landed and emits land.landed. The same unchecked continuation can run after shutdown or a lost claim.
findings.suggestion: After the lookup, recheck the abort signal and condition the terminal update on the entry still being owned and in the expected state.
findings.failure_scenario: A user cancels a merging entry after GitHub confirms the merge while the metadata lookup is still pending; the lookup aborts, then the queue overwrites cancelled with landed.

findings.title: The reported change-view request still does not identify the failing part
findings.detail: The request specifically asks for a useful diagnosis for limitless_get_change with a run and file: 1 after the head moves. This input fails the pagination refinement before the backend checks either the file index or current head, and now reports only that headSha and baseSha are required. It still does not identify an unknown index, report the changed head, or identify an unavailable commit as requested.
findings.suggestion: Handle this unpinned request so its response identifies the applicable change-view failure and includes the current head when it has changed.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling limitless_get_change with {"run":"<run>","file":1} immediately after a conflict round moves the head returns only the pagination-pins message.

structured.summary: Reviewed the merge, MCP review and change-view, and CLI authentication paths. The targeted command passed 62 notifier tests, but the MCP, CLI and land-queue test files could not load because the MCP SDK was unavailable in the sandbox. Found merge recovery, cancellation and change-view accuracy defects.

findings.title: A failed metadata lookup leaves the merge feed permanently incomplete
findings.detail: After a successful merge, a failed or stale GitHub lookup is converted to null and landed() immediately sets merged=true. That transition emits run.merged with null metadata. Later reconciliation only updates the run fields from a saved snapshot; it does not correct the already emitted feed event, and it never fetches missing metadata itself. This leaves the exact feed discrepancy described in the request, even if a later poll supplies the fields.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the merge event receives confirmed metadata, or provide a durable correction path for both the run and its feed event when the lookup is unavailable.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds but the subsequent gh pr view times out or still reports OPEN. The parent run emits run.merged with null mergedBy and mergedAt; a later merged snapshot cannot repair that event.

findings.title: Cancellation during the new lookup is overwritten by landed
findings.detail: The new awaited lookup catches abort errors and unconditionally calls landed(). If cancel() runs while the lookup is in flight, it aborts the signal and records cancelled, but this continuation changes the entry to landed and emits land.landed. The same unchecked continuation can run after shutdown or a lost claim.
findings.suggestion: After the lookup, recheck the abort signal and condition the terminal update on the entry still being owned and in the expected state.
findings.failure_scenario: A user cancels a merging entry after GitHub confirms the merge while the metadata lookup is still pending; the lookup aborts, then the queue overwrites cancelled with landed.

findings.title: The reported change-view request still does not identify the failing part
findings.detail: The request specifically asks for a useful diagnosis for limitless_get_change with a run and file: 1 after the head moves. This input fails the pagination refinement before the backend checks either the file index or current head, and now reports only that headSha and baseSha are required. It still does not identify an unknown index, report the changed head, or identify an unavailable commit as requested.
findings.suggestion: Handle this unpinned request so its response identifies the applicable change-view failure and includes the current head when it has changed.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling limitless_get_change with {"run":"<run>","file":1} immediately after a conflict round moves the head returns only the pagination-pins message.

findings.title: Merge metadata is permanently lost if the follow-up lookup fails or is interrupted
findings.detail: The queue marks both runs merged and the land entry landed before fetching merge metadata. If the daemon restarts during that fetch, or the fetch fails or times out, the landed entry will not resume. Reconciliation only consults an already-saved merged snapshot, while githubTracked excludes merged runs, so an earlier open snapshot will never be refreshed. Both the run fields and their run.merged feed items can therefore remain null indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Make metadata recovery durable after landing, for example by retaining a bounded reconciliation path for merged runs whose metadata is missing.
findings.failure_scenario: A merge succeeds while the saved GitHub snapshot still says OPEN; the daemon restarts after landed() commits but before mergeMetadata() returns. On restart the entry is already landed and the PR is no longer tracked, leaving mergedBy and mergedAt null.

findings.title: Retry metadata collection after an interrupted merge lookup
findings.detail: The queue marks the runs merged before its metadata lookup. If the daemon restarts during that lookup, the lookup fails, or GitHub returns incomplete metadata, reconciliation only examines an existing saved snapshot and never fetches a fresh one. The poller also excludes merged runs from tracking, so an absent or pre-merge snapshot cannot repair the fields later. This leaves the parent and round run.merged fields null indefinitely. The focused command `bun test test/github-notifier.test.ts -t 'merged runs with permanently missing metadata never spend reconciliation requests'` passed with `1 pass` and `0 fail`; that test confirms reconciliation makes no requests for these runs.
findings.suggestion: Persist pending metadata collection or perform a bounded, retryable reconciliation lookup for merged runs whose metadata is missing, including after restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A land succeeds, then the daemon restarts before the subsequent GitHub metadata request completes. The saved PR snapshot still says OPEN, both runs are already marked merged, and neither reconciliation nor polling fetches the merged metadata.

findings.detail: The initial run.merged item is published with null metadata, then its database row is edited in place when the GitHub lookup completes. findings.suggestion: Provide a cursor-visible update when merge metadata arrives, or obtain the metadata before publishing the merge item while retaining a durable recovery path.

findings.title: Review prompts still expose multiline credentials in diffs
findings.detail: The new protection applies only to the MCP change view. Verify-change reviews also place reviewDiff.patch directly into the model prompt, and conflict-resolution reviews use a separately rendered first-parent patch. Their existing credential redaction matches the complete literal, which the diff line prefixes interrupt. The request explicitly requires other diff-rendering outputs to receive the same treatment or be listed as follow-ups; no such follow-up was provided.
findings.suggestion: Apply a shared patch-aware credential filter to these diff renderers, or explicitly identify them as follow-ups as the request permits.

findings.title: Diffs embedded in reports bypass multiline credential filtering
findings.detail:

+beta-secret
```"; console.log(loadOutputPrivacy()?.(report));'` printed both `+alpha-secret` and `+beta-secret` unchanged.

Reviewed patch reconstruction, paging, and other diff output paths. The targeted integration test could not start because the MCP SDK dependency is missing from this checkout; a direct check reproduced the clipped-hunk leak.

findings.title: A clipped credential can expose a changed line
findings.detail:
The clipped-prefix check withholds only context lines, and the adjacent-pair check requires the credential fragment to occupy a whole patch line. If a changed line contains text before the first credential fragment, that line remains visible. A direct probe returned hidden line indexes [3, 4, 5] while leaving `-key=alpha-secret` visible: `bun -e '…privatePatchLines("@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-key=alpha-secret
+public
 beta-secret
 gamma-secret
 delta-secret
", ["alpha-secret
beta-secret
gamma-secret
delta-secret
epsilon-secret"])…'`.
findings.suggestion: Map clipped credential matches back to all affected old-side and new-side patch lines, including additions and deletions, and cover fragments embedded within a line.
findings.failure_scenario: A five-line credential begins after `key=` on a deleted line; the following three credential lines are context and the fifth lies beyond the hunk. The deleted line containing the first credential fragment is returned to the MCP client.

findings.title: Other diff output still persists multiline credentials unredacted
findings.detail: The change only filters the MCP change-view patch. The pipeline still stores `diff.patch` directly from the raw Git diff, where line prefixes prevent literal credential redaction from matching a multiline value. This leaves registered credential fragments in persisted output, and the request explicitly requires other diff renderings to receive the same treatment or be identified as follow-ups.
findings.suggestion: Apply a shared patch-aware credential filter at the persisted diff output boundary and other diff-rendering boundaries, or explicitly identify the remaining outputs as follow-ups as requested.
findings.failure_scenario: A changed file contains a registered two-line credential. During audit, the raw patch containing both prefixed credential lines is stored as the run's `diff.patch` artifact.

findings.title: A single middle line of a multiline credential remains visible at a hunk edge
findings.detail:
The clipped-hunk handling protects credential prefixes, suffixes, and pairs of middle lines, but not an isolated middle line. A direct check returned `hidden lines: []` for a patch ending in ` middle-secret` with the registered credential `first-secret
middle-secret
last-secret`. The command was `bun -e 'import { readFileSync } from "node:fs"; import { normalizedLayers } from "./src/gates/private.ts"; const source = readFileSync("src/integrations/mcp-change.ts", "utf8"); const fn = source.slice(source.indexOf("function privatePatchLines"), source.indexOf("
function catalogueKey")); const build = new Function("normalizedLayers", `${new Bun.Transpiler({loader:"ts"}).transformSync(fn)}; return privatePatchLines`); const scan = build(normalizedLayers); const patch = "@@ -1,4 +1,4 @@
-old
+new
 public1
 public2
 middle-secret
"; console.log("hidden lines:", [...scan(patch, ["first-secret
middle-secret
last-secret"])]);'`.
findings.suggestion: Protect isolated credential lines exposed as clipped context, and add a regression test for a hunk containing only a middle line.
findings.failure_scenario: A change three lines before the middle of a multiline key causes Git to include only that key line as trailing context; the change view returns it unredacted.

findings.title: Conflict review prompts still contain unredacted multiline credentials in diffs
findings.detail: The new protection is local to the change view. The conflict-resolution review path still passes a line-prefixed first-parent diff through literal credential redaction before embedding it in the model prompt. A multiline credential split by diff prefixes therefore survives. The request requires other diff-rendering outputs to receive the same treatment or be listed as follow-ups, and no follow-up was supplied.
findings.suggestion: Apply shared patch-aware redaction to this diff before it is sent to the model, or explicitly record this output as a follow-up as requested.
findings.failure_scenario: A conflict-resolution diff includes two added lines comprising a registered multiline credential; both lines are sent in the review prompt.

findings.suggestion: Map matches on each reconstructed file side back to the affected patch lines and withhold those lines while retaining unrelated patch content.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file contains public lines before and after a registered two-line credential. The change view returns only `[withheld: private text; 1 file]`, so neither public line is visible.

findings.suggestion: Apply line-prefixed diff redaction to report quotations before paging, or explicitly identify this output as a follow-up as permitted by the request.

findings.suggestion: Map each match to its contributing old-side and new-side patch lines and withhold those lines before paging, retaining unrelated patch lines.

Reviewed retry selection, JUnit parsing, slot handling, configuration provenance, and classification. The focused retry-file tests passed. The executor and feedback tests could not load because the installed dependencies lack zod's overwrite method and the MCP SDK client module.

findings.title: A security check can be classified as flaky after a passing retry
findings.detail: Retry classification treats every check alike. A failing security check followed by a passing full retry becomes non-blocking `flaky`, contrary to the explicit requirement that a security-check failure never become a pass. A focused `bun -e` call to `retryRegressions` with a failed check named `security` and a passing fake retry returned `"verdict":"flaky","blocking":false`.
findings.suggestion: Represent security checks explicitly and preserve a blocking failure across retries, including baseline handling. Add a fake-runner test for this case.
findings.failure_scenario: A security scan reports a vulnerability on the first post-change run but passes on retry; the gate becomes non-blocking.

findings.title: Bun treats targeted file arguments as substring filters
findings.detail: `bun test {files}` does not restrict execution to the listed paths: Bun also runs test files whose paths contain an argument. A focused fixture run with `bun test a.test.ts` ran both `a.test.ts` and `a.test.ts.extra.test.ts`. Thus an unrelated failing file can make a targeted retry appear to confirm the original failure, and additional matched files can bypass the file-count and duration bounds used to skip the gate slot.
findings.suggestion: Use an invocation that selects exact paths, and verify its behavior with overlapping test-file names before allowing a retry to bypass the slot.
findings.failure_scenario: The original failed file `a.test.ts` passes alone, but `a.test.ts.extra.test.ts` matches the same Bun filter and fails intermittently; the retry is classified as a confirmed regression without the required full check.

findings.title: A security check can still become a nonblocking flaky result
findings.detail: Retry classification has no distinction for security checks: any regressed check whose full retry passes becomes flaky and nonblocking. This leaves the request's explicit security-check requirement unmet, including when a targeted retry passes first.
findings.suggestion: Represent security checks in trusted gate configuration and preserve a blocking failure when any attempt of such a check fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A security check passes on the baseline, fails after the change, and passes its retry. The comparison is marked flaky with blocking false.

findings.title: Failures naming a changed file never receive the targeted retry
findings.detail: The existing pointsAt exclusion runs before the new targeted-retry selection. Consequently, a structured test failure that names a changed test file is returned immediately without the requested confirmation, even though its failing files are known. Test output commonly includes a file and line number, so this is not limited to malformed reports.
findings.suggestion: Allow known structured failing files through to targeted confirmation, while preserving any intended exclusion for checks without structured file information.
findings.failure_scenario: A changed test file fails and the output includes test/example.test.ts:12; the JUnit report identifies that file, but retryRegressions skips it and runs no targeted retry.

findings.title: A security check can be classified as flaky after a retry
findings.detail: The retry verdict treats every passing full retry as nonblocking, with no distinction for security checks. This leaves the request’s explicit requirement that a security-check failure never become a pass unimplemented.
findings.suggestion: Identify security checks in trusted gate configuration and retain a blocking failure when one fails, regardless of retry results.
findings.failure_scenario: A security check passes on the baseline, fails after the change, and passes on its full retry. The comparison becomes flaky and nonblocking, allowing the failed security check through.

findings.title: Raw JUnit filenames can be persisted in the baseline cache
findings.detail: JUnit filenames and timing-map keys are added to gate results without redaction. During preparation, a passing retry can make the baseline cacheable, and the engine writes that result to the cache before calling redactGateData on the baseline. A registered credential included in a reported filename is therefore stored unredacted in the cache, including through firstAttempt or targetedRetry.
findings.suggestion: Redact gate data before every cache write, while retaining any raw filenames needed for the immediate retry only in memory.
findings.failure_scenario: A baseline test fails in a file whose path contains a registered credential, then the full retry passes. The cacheable baseline includes the first attempt’s raw failedFiles and failedFileTimes keys and is stored before sanitization.

findings.title: A passing retry makes a failed security check nonblocking
findings.detail: The retry verdict has no security-check distinction: any failed check becomes flaky and nonblocking when its full retry passes. This misses the request's explicit requirement that a security check's failure never become a pass. A focused reproduction using retryRegressions with a failed check named security and a passing retry returned {"verdict":"flaky","blocking":false}.
findings.suggestion: Represent security checks explicitly in trusted gate configuration and preserve a blocking failure when any attempt fails; cover both targeted and full retries.
findings.failure_scenario: A security scan finds a vulnerability on its first run but passes on retry; the pipeline records it as flaky and allows the run to proceed.

findings.title: Bun's JUnit report can omit failed files
findings.detail: Bun omits a file that throws while loading from its JUnit report when another file contains a normal failing test. The parser accepts the remaining file list as complete, so the targeted retry can fail and terminate confirmation without rerunning the omitted file. A focused run with a.test.ts containing a failing assertion and b.test.ts throwing at module load reported two failed tests on the console, but report.xml contained only the a.test.ts suite. This violates the explicit fallback requirement when failing files cannot be determined.
findings.suggestion: Use a structured source that accounts for Bun's load errors, or detect that the report cannot account for the process failure and fall back to the full retry.
findings.failure_scenario: One test file fails an assertion while another fails to import; the report names only the assertion failure, and a failing targeted retry prevents a full check from confirming the complete failure.

Reviewed the pairing and heartbeat split, its TLS handling, persistence, and sandbox integration. The targeted tests could not start: `bun test test/workers.test.ts test/config-routing.test.ts` reported a missing `@simplewebauthn/server` module and an incompatible Zod installation (`z.number().overwrite is not a function`).

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the code shown to the worker comes from that unauthenticated connection. A network attacker can submit a separate pairing request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the real request's claim secret. The owner sees the same code and approves it, after which the attacker can claim the worker token. Pinning the certificate observed on the first connection does not prevent this substitution.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-confirmed pairing code to both sides' identities and the coordinator certificate, so a relayed request with a substituted certificate cannot produce the same confirmation.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts a worker's first connection on the LAN, creates their own pending request at the coordinator, and relays its pairing code. The owner approves that code and the attacker obtains the approved token.

findings.title: Interrupted first certificate generation prevents subsequent daemon starts
findings.detail: Certificate generation publishes an empty key file before awaiting OpenSSL. If the daemon is restarted or OpenSSL fails before both files are complete, the next start either throws `Incomplete worker TLS material` or attempts to load incomplete material. Because the worker listener starts before the owner API and integrations, the configured daemon cannot start again without manual file repair.
findings.suggestion: Generate and validate both files under temporary names, publish them only after success, and recover safely from interrupted generation.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon during its first worker TLS certificate generation, leaving key.pem without a complete cert.pem; every subsequent daemon start fails.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The first connection accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is generated by the coordinator independently of the certificate. A network intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged while reading the pairing secret, then claim the approved token itself. Comparing the codes therefore does not establish that the worker pinned the intended coordinator.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and the pairing exchange, so an intermediary cannot relay a matching code while terminating TLS.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker on the worker's network terminates the initial TLS connection, forwards the pair request to the real coordinator, relays its code to the worker, and uses the observed pairing secret to claim the token after owner approval.

findings.title: Persisted TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The key's read-deny registration exists only while `certificate()` is held by an active listener. If the owner disables the listener after using it, the key remains on disk but daemon startup skips registration. Agent sandbox policies built by that daemon can then omit the key from their private-file deny list. The same process-local registration cannot protect worker credentials from agents launched by a separate daemon process.
findings.suggestion: Register the persisted worker key and worker credential paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, regardless of listener or worker-loop state.
findings.failure_scenario: The listener is enabled once, then disabled in configuration and the daemon restarts. A tool-enabled reader runs with access to the data directory and reads the still-present worker TLS private key.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation can prevent every subsequent daemon start
findings.detail: Certificate generation publishes an empty key file before invoking OpenSSL. A crash, restart, or failed OpenSSL invocation can leave that file without a certificate, or leave incomplete material. Subsequent starts reject the incomplete pair and never regenerate it, so enabling the worker listener can prevent the daemon from starting until manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths, validate them, and publish the completed pair atomically or recover safely from incomplete generation.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is restarted after creating `key.pem` but before OpenSSL writes `cert.pem`. Each subsequent start with `workers.listen` configured fails with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

Reviewed the pairing and heartbeat implementation as the first permitted split of the request. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout's dependencies were unavailable or incompatible: @simplewebauthn/server was missing and the resolved Zod lacked number().overwrite.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The first request accepts any certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An active network attacker can relay the pairing request and its returned code to the real coordinator while recording the pairing secret. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it, after which the attacker can claim the worker token. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is stored but never used to authenticate the claim.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator identity and worker identity, and ensure the claim secret cannot be learned by an intermediary on the unauthenticated connection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts a worker's first connection, proxies the pairing exchange, and claims the approved token using the observed secret.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation prevents subsequent daemon starts
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If the process stops or OpenSSL fails before both files are complete, the next startup sees incomplete material and throws; if both files exist but are incomplete, parsing or TLS startup can fail instead. No recovery removes the partial files, so enabling the worker listener can leave the daemon unable to start until an operator repairs the directory.
findings.suggestion: Generate the key and certificate in temporary paths, validate them, and publish them only after successful completion; clean up incomplete generation on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is restarted during its first OpenSSL certificate generation, leaving key.pem without a complete cert.pem; every later daemon startup fails.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not protected in other daemon processes
findings.detail: protectPrivateFile registers paths only in the current process. Pairing releases those registrations before exiting, and runWorker registers them only in the worker CLI process. A separate Limitless daemon on that machine therefore does not include the worker token or fingerprint in its agent sandbox deny lists. Likewise, a coordinator daemon started with the listener disabled does not register an existing TLS key. These files can consequently be read by tool-enabled agents running under that daemon; mode 0600 does not protect against agents running as the same user. The real-Seatbelt test masks this by registering all files in the same process that launches the gates.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential and TLS key paths in every daemon before it starts agents, regardless of whether the worker CLI or listener is active, and test using separate processes and an existing credential.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is paired as a worker and also runs a Limitless daemon. After the pairing command exits, an agent launched by that daemon reads the worker token from the data directory and can authenticate as the worker.

Reviewed the permitted pairing and heartbeat split, including TLS setup, approval, revocation, and restart behavior. Targeted tests could not run because the checkout has missing or incompatible dependencies: @simplewebauthn/server is unavailable and the installed Zod lacks number().overwrite().

findings.title: Heartbeat data can persist a worker token in plaintext
findings.detail: Authenticated heartbeat fields are written to SQLite without credential redaction. In particular, `osVersion` accepts a 64-character string, so a worker can send its bearer token there and cause it to be stored in `capabilities`, despite the pairing design storing only the token hash. Sanitizing the owner API response later does not remove the stored secret.
findings.suggestion: Redact credential-bearing heartbeat data before persistence while retaining a valid, usable capabilities record.
findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a valid heartbeat with its token as `osVersion`; the coordinator stores that token in plaintext in the workers table.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation leaves the listener unable to start
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key file before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails or the process stops before the certificate is written, the next startup sees incomplete TLS material and refuses to start the daemon. The partial material is never cleaned up automatically.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names and publish them only after successful generation, or safely recover incomplete first-start material.
findings.failure_scenario: OpenSSL fails or the daemon is interrupted during initial certificate generation; subsequent daemon starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

findings.title: Certificate replacement cannot be followed by pairing again under the same name
findings.detail: The guide tells operators to pair again after changing the coordinator certificate, but an existing approved worker name is always rejected. Replacing the coordinator key also changes the derived token, so the existing pairing cannot simply continue.
findings.suggestion: Document the required revocation before re-pairing, or provide an explicit safe re-pairing path.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate is replaced and an existing worker runs `worker pair` with its normal name; the request is rejected as already paired.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents subsequent daemon starts
findings.detail: Certificate generation writes directly to the final key and certificate paths. If OpenSSL fails or the process is interrupted after creating one file, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or attempts to parse incomplete material. Since the worker listener starts before the owner API and integrations, this prevents the daemon from starting until an operator removes or repairs the files.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names, validate them, and publish them only after generation succeeds; clean up incomplete temporary material on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The first start with workers.listen configured is interrupted after key.pem is created but before cert.pem is complete. Every subsequent daemon start fails during certificate initialization.

findings.title: A changed coordinator certificate leaves the worker retrying silently
findings.detail: The heartbeat loop catches all request errors, including a pinned fingerprint mismatch, and retries indefinitely without reporting the cause. After coordinator certificate replacement, the documented recovery is to pair again, but the worker gives no indication that its pin has changed.
findings.suggestion: Surface fingerprint mismatch as a terminal, actionable error while retaining retries for transient connection failures.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator's TLS certificate is replaced and an existing worker reconnects. Every heartbeat fails the pin check, but the worker remains running and silently retries instead of telling the owner to pair again.

findings.title: Restart discards leased retry jobs instead of reattaching
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A durable LAN job for a timeout rerun or targeted/full retry is cancelled on resume and replaced with a new job, even if the original worker is still running it or has completed it. This violates the requested restart behavior and repeats gate work during ordinary daemon restarts.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to reattach the matching LAN handle for every gate purpose, and add a restart test covering a retry job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a worker is executing a `baseline-retry` or `timeout` job. On resume, `stored` is undefined, so the existing job is cancelled and another job is enqueued.

findings.title: A failed check can become a clean pass after an infrastructure retry
findings.detail: Check events from the first worker are persisted, but when its lease fails the eventual result is returned without considering those events. If a worker reports a failed check and disconnects before posting its final result, a passing retry or local fallback becomes the clean GateRun. This loses the observed failure and violates the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve failed check evidence across attempts and incorporate it into the final result using the existing flaky-result semantics.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing test event, loses its connection before submitting the GateRun, and a second worker passes the same test; the coordinator returns only the passing result.

findings.title: Restart discards durable jobs for retry purposes
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. LAN jobs for baseline retries, regression retries, and timeout reruns are checkpointed in the same way, but a restart treats their handles as stale, cancels them, and enqueues new work. Daily daemon restarts can therefore repeat gate commands and lose already completed work instead of reattaching as requested.
findings.suggestion: Provide a durable resume path for every LAN gate purpose, preserving the request and setup needed to reattach safely.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a worker is executing a baseline-retry job; the resumed run cancels that job and starts another execution.

findings.title: Persisted LAN handles cannot resume after rollback
findings.detail: The change stores a `lan` execution handle in run state, but the previous release only constructs a local executor and rejects any stored handle of another kind. Rolling back after a LAN job has been checkpointed makes the older daemon fail that run with `Unavailable gate executor: lan`, even if the configuration is restored to local.
findings.suggestion: Use a checkpoint representation and rollback path that the previous release can resume, or ship the necessary compatibility handling in an earlier release.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy starts a LAN gate job, then rolls back while the job is pending; the previous daemon resumes the run and fails on its stored LAN handle.

findings.title: Infrastructure retry can turn a reported failing check into a pass
findings.detail: A worker can post a failing check event and then lose its lease before posting the final result. The failure transition retains that event only as diagnostic history; the next worker's passing result becomes the job result without preserving the earlier failure. The pipeline therefore treats the check as a clean pass, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Carry validated check failures across infrastructure attempts and ensure a later pass cannot erase them from the gate verdict.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts a failed test check and disconnects before posting its GateRun. Worker B runs the same flaky test successfully and posts a passing GateRun; the job completes with the passing result.

findings.title: Persisted LAN handles cannot resume after rollback
findings.detail: A run can persist a LAN execution handle before a deploy rolls back to the previous release. Resetting the configuration to local, as the guide instructs, lets the previous release start, but its executor cannot attach a stored LAN handle and fails the resumed run. Daily deploy restarts make this a realistic version-skew window.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible resume path for persisted LAN work, such as a representation the previous release can safely rerun locally, and test rollback while a LAN job is outstanding.
findings.failure_scenario: A run checkpoints a `lan` handle while waiting for a worker; the deploy is rolled back and `[gates] executor` is reset to `local`. The old release resumes the run and rejects the stored handle as an unavailable executor.

findings.title: Allow the Bun executable that verifier commands actually resolve
findings.detail: The read exception is built from the daemon's process.execPath, but a verifier normally invokes `bun` through its shell PATH. Those can point to different installations. In that case the PATH-resolved Bun remains under the private-root read deny, so the original test failure persists. The live smoke check also uses process.execPath directly for both its launcher and test command, so it can pass without exercising the affected executable.
findings.suggestion: Resolve and validate the Bun executable available to the verifier's shell, and have the live probe execute `bun test` through that same command path.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts using one Bun installation while the verifier's PATH selects another Bun executable under the home directory; the smoke probe passes using the daemon executable, but the verifier's `bun test` remains denied or hangs.

findings.title: Allow the Bun executable that verifier commands actually resolve
findings.detail: The allowance is derived from the daemon's process.execPath, but verifier shell commands resolve `bun` through their own PATH. Those can refer to different installations. In that case the actual Bun executable remains under a denied private root and the reported verifier hang remains. The new smoke check also invokes process.execPath explicitly, so it can pass without detecting this mismatch.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the Bun executable using the verifier's effective shell PATH and grant its canonical path, with the same credential-overlap checks. Make the live probe execute `bun test` through that PATH.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts with one Bun installation, while its inherited or shell-adjusted PATH selects a different Bun under the user's home directory. A verifier runs `bun test`; only the daemon's executable is allowed through the read deny.

findings.title: Bun allowance is not applied to actual verifier invocations
findings.detail: The new allowance is conditional on `spec.confineReads`, but the production `verify` invocation in `src/pipeline/engine.ts` does not set that option. Consequently, this change does not alter the filesystem settings for the verification stages named in the request. The new smoke check sets `confineReads: true`, so it exercises a different configuration and can pass while the reported verifier hang remains. The only pipeline invocation that explicitly sets `confineReads` is the holdout author.
findings.suggestion: Reproduce and fix the configuration used by the production verifier, and make the smoke check exercise that same configuration and command path.
findings.failure_scenario: A verification stage needs to run `bun test` itself: its readonly invocation omits `confineReads`, so the new Bun read allowance is absent and the original sandbox behavior remains.

findings.title: Allow the Bun executable that verifier commands resolve
findings.detail: The read exception covers only the daemon's process.execPath. A verifier normally runs `bun test` through its shell PATH, which can resolve a different Bun installation under a denied private root. That executable remains unreadable, so the reported hang or failure persists. The smoke probe also uses process.execPath explicitly, so it can pass while the verifier's ordinary command fails.
findings.suggestion: Resolve and validate the Bun executable available to the verifier's shell, grant the necessary narrowly scoped read access, and exercise `bun test` through that same PATH in the smoke check.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts with one Bun binary, while its shell PATH selects another Bun binary under the user's home directory; the smoke probe passes using the first binary, but a verifier running `bun test` cannot read the second.

Traced PR body, round comment, and squash publication paths and probed the sanitizer directly. The targeted test could not run because the checkout lacks the entities dependency.

Reviewed the publication rewrite and delivery callers. Targeted tests could not start because the checkout lacks the entities dependency; an independent probe reproduced the rewrite failures below.

findings.title: Absolute paths in link labels bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes the entire Markdown link, but only its destination is inspected. When the destination is relative or external, the original link is returned unchanged, including any absolute worktree or data-directory path in its visible label. A direct sanitizer probe returned `[/factory/data/work/run/foo.ts](docs/foo.md)` unchanged. This can publish the owner's local path or cause the private-strings check to block delivery.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path text in link labels independently of the destination while preserving ordinary links.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[/factory/data/work/run/foo.ts](docs/foo.md)`; the absolute path remains in the published text.

findings.title: File URL links retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: The sanitizer does not recognize `file://` destinations as local paths, and the bare-path alternative cannot start after the URL's slash. A direct sanitizer probe returned `file:///factory/data/work/run/foo.ts` unchanged. Markdown links using the same URL are likewise returned unchanged. These links disclose the local path or block delivery when the username is listed as private.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URLs and convert their decoded worktree or data-directory paths using the same boundary checks.
findings.failure_scenario: A report links to `file:///factory/data/work/run/foo.ts`; the published text retains the absolute path.

findings.title: Absolute paths inside Markdown link labels bypass sanitization
findings.detail: The matcher consumes an entire Markdown link and checks only its destination. If the destination is relative or remote, it returns the link unchanged even when its visible label contains a worktree or data-directory path. This can publish the owner's username, or block delivery once the username is added to private strings. An independent probe returned `[see /factory/data/work/run/a.ts](docs/a.md)` unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize path occurrences in link labels as well as destinations, while preserving ordinary link destinations.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains `[see /Users/name/.limitless/work/run/test/a.ts](docs/a.md)`; the absolute path remains in the published body or fails the private-text check.

findings.title: File URL destinations retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: A Markdown destination beginning with `file://` is matched as a link, but rewrite only recognizes destinations that start directly with a configured root. The entire local URL is therefore returned unchanged. An independent probe returned `[x](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Recognize local file URLs, convert their paths to repository-relative destinations or data placeholders, and handle URL encoding before checking the root.
findings.failure_scenario: A report includes `[source](file:///Users/name/.limitless/work/run/src/a.ts)`; publication exposes the local path or is blocked by the private-string check.

findings.title: Line-number links are rewritten to nonexistent filenames
findings.detail: The rewrite treats a `:line` suffix as part of the filename. A link such as `[x](/factory/data/work/run/a.ts:12)` becomes `[a.ts:12](a.ts:12)`, which points GitHub at a file named `a.ts:12` rather than the source file. This is a common report-link format and leaves the original broken-link problem unresolved.
findings.suggestion: Parse location suffixes separately and convert line numbers to GitHub line anchors when producing the repository-relative destination.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer reports `[a.ts](/Users/name/.limitless/work/run/a.ts:12)`; the PR links to `a.ts:12`, which does not exist.
