output.summary:
Reviewed the publication sanitizer and its delivery and land-queue call sites. The targeted test command could not start because the checkout lacks the entities dependency; isolated sanitizer inputs exposed privacy and rendering defects.

Reviewed the publication sanitizer and its delivery and land-queue call sites. The targeted publication test could not run because the checkout lacks the entities package; direct checks of the sanitizer exposed path-handling defects.

findings.title: Local paths inside other Markdown links and file URLs escape sanitization
findings.detail: The link alternative consumes an entire Markdown link and returns it unchanged when its destination is relative, even if its label contains an absolute worktree path. File URLs also escape: their destination does not start with a configured root, and the bare-path matcher rejects the preceding slash. These forms can publish the owner's local path; once the username is in private-strings.txt, they instead block delivery.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize local paths in link labels as well as destinations, and recognize local file URLs without rewriting ordinary remote URLs.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, the sanitizer leaves both `[/factory/data/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` and `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/a.ts)` unchanged. An isolated Bun invocation of the function produced those exact outputs.

findings.title: Data directory placeholder is emitted as an HTML tag
findings.detail: The replacement inserts literal `<data>` into published Markdown. GitHub interprets that sequence as an HTML tag, so readers do not see the requested plain-text placeholder and the displayed path loses its directory prefix. The tests check the raw body rather than its rendered form.
findings.suggestion: Escape the placeholder for Markdown, for example as `<data>`, while retaining the intended visible text.
findings.failure_scenario: A report containing a link to `/factory/data/runs/log.txt` is published as `<data>/runs/log.txt`; GitHub renders the tag as HTML rather than displaying `<data>` as text.

findings.title: Markdown links can retain absolute local paths
findings.detail: The link matcher consumes the whole link but only checks its destination. An absolute path in the link label is left untouched when the destination is relative. A file:// destination is also left untouched because it does not start with a configured root. Either form can publish the owner's username and data layout, or block delivery after the username is added to private-strings.txt.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize local paths in link labels as well as destinations, and recognize local file URLs before deciding whether a link points into a configured root.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run, both `[/factory/data/work/run/src/a.ts](src/a.ts)` and `[file](file:///factory/data/work/run/src/a.ts)` are returned unchanged.

findings.title: Dot segments let paths outside the worktree become repo-relative
findings.detail: Containment is decided by a lexical prefix without resolving dot segments. A path that starts with the worktree but traverses out of it is consequently published as a repo-relative path instead of using the required data-directory placeholder.
findings.suggestion: Normalize local path components before determining which configured root contains the target.
findings.failure_scenario: With worktree /factory/data/work/run and data directory /factory/data, `/factory/data/work/run/../other/secret.txt` becomes `../other/secret.txt` instead of `<data>/work/other/secret.txt`.

findings.title: Round delivery rewrites previously published PR body text
findings.detail: The sanitizer is applied to the existing PR body together with the new round section. When that body contains an old local path, appending a round silently rewrites previously published text, although rewriting already published PR bodies is explicitly out of scope.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize the new round section before appending it, without modifying the existing body.
findings.failure_scenario: A review round is delivered to a PR whose existing body contains a path under the current run's worktree or data directory; the subsequent PR edit changes that existing text as well as adding the round.

findings.title: Merge helper can issue a merge after ownership changes
findings.detail: The ownership check precedes the call to mergePullRequest, but that helper awaits a GitHub PR lookup before issuing `gh pr merge`, and may await further lookups and retries. A reclaim during one of those awaits is invisible until the heartbeat aborts, so the old worker can still issue the merge command. Checking again after the helper returns is too late.
findings.suggestion: Pass a claim-validity guard into the merge helper and check it immediately before each merge command, including retries.
findings.failure_scenario: The worker starts the helper, its PR view is deferred, another owner reclaims the entry, and the view returns before the next heartbeat; the old worker issues `gh pr merge`.

findings.title: Push helper can push after ownership changes
findings.detail: The transaction checks ownership before entering pushExistingBranch, but that helper awaits commit resolution, transport setup, remote inspection and ancestry checking before launching the push. A claim can be reclaimed during those waits and the old worker will still push before its next heartbeat.
findings.suggestion: Check claim ownership inside the push helper immediately before launching the push.
findings.failure_scenario: After the ownership transaction, the remote lookup inside pushExistingBranch is delayed; another worker reclaims the entry, then the lookup completes and the old worker pushes the merge commit.

findings.title: Lost worker can delete the new owner's checkout
findings.detail: The unconditional finally block discards a checkout whose path is shared by all attempts for the entry. After a reclaim, the new owner can replace that checkout, then the old worker's cleanup removes the new owner's worktree and files. The new ownership checks cause the old worker to exit through this cleanup when it detects a lost claim.
findings.suggestion: Give each claim its own checkout and cleanup path, or otherwise ensure cleanup cannot remove a newer owner's checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: A CI response is delayed, the entry is reclaimed and the new worker creates `land-<id>`, then the old response returns and its finally block removes that worktree while the new worker is using it.

findings.title: A worker that loses its claim can delete the new owner's checkout
findings.detail: The new ownership checks throw when a delayed operation returns after a reclaim, but the unconditional finally block still calls discard. Both attempts use the same worktree path derived solely from the entry ID, so this cleanup can remove the replacement worker's checkout while it is checking or preparing a merge. The replacement can then fail and block an otherwise valid land. This also leaves the request's requirement that a worker that lost its claim writes nothing unmet.
findings.suggestion: Give attempts independently owned worktree paths, or coordinate cleanup so an old attempt cannot remove a checkout belonging to a newer claim. Cover a reclaim while the old worker is awaiting an operation and the replacement has already created its checkout.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A awaits CI, its claim is reclaimed by worker B, and B recreates `land-<entry id>`. A's CI response arrives before its heartbeat; assertClaim throws and A's finally block removes B's worktree.

findings.title: PR numbers cannot select an unowned pull request

findings.suggestion: Resolve supported PR references to a configured repository and canonical PR URL, with a clear error when the reference is ambiguous.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator runs `limitless land 599 --sha <full-head-sha>` for a hand-opened PR; the command returns `run not found` instead of queueing it.

findings.title: Rollback permanently blocks active unowned lands
findings.detail: An unowned entry is persisted with an empty run ID. The previous release's land worker claims active entries and requires `getRun(entry.runId)` to succeed, so after a rollback it marks such an entry blocked as `run  is gone`. Returning to the new release does not resume the now-terminal entry. This breaks compatibility during the daily restart and rollback window.
findings.suggestion: Represent or schedule unowned entries so the previous release cannot claim and terminally block them, while retaining a resume path after upgrade.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy is rolled back while a hand-opened PR is queued or waiting for CI; the older daemon claims it and permanently blocks the land.

findings.title: Runless land entries are not shown in the UI
findings.detail: The change publishes feed records and exposes the queue API, but adds no UI consumer for land entries or feed items. The dashboard renders runs, and a runless land has no run to appear there. The request explicitly requires the UI to show these entries.
findings.suggestion: Add a UI view or existing-view integration that displays runless land entries and their state.
findings.failure_scenario: A user queues a hand-opened PR and opens the UI to monitor it; no entry or status for that land is displayed.

findings.title: Rollback blocks active runless land entries
findings.detail: Runless entries are persisted with an empty run ID. After a rollback, the previous release reads that value as a run ID, fails to find the run, and permanently marks the active entry blocked. This breaks the requested compatibility with the previous release and loses the automatic continuation of an interrupted land.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible representation and processing strategy for active runless entries.
findings.failure_scenario: A runless land is queued or waiting for CI when a deployment rolls back; the previous daemon resumes it and blocks it with 'run  is gone'.

findings.title: Bare PR numbers cannot request an unowned land
findings.detail: The new path accepts only a full GitHub URL, although the CLI accepts a PR number and the request specifies `limitless land <pr> --sha <full sha>`. A bare number is looked up only among factory runs and then rejected as 'run not found'.
findings.suggestion: Resolve a bare PR reference against the configured repository context, with a clear error if it is ambiguous.
findings.failure_scenario: Running `limitless land 599 --sha <current-head>` for a hand-opened PR returns 'run not found' instead of queuing it.

findings.title: Fork pull requests are rejected
findings.detail: The request accepts open PRs on configured GitHub repositories without excluding fork PRs, but this unconditional check rejects every cross-repository PR. Such PRs are a normal type of hand-opened contribution.
findings.suggestion: Support fork heads with the same pinned-head and confined-check guarantees, or obtain an explicit scope change.
findings.failure_scenario: An open PR targets a configured repository from a contributor's fork; a request with its exact current SHA fails with 'cross-repository pull requests cannot be landed'.

findings.title: Runless entries have no UI representation
findings.detail: The change creates entries with no owning run, but adds no UI for listing or viewing them. The existing UI associates land activity with run detail, so a runless land cannot appear there. This leaves the explicit UI requirement unmet.
findings.suggestion: Expose runless queue entries and their state in the UI, including a way to identify their PR and lack of an owning run.
findings.failure_scenario: A user queues a hand-opened PR and opens the UI to monitor it; there is no run page or land queue view showing that entry.

Reviewed cleanup persistence, recovery, startup and resume paths. The targeted cleanup test command passed 8 cases; 3 integration cases could not run because the checkout could not resolve @modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js.

findings.title: Recovery drops descendants that were not recorded before the crash
findings.detail: Recovery kills only the persisted members and then deletes the invocation's records. During live cleanup, a marked process can fork after the discovery snapshot but before it is frozen; the normal cleanup loop relies on a subsequent scan to discover that child. If the daemon crashes after the freeze and before that scan, the new descendant has no record. Recovery kills the recorded parent, clears the records, and allows the next invocation to run while the unrecorded descendant can still write to the checkout.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation ownership information to resume discovery as well as killing recorded members, and retain the cleanup record until a recovery sweep confirms that no marked descendants remain.
findings.failure_scenario: A tool-enabled invocation forks a detached child between markedProcesses returning and its parent's SIGSTOP. The daemon dies before the next scan. On restart, recovery kills the recorded parent and clears the cleanup, leaving the child running in the checkout.

findings.title: Recovery cannot find descendants omitted from the recorded snapshot
findings.detail: Recovery kills only PIDs already written to process_cleanups and then deletes the invocation's records. The live sweep explicitly rescans after freezing because a process can fork between inspection and the freeze. If the daemon dies before that rescan, the new descendant has no record and recovery neither discovers it nor blocks the checkout. A crash before the first record is written leaves no indication of cleanup at all. The resumed run can therefore start while an old descendant continues writing to its checkout.
findings.suggestion: Persist an invocation-level pending record before cleanup begins, retain enough ownership information to repeat discovery after restart, and clear it only after the complete marked set has been confirmed gone.
findings.failure_scenario: A marked process forks after the first scan, is frozen, and the daemon dies before the next scan. Recovery kills the recorded parent, clears the record, and starts the next command while the unrecorded child remains running.

findings.title: Rollback resumes runs without honoring pending cleanup records
findings.detail: The new table is additive, but the previous release has no recovery or checkout guard. If deployment rolls back after the new daemon crashes during cleanup, the older daemon ignores the persisted rows and can resume the run while its recorded descendants remain alive or stopped. This violates the repository's requirement that the previous release remain safe after rollback.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible mechanism that prevents the older release from resuming an unresolved checkout, or stage the compatibility guard in an earlier release.
findings.failure_scenario: The new daemon records and freezes a descendant, crashes, and deployment rolls back. The previous daemon resumes the run without reading process_cleanups.

findings.title: Linux birth identities can match an unrelated process after reboot
findings.detail: On Linux the stored birth value is the process start tick relative to boot, with no boot identifier. After a host reboot, an unrelated process can receive the same PID and start tick as a pending record; recovery will treat it as the original member and send SIGKILL.
findings.suggestion: Include the Linux boot identity in the persisted birth identity and treat a different boot as proof that the original process is gone.
findings.failure_scenario: A cleanup record survives a reboot, and a new process has both the recorded PID and the same boot-relative start tick. Daemon startup kills that unrelated process.

findings.title: Recovery cannot find descendants omitted from the recorded snapshot
findings.detail: Recovery kills only PIDs already written to process_cleanups and then deletes the invocation's records. The live sweep explicitly rescans after freezing because a process can fork between inspection and the freeze. If the daemon dies before that rescan, the new descendant has no record and recovery neither discovers it nor blocks the checkout. A crash before the first record is written leaves no indication of cleanup at all. The resumed run can therefore start while an old descendant continues writing to its checkout.
findings.suggestion: Persist an invocation-level pending record before cleanup begins, retain enough ownership information to repeat discovery after restart, and clear it only after the complete marked set has been confirmed gone.
findings.failure_scenario: A marked process forks after the first scan, is frozen, and the daemon dies before the next scan. Recovery kills the recorded parent, clears the record, and starts the next command while the unrecorded child remains running.

findings.title: Rollback resumes runs without honoring pending cleanup records
findings.detail: The new table is additive, but the previous release has no recovery or checkout guard. If deployment rolls back after the new daemon crashes during cleanup, the older daemon ignores the persisted rows and can resume the run while its recorded descendants remain alive or stopped. This violates the repository's requirement that the previous release remain safe after rollback.
findings.suggestion: Provide a rollback-compatible mechanism that prevents the older release from resuming an unresolved checkout, or stage the compatibility guard in an earlier release.
findings.failure_scenario: The new daemon records and freezes a descendant, crashes, and deployment rolls back. The previous daemon resumes the run without reading process_cleanups.

findings.title: Linux birth identities can match an unrelated process after reboot
findings.detail: On Linux the stored birth value is the process start tick relative to boot, with no boot identifier. After a host reboot, an unrelated process can receive the same PID and start tick as a pending record; recovery will treat it as the original member and send SIGKILL.
findings.suggestion: Include the Linux boot identity in the persisted birth identity and treat a different boot as proof that the original process is gone.
findings.failure_scenario: A cleanup record survives a reboot, and a new process has both the recorded PID and the same boot-relative start tick. Daemon startup kills that unrelated process.

findings.title: Recovery loses descendants that have not yet been recorded
findings.detail: Ownership records are inserted one PID at a time during discovery, and recovery only visits those records. If the daemon dies before the first insert, between inserts, or after freezing the first discovered set but before a subsequent sweep discovers a newly forked descendant, recovery has no record of the remaining processes. It deletes the records it does have and permits the run to continue while an unrecorded descendant can still write to the checkout. The same gap occurs if inspection or an ownership write fails before all members are recorded and the daemon later restarts.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation-level recovery state before cleanup begins to rediscover and safely finish the entire marked process set, and retain that state until discovery and termination are confirmed complete.
findings.failure_scenario: An invocation has two marked descendants. Cleanup records the first PID, then the daemon crashes before recording the second. On restart, recovery kills the first, deletes the invocation's records, and starts the next step while the second descendant remains running.

findings.title: Recovery loses descendants that have not yet been recorded

findings.suggestion: Persist enough invocation-level ownership and discovery state to resume discovery and confirm the entire marked process set is gone before clearing the cleanup record.
findings.failure_scenario: A descendant forks between the initial process scan and freeze; the daemon crashes after SIGSTOP and before the next scan. On restart, the recorded parent is killed, the new descendant is not recovered, and the resumed run starts another command.

findings.title: A failed initial ownership write leaves no durable block on restart
findings.detail: When the first ownership insert fails, ownershipWriteFailed prevents the error path from killing the child. The in-memory termination error blocks the current scope, but no cleanup record exists to alert a restarted daemon or resumed run. The child remains alive and the next invocation can start in the same checkout. The new test explicitly confirms that the child survives this failure, but only checks the current scope.
findings.suggestion: Make a durable invocation-level cleanup intent exist before cleanup can fail, and retain a recoverable block when member persistence fails.
findings.failure_scenario: SQLite rejects the first cleanup insert while a child is running, then the daemon restarts after storage becomes available. There are no pending rows, so recovery succeeds without stopping the child and the run continues.

findings.title: Decode filenames before redacting credentials in publication diagnostics
findings.detail: The new diagnostic applies literal credential redaction directly to the Git path. A percent-encoded registered credential is therefore returned in the refusal message and can be stored or displayed in encoded form. The repository's privacy rules require decoding before redaction.
findings.suggestion: Redact credentials across decoded filename representations before emitting the diagnostic, while retaining a safe path description where possible.
findings.failure_scenario: A published file path contains a registered credential encoded as percent escapes, and its patch exceeds the private-text decoding limit. The refusal includes the encoded credential in the reported path.

findings.title: An approved round can publish scratch output before the implementer sees the warning
findings.detail: The advisory is added only when another implementation round starts. A warning does not itself cause another round, so if gates pass and review approves, the run proceeds to publication with the scratch file still in its history. This leaves the reported failure mode in place when no other issue happens to trigger a retry.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the implementer receives an opportunity to address these warnings before publication while keeping intentional additions advisory.
findings.failure_scenario: The first implementation adds .tmp-gate/report.xml, gates pass, and review approves. No second implementer invocation occurs, so the warning is never fed back to the implementer before publication.

findings.title: Encoded credentials in diagnostic paths are emitted without redaction
findings.detail: The new refusal message passes the raw Git path to redactCredentials, which only matches literal registered credentials. A percent-encoded credential in the path therefore survives and is included in the error that can be stored or shown. The private-string redactor does not protect registered credentials unless they also happen to be in the separate private-strings list.
findings.suggestion: Decode or otherwise recognize credential encodings before emitting the path, and redact safely without exposing the encoded value.
findings.failure_scenario: A file path contains a percent-encoded registered token and its content exceeds the decoding limit. The publication refusal includes the encoded token in the reported path.

findings.title: Eval trials are counted as single provider calls even when they contain several
findings.detail: The fallback creates one workload record per trial, and recorded implementation rounds also each become one record. Eval execution can make multiple provider calls within a trial or round, including panel finders, verifiers and retries. Their combined usage is attributed to the trial or round target and counted as one invocation, so counts, provider/model attribution and success shares do not represent the work performed.
findings.suggestion: Use per-call evidence where it is stored; where it is unavailable, expose the limitation without reporting a trial or round as an invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel review invokes two finders and a verifier on different models. The statistics report one invocation on the trial model and attribute the combined cost and tokens to it.

findings.title: Implementation evals discard stored cache token totals
findings.detail: Every trial with recorded rounds forces cache-read and cache-write tokens to null, even though the runner stores both totals on the trial. Since an unknown value makes the entire aggregate null, a single implementation eval causes its provider's eval cache and uncached-input totals to become unavailable.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the trial's stored cache totals at an aggregation level where they can be attributed correctly, including the common single-round case.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation eval has one recorded round and details.cacheReadTokens of 100. Its provider's eval cache-read total is returned as null instead of 100.

findings.title: Discard recorded cache totals for every implement eval
findings.detail: Whenever a trial has rounds, the aggregation forces both cache measurements to null, even though the runner records cumulative cache-read and cache-write totals in the trial details. Because sums become null when any contributing row is unknown, one implement eval makes the provider's entire eval cache and uncached-input totals unavailable. This misses the requested cached-token statistics even for a single-round trial where the stored totals are attributable without ambiguity.
findings.suggestion: Use the stored trial cache totals when they can be attributed to a provider and model, and retain unknown values only where a multi-target split cannot be recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: An implement eval completes one round with 100 cache-read tokens and 20 cache-write tokens. Its provider's eval totals report null for both cache measurements and uncached input.

findings.title: Attribute multi-provider review eval work to the trial target
findings.detail: A review trial without implement rounds is represented as one invocation of the trial's target model. Panel reviews can invoke finders and verifiers on other providers, and sample reviews can make multiple calls; the runner combines their usage and cost into the trial totals. This code therefore assigns those calls' cost and tokens to the wrong provider and model and reports one invocation instead of the calls made.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individually recorded call evidence where available, and avoid presenting combined trial costs as solely attributable to the target when the trial used other models.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel eval uses provider A as its target and provider B as a verifier. The resulting statistics charge the combined trial cost and tokens to A, count one invocation, and omit B's work.

findings.title: Multi-call evals are counted and attributed as one provider invocation
findings.detail: An eval trial can run multiple review samples, panel finders, and verifiers against different providers. The runner combines their usage into the trial, but this branch reports one invocation under the trial target's provider and model. Consequently, other providers' calls disappear and their cost and tokens are attributed to the wrong provider.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individual call evidence where it is available, and represent unattributable combined usage explicitly rather than assigning it all to the trial target.
findings.failure_scenario: A panel review invokes provider A as its target and provider B as a verifier. The result reports one invocation and both calls' combined usage for A, with no invocation for B.

findings.title: Implement evals never report cached or uncached input tokens
findings.detail: Every recorded implement round takes this branch, which forces both cache fields to null. The runner accumulates cache-read and cache-write counts on the trial, but they are discarded even for a single-round trial where those totals directly describe the round. Since one null makes the entire aggregate null, a normal implement eval also makes the provider's overall eval cache and input totals unavailable.
findings.suggestion: Use the persisted trial cache totals where they can be attributed, and preserve known aggregate totals for multi-round trials without inventing per-round splits.
findings.failure_scenario: A single-round implement eval records 100 input tokens and 50 cache-read tokens. Its provider's eval totals report null for input and cached tokens instead of the recorded amounts.

findings.title: Eval wall time includes preparation and grading
findings.detail: For trials without rounds, duration_ms is the elapsed trial duration; for implement rounds, durationMs is updated after grading. These durations include work outside the provider invocation, so the reported total and p50 do not measure provider wall time and can be dominated by tests or other grading work.
findings.suggestion: Use persisted invocation durations when available and distinguish unavailable provider durations from whole-trial or grading durations.
findings.failure_scenario: An implement provider call takes one minute and its grading gates take ten minutes. The reported provider wall time is approximately eleven minutes.

findings.title: Eval rounds discard cache totals that are stored on the trial
findings.detail: Every eval with recorded rounds reports unknown input, cache-read, and cache-write tokens, even when the trial stores those totals. A single-round implementation eval has an unambiguous provider and model, yet its requested token breakdown is unavailable in both the API and CLI. Since null propagates through summarize, one such record also makes the provider's aggregate cache totals unknown.
findings.suggestion: Use the stored trial cache totals when they can be attributed to the reported provider and model, and preserve known aggregate totals where round-level splits cannot be reconstructed.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation eval records one round with cacheReadTokens and cacheWriteTokens in its trial details; the resulting eval statistics report all three input and cache fields as null.

findings.title: Panel eval work is attributed to the trial's model
findings.detail: A review-system trial can invoke finders and verifiers on other models and providers, but its fallback record assigns the combined trial tokens and costs to details.provider and t.model_id and counts one invocation. This produces wrong per-provider and per-model workload and successful-share figures for panel evaluations.
findings.suggestion: Aggregate individually persisted call evidence where available, and avoid presenting combined panel spend as belonging entirely to the primary model.
findings.failure_scenario: A review panel uses one provider for its primary reviewer and another for a verifier; all combined trial spend and tokens appear under the primary provider and the verifier has no invocation.

findings.title: In-progress invocations lower the successful share
findings.detail: The denominator includes running invocations while only status ok contributes to the numerator. Consequently, starting an invocation immediately makes the reported historical success share decline even though no failure has occurred.
findings.suggestion: Calculate the share over completed invocations and define the empty completed set explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: A provider has one completed successful invocation and one currently running invocation; its successful share is reported as 0.5.

Reviewed signature selection, excerpts, rerun resolution, and credential redaction. The targeted tests could not load because the checkout is missing the entities dependency; a direct redaction probe reproduced a credential leak.

findings.title: Windowed redaction exposes short credentials that match a signature line
findings.detail: Credentials shorter than eight characters are redacted only when the entire input to redactCredentials equals the credential. The new publication function passes surrounding log text as well, so a short credential that is exactly the selected line is no longer redacted before it is stored and published. The previous implementation passed the selected line directly to redaction. Reproduction: `bun -e 'import { registerCredential } from "./src/util/proc.ts"; import {ciSignature} from "./src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts"; registerCredential("TEST_REVIEW", "error:"); console.log(JSON.stringify(ciSignature("test", "prefix\nerror:\nend", "fallback")));'` outputs a signature line of `error:` and an excerpt containing `error:`.
findings.suggestion: Preserve exact-match redaction for the selected publication window while retaining enough surrounding context to redact longer credentials that cross its boundaries.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential is `error:` and a CI log contains `prefix\nerror:\nend`; the credential is included unredacted in the signature and excerpt.

findings.title: Windowed redaction exposes short credentials
findings.detail: Windowed redaction passes surrounding log text to redactCredentials. Credentials shorter than eight characters are redacted only when the entire input equals the credential, so a short credential that was previously redacted as an image value now remains visible and can be persisted in the CI signature. A direct Bun probe returned `previous: [redacted]` and `window: abc123` for the same registered credential.
findings.suggestion: Preserve exact-value redaction for the selected publication window while also protecting credentials that cross its boundaries.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential is `abc123` and a job log contains `Image: abc123` followed by a failure. The image value and serialized signature contain `abc123`.

findings.title: Windowed redaction exposes short credentials that fill the published value
findings.detail: Short credentials are redacted only when they equal the entire input to redactCredentials. The new windowed caller supplies surrounding log text as padding, so a short credential that exactly equals the published image value is no longer recognized. The previous code redacted the extracted image value before storing it in the signature. A targeted probe registering `abc123` printed `[redacted]` for ordinary redaction but `abc123` for the equivalent padded window.
findings.suggestion: Apply the exact-value short-credential rule to the selected window as well as the padded input, while retaining padding for credentials crossing its boundaries.
findings.failure_scenario: A registered credential shorter than eight characters appears as the complete value of an `Image:` log line. The resulting image and serialized CI signature contain the credential and can be persisted or emitted.

findings.title: A long Bun test name can remove the chosen failure line from the excerpt
findings.detail: When an assertion error precedes a Bun failure line, the excerpt takes the end of the intervening block. If the failure line itself is longer than the available tail budget, this drops its `(fail)` prefix and the beginning of the test name, even though those characters form the chosen signature. A direct probe with `bun -e 'import {ciSignature} from "./src/integrations/ci-classifier.ts"; const x=ciSignature("test", "error: assertion failed\n(fail) " + "x".repeat(3000), "fallback"); console.log(JSON.stringify({line:x.line.slice(0,30),hasFail:x.excerpt.includes("(fail)"),length:x.excerpt.length}));'` returned `{"line":"(fail) xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx","hasFail":false,"length":1999}`.
findings.suggestion: Reserve space for the beginning of the chosen signature line before filling the remaining excerpt budget with surrounding context.
findings.failure_scenario: A Bun assertion is followed by a `(fail)` line whose test name exceeds the excerpt's remaining tail budget; the fix round receives an excerpt that does not identify the failing test.

findings.title: Event sequence restarts at zero when a job is retried

findings.title: Rejected event batches do not report job failure
findings.detail: A rejected post aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure endpoint because the signal is aborted, leaving the coordinator to expire the lease rather than receiving the required failure. This also loses the actual rejection reason.

findings.failure_scenario: The events endpoint rejects a batch with HTTP 400 or 409 while the harness is running. The harness is aborted, but no failure request is sent and the job remains leased until expiry or another coordinator sweep.

findings.title: Previously queued requests without a branch cannot run
findings.detail: The newly added branch field is optional in the persisted request, but the worker rejects its absence. Agent jobs queued by the previous release therefore fail after a worker upgrade, even though their requests were valid when stored.
findings.suggestion: Provide a compatible branch value for older requests or migrate/handle them explicitly before enforcing the new requirement.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator queues an agent job before deployment using the previous AgentJobRequest shape. After deployment, a worker leases it and reports `Missing or invalid agent branch` instead of running it.

findings.title: Heartbeat fencing can run a full heartbeat interval late
findings.detail: The periodic fence checks at heartbeat intervals and uses a strict greater-than comparison. With the default 60-second lease and 10-second heartbeat interval, a partitioned agent can keep running for nearly 70 seconds after the last successful heartbeat, exceeding the requested one-lease-period limit.
findings.suggestion: Schedule fencing against the exact deadline after each successful heartbeat, and abort when that deadline is reached.
findings.failure_scenario: A heartbeat succeeds just after a fence tick and all subsequent heartbeats fail. The tick immediately before the 60-second deadline does nothing, and the agent continues spending quota until the next tick.

findings.failure_scenario: A job queued by the previous coordinator is leased after deployment; the worker reports `Missing or invalid agent branch` instead of running it.

findings.title: Event batches can exceed the coordinator's body limit
findings.detail: Batching limits the number of events but not their serialized size. findings.title: Event sequence numbers restart on a retried job
findings.detail: Each worker attempt starts its event sequence at zero, but the coordinator retains event rows across attempts and ignores inserts that conflict on job ID and sequence. findings.title: A rejected event batch does not report job failure
findings.detail: The rejection handler aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure POST because the job signal is already aborted. If the coordinator still holds the lease, the job remains leased until expiry instead of promptly failing and becoming eligible for another worker.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish an event-post failure from cancellation and send a bounded failure report while the lease is still held.
findings.failure_scenario: The events endpoint rejects a batch with HTTP 413 or 400 while the lease remains valid. The harness is aborted, but no failure is posted and the coordinator waits for lease expiry.

findings.title: Fencing can occur up to a heartbeat interval after lease expiry
findings.detail: The fence checks elapsed time only on a periodic interval. A successful heartbeat can occur just after a check, so after heartbeats stop the worker can continue running the harness for almost an extra heartbeat interval beyond the lease period. The default interval is 10 seconds. This misses the explicit requirement to abort after one lease period without a successful heartbeat.
findings.suggestion: Reset a one-shot fencing timer on each successful heartbeat so it fires at the lease deadline.
findings.failure_scenario: A heartbeat succeeds just after a fence tick and subsequent heartbeats fail. At the tick near 60 seconds the elapsed time is still below the lease period, so the harness runs until the next tick, nearly 70 seconds after the last successful heartbeat.

findings.title: Event sequence numbers restart when a job is retried

A successful retry therefore silently loses batches whose sequence numbers overlap the failed attempt, and its stored event stream can mix attempts.

findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts batch 0 and then loses its lease. Another worker retries the job and posts batch 0; the server returns success but retains the first worker's batch instead.

findings.title: Event sequence numbers restart on a retried job
findings.detail: Each worker attempt starts its event sequence at zero, but the coordinator retains event rows across attempts and ignores inserts that conflict on job ID and sequence. If an attempt posts events and then fails or loses its lease, a subsequent worker's batches collide with those rows and are silently discarded. The job can finish with events from the failed attempt and missing events from the successful one.
findings.suggestion: Make event identity attempt-aware, or establish a coordinator-managed sequence that continues across attempts.
findings.failure_scenario: Worker A posts sequence 0 and disconnects; worker B leases the same job, posts its own sequence 0, and completes. The stored sequence 0 still contains worker A's events.

findings.title: A rejected event batch does not report job failure
findings.detail: The rejection handler aborts the job controller. The catch block then skips the failure POST because the job signal is already aborted. If the coordinator still holds the lease, the job remains leased until expiry instead of promptly failing and becoming eligible for another worker.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish an event-post failure from cancellation and send a bounded failure report while the lease is still held.
findings.failure_scenario: The events endpoint rejects a batch with HTTP 413 or 400 while the lease remains valid. The harness is aborted, but no failure is posted and the coordinator waits for lease expiry.

findings.title: Fencing can occur up to a heartbeat interval after lease expiry
findings.detail: The fence checks elapsed time only on a periodic interval. A successful heartbeat can occur just after a check, so after heartbeats stop the worker can continue running the harness for almost an extra heartbeat interval beyond the lease period. The default interval is 10 seconds. This misses the explicit requirement to abort after one lease period without a successful heartbeat.
findings.suggestion: Reset a one-shot fencing timer on each successful heartbeat so it fires at the lease deadline.
findings.failure_scenario: A heartbeat succeeds just after a fence tick and subsequent heartbeats fail. At the tick near 60 seconds the elapsed time is still below the lease period, so the harness runs until the next tick, nearly 70 seconds after the last successful heartbeat.

findings.title: Restart grace expires after heartbeat freshness, before a lease period
findings.detail: A leased job with an old heartbeat is failed once the coordinator has been up for more than `fresh` (30 seconds), even though its restart-adjusted lease remains valid for 60 seconds. This does not deliver the requested behavior that a worker gets one lease period after restart to reconnect. A worker that reconnects between those deadlines has its job retried or cancelled, and a pushed result can no longer be accepted.
findings.suggestion: Ensure restart grace protects an existing leased job for the full lease period, including against the heartbeat freshness check.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator restarts after a long outage; the worker remains unreachable for 35 seconds after listener startup and then sends its heartbeat or result. The first sweep after 30 seconds has already failed its lease.

findings.title: A dirty worktree can bypass detection of an unreported worker push
findings.detail: When reconciliation rejects an open job, the executor cancels it and calls `prepare()`. That hook returns null immediately for a dirty worktree, before checking the remote branch, so the executor runs locally even if the cancelled worker already pushed an unreported commit. The request requires such a push to end in NeedsHuman; local work instead proceeds with the remote branch having moved outside the coordinator's recorded publication state.
findings.suggestion: Check the remote branch for an unreported push before falling back locally after cancelling a reconciled job, including when preparation cannot proceed because the worktree is dirty.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker pushes W but has not reported it when the coordinator restarts. The coordinator worktree is dirty, so resume rejects the lease, cancels it, and preparation returns null without inspecting the branch; a local implementer starts instead of NeedsHuman.

findings.title: Keep local panel finders off workers
findings.detail: The production review call supplies checkout metadata to every finder, including finders configured with local: true. The executor has no local-finder flag; it only excludes targets with backend, openai or decisions fields. A local finder can therefore be sent to a worker when routing selects an otherwise eligible Claude or Codex target. findings.title: Validation preserves setup files that grading removes
findings.detail: Validation injects and runs the hidden tests immediately after setup. Actual implement grading resets the checkout and runs git clean after gates and before hidden tests. A hidden test that depends on a non-ignored file created by setup can therefore pass validation at head but fail even for the original implementation during grading. The new fixture itself creates and reads an untracked `ready` file, so its accepted case exhibits this mismatch.
findings.suggestion: Reproduce the grading checkout cleanup before injecting hidden files during both validation runs, and cover the resulting behavior with a fixture.
findings.failure_scenario: Setup writes an untracked `ready` file and the hidden test reads it. Validation reports base fail and head pass, but grading removes `ready` with git clean and the head's hidden test fails.

findings.title: The documented CLI never retrieves available production complexity
findings.detail: Production complexity is read only through the optional lookupRun dependency, but the CLI never supplies it. Consequently every generated case defaults to medium even when the report identifies a locally available production run with a different triage complexity. This misses the request's explicit requirement to record complexity when it can be found.
findings.suggestion: Connect the CLI to the existing run-record lookup and preserve the recorded complexity when available; handle values the case schema cannot represent explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: Generate a case for a factory PR whose run footer names a locally recorded small-complexity run. The generated case is labeled medium.

findings.title: The CLI never looks up available production complexity
findings.detail: The production lookup is only injectable programmatically; the actual CLI supplies no lookupRun. Every generated case therefore gets medium even when the run footer identifies a locally available run with a different triage complexity. This misses the explicit requirement to capture complexity when it can be found and produces misleading dataset labels.
findings.suggestion: Wire the CLI to a read-only run-record lookup and preserve the recorded complexity in the case format.
findings.failure_scenario: A merged factory PR identifies a run whose persisted triage complexity is small; the CLI records medium and says lookup was not configured.

findings.title: Interrupted publication permanently blocks the next case ID
findings.detail: Hidden files are created before the atomic cases.json rename. If the process is interrupted between those operations, the hidden directory survives without a corresponding case. On the next invocation the same ID is selected and rejected because its destination exists, so generation cannot proceed without manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Stage hidden files separately and make interrupted publication recoverable on the next invocation.
findings.failure_scenario: The process is stopped after creating hidden/impl-013 but before renaming cases.json; every subsequent attempt to add a case selects impl-013 and fails.

Reviewed snapshot creation, execution, reuse, retries, and evidence. Focused tests could not load because installed dependencies are incomplete or incompatible: `entities` is missing and the installed Zod lacks APIs used by the repository.

findings.title: Timed-out gate executions are never recorded or reused
findings.detail: The completed predicate rejects every timed-out result, so a full suite that reaches its timeout is discarded even when the round ends on the exact same tree and configuration. The gates stage then runs the suite again instead of carrying its failure and classification forward, contrary to the explicit reuse requirement.
findings.suggestion: Persist completed timeout results with their timeout and retry information, and reuse them under the same key.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer requests the suite, it runs for the configured timeout, and the implementer makes no further changes. The following gates stage runs the same suite again.

findings.title: Snapshot execution can attest to a tree it no longer checks
findings.detail: The snapshot checkout's HEAD is never checked after setup or the test command. A gate can change HEAD before running its tests, yet the result is stored under the original snapshot tree and later accepted as evidence for that tree. The normal gates path explicitly checks HEAD before recording evidence.
findings.suggestion: Verify that the snapshot checkout still has the expected commit and tree after the execution and retries before recording reusable evidence.
findings.failure_scenario: A setup script or test command checks out another commit and passes there. The original snapshot tree is committed by the round, and its gates stage reuses that unrelated pass.

findings.title: Signal-style exit statuses are replaced with 1
findings.detail: The wrapper returns 1 for every gate exit code above 128, even though the request requires returning the gate's exit status to the session. This changes the command result observed by the implementer.
findings.suggestion: Return the actual valid gate exit status; use a fallback only when no exit status exists.
findings.failure_scenario: A test command exits 137, but the session receives exit status 1.

findings.title: Timed-out gate executions are never recorded or reused
findings.detail: The record is written only when `completed(result)` succeeds, and that predicate rejects timed-out results. The gates stage therefore runs the same test check again for the same tree, configuration, and environment after an in-session timeout. The in-session path also does not perform the gates stage's timeout rerun, so its retry behavior differs from a normal gate execution. The request explicitly requires failures and retries to carry over and the test check to run nothing when a matching execution exists.
findings.suggestion: Apply the normal gate timeout and retry policy to the in-session execution, then persist and reuse its final timeout result and retry history.
findings.failure_scenario: A full suite exceeds its configured timeout during an implement session, and the implementer finishes without changing the tree. No record is stored, so the gates stage runs the full suite again.

findings.title: Snapshot tests observe a different commit from the round gate
findings.detail: The separate checkout uses a synthetic commit with its own message, author, timestamp, and SHA. A test that inspects `HEAD`, commit metadata, or `git describe` can therefore produce a different result from the eventual round commit even though their trees match. That result is subsequently reused as evidence for the real commit.
findings.suggestion: Ensure checks that depend on commit identity cannot be reused across the synthetic and actual commits, or arrange for the snapshot and round to use the same commit identity.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository's test checks the latest commit message or embeds `git rev-parse HEAD`; it passes against `Factory gate snapshot` but would fail against the round's actual commit.

A setup or test command can switch or replace HEAD and pass against another revision; the result is then stored under the original tree and can suppress the actual test gate and supply verify evidence for that tree.
findings.suggestion: Record the synthetic snapshot commit before execution and refuse to persist or reuse the result if HEAD changes during the gate.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured setup or test script checks out another commit before running tests, then exits successfully; the unchanged session tree later reuses that passing result.

findings.title: Reject results when the snapshot gate changes HEAD

findings.suggestion: Record the snapshot checkout's initial HEAD and refuse to persist the result if HEAD differs after execution and retries.
findings.failure_scenario: A test script checks out another commit and passes there. The result is stored under the original snapshot tree, then reused for the round commit and can satisfy verify substitution even though the tests ran against another commit.

findings.title: Include the test worker count in the environment key

findings.detail: The handler is disabled whenever the configured gate executor is not local, even when the implement session itself is local. output.summary:
Reviewed the executor, lease, restart, and rollback paths. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` could not start because the checkout is missing the `entities` dependency; it reported `Cannot find package 'entities' from 'src/gates/private.ts'`. No test assertions ran.

Reviewed job leasing, restart recovery, release matching, fallback, and executor selection. The targeted executor test could not start: `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` reported `Cannot find package 'entities'` before running any tests.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release leaves the executor running
findings.detail: Release changes are detected solely through `executor.daemonRelease`, but the previous release never writes that setting. After a rollback, the setting still names the executor's release, so it continues renewing and running its gate while the older daemon resumes using its own local gate path. The older daemon also lacks the new in-place handle and job isolation logic. This can run two gates in the same worktree and let their commands interfere.
findings.suggestion: Make executor ownership detect coordinator release changes even when the coordinator is an older release, and ensure rollback cannot resume work in the worktree until the executor's processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: A deployment is rolled back while a long in-place gate is running. The previous daemon starts without updating the release setting, while the executor continues its check and the old daemon resumes the run.

findings.title: Targeted retry jobs are never reattached
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only `baseline`, `initial`, and `rebase`. Handles for `baseline-retry-targeted`, `regression-retry-targeted`, and the other retry purposes are therefore cancelled after restart even when their stage, round, SHA, executor release, and lease match. The resumed stage repeats earlier work rather than receiving the running retry's result.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry-stage state to resume the matching retry and attach to its existing job.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts during a long targeted regression retry. On resume, it rejects the live retry handle and runs gates again.

findings.title: Queued jobs are reattached without an executor lease
findings.detail: The resume check accepts a queued job whenever any matching executor process exists. The request explicitly limits reattachment to jobs whose executor still holds a lease. A queued job has no owner or lease, so a restart can attach to work that never started and wait for pickup instead of starting fresh.
findings.suggestion: Require a live, unexpired lease held by a matching executor before reattaching.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon stops after enqueueing a job but before the executor leases it; on restart `canResume` accepts the queued job because an executor process exists.

findings.title: Executor availability does not use a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor availability is determined only by whether its PID and birth time still match. The executor records no heartbeat, so a live but stalled process is treated as available indefinitely. New gates enqueue and wait for the pickup timeout instead of immediately falling back, and a stalled executor holding a job can make `waitStopped` wait indefinitely after its lease is failed.
findings.suggestion: Record and check a fresh executor heartbeat, and make stop confirmation recover or fail closed when the owner is alive but no longer making progress.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor process remains alive but its event loop stops progressing during a gate. The daemon detects an expired lease, then waits in `waitStopped` forever because the PID still exists.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release leaves the executor running
findings.detail: Release changes are detected only through the `executor.daemonRelease` setting, which is written by the new daemon. The previous release does not write that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release's SHA in the database. Its executor continues running and leasing jobs while the older daemon resumes runs without knowledge of in-place jobs. Both processes can then operate on the same worktree, and the old daemon can accept or produce results while the surviving gate changes files.
findings.suggestion: Detect the actual current daemon release through a mechanism that the previous release also updates, and stop and confirm cleanup before allowing rollback recovery to use the worktree.
findings.failure_scenario: A new-release executor is running a gate when a deploy rolls back to the base release. The old daemon starts without changing `executor.daemonRelease`, while the executor continues its gate and the daemon resumes the same run.

findings.title: Interrupted targeted retries are always cancelled instead of reattached
findings.detail: Resume eligibility is restricted to `baseline`, `initial`, and `rebase`, although targeted and full retry executions also receive durable in-place handles. A restart during one of those checks cancels the surviving executor job and starts the retry over. This misses the explicit requirement to reattach targeted retries and can repeat a long-running check.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to resume the matching retry purpose and attach to its existing leased job.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression triggers `regression-retry-targeted` and the daemon restarts while the executor is running it. On resume, the purpose is excluded by this list, so the job is cancelled and its command runs again.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat or freshness check
findings.detail: An executor is considered available solely because its PID and birth identity still exist. There is no heartbeat timestamp or expiry. A live but stalled executor is therefore advertised as available indefinitely; jobs are queued to it and only fall back after the pickup timeout. If it stalls while holding a job, `waitStopped` also waits indefinitely for that live process, preventing fallback or another gate in that worktree.
findings.suggestion: Track executor heartbeat freshness and use it for selection and sweep decisions, while retaining process confirmation before reusing a worktree.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor process remains alive but its event loop stops responding. The daemon sees it as available, queues a gate, and can remain blocked waiting for a leased job to be confirmed stopped.

findings.title: LAN configuration bypasses the in-place executor for local gates
findings.detail: When `gateExecutor` is `lan`, the enabled flag is ignored. The LAN executor falls back directly to `localExecutor` for repositories outside its configured list, so those local gates still run in the daemon and die on restart even when the in-place executor is enabled and available.
findings.suggestion: Route the LAN executor's local fallback through the in-place executor when enabled, preserving LAN routing for configured repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure LAN gates for one repository and enable the executor, then run a gate for another repository. The gate runs in-process and is restarted after a daemon restart.

findings.title: Rollback leaves the executor running jobs against the old daemon
findings.detail: The executor detects a release change solely through this setting, but the previous release does not write it. After a rollback, it remains set to the newer release, so the newer executor continues leasing and running its jobs. The previous daemon also cannot recognize an `inplace` handle: it can fail with `Unavailable gate executor: inplace` or proceed with worktree cleanup while the executor is still using that worktree. This violates both release isolation and the one-job-per-worktree guarantee.
findings.suggestion: Use a release and daemon-liveness signal that also detects a rollback to a release that does not know about this setting, and provide a rollback-safe way to stop or recover in-place work before the older daemon resumes it.
findings.failure_scenario: A deployment starts an in-place gate and then rolls back to the base release while the check is running. The stored release remains the newer SHA, so the executor continues and the older daemon resumes without understanding its handle.

findings.title: Restarting during a targeted retry cancels it instead of reattaching
findings.detail: Resume is restricted to baseline, initial, and rebase purposes. Targeted retries and timeout retries are dispatched as in-place jobs but their saved handles are always rejected on restart. The resumed stage cancels the live job and repeats earlier gate work, despite the request explicitly including targeted retries in restart attachment.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough stage progress and retry context to resume each dispatched purpose, and attach when its stage, round, purpose, SHA, and lease match.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a long `regression-retry-targeted` job is running. The resumed gate stage rejects its handle and cancels the running retry rather than receiving its result.

findings.title: One executor serializes all jobs even when multiple gate slots are available
findings.detail: The polling loop awaits a job's entire execution before leasing another. With one long-running executor and multiple configured gate slots, all subsequent in-place jobs remain queued until pickup expiry and fall back to daemon-owned gates. Those gates then lose restart survival even though an executor and free capacity were available. Queue order also prevents the requested slot priority from governing those jobs.
findings.suggestion: Allow the executor to manage concurrent leased jobs up to the shared slot capacity, with each job independently acquiring its requested priority and renewing its lease.
findings.failure_scenario: With two gate slots, one executor starts a 15-minute suite. A second run queues another suite; it is not leased during the pickup window and falls back to the daemon despite the second slot being free.

findings.title: Executor availability is based on process existence, not a fresh heartbeat
findings.detail: Executor rows have no heartbeat timestamp, and availability only checks whether the recorded PID and birth identity still exist. A suspended or wedged executor is therefore treated as alive indefinitely. New gates are enqueued and wait for pickup expiry instead of immediately using the required no-fresh-heartbeat fallback.
findings.suggestion: Record and renew an executor heartbeat and require it to be fresh when selecting an executor and sweeping its jobs.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor process remains alive but is suspended or its event loop stalls. A daemon starts a gate and treats it as available, then waits through the pickup timeout before running locally.

findings.title: Executor stores output without the daemon’s registered credentials
findings.detail: The executor runs in a separate process and calls `loadConfig`, which registers configured provider keys, but it does not register credentials acquired dynamically by the daemon, such as the API token, GitHub token or worker tokens. `runLocalGates`, `workers.event` and `workers.complete` therefore cannot redact those values in the executor process before writing check output and results to `gate_jobs`. The daemon’s later redaction cannot undo the persisted disclosure.
findings.suggestion: Provide the executor with the complete current redaction set through a protected mechanism, and redact before any output or result is persisted.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a credential that the daemon registered at runtime, such as a GitHub token appearing in test output. The executor does not recognize it and stores it unredacted in the job events and result.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not stop executor jobs
findings.detail: Release detection depends exclusively on the `executor.daemonRelease` setting written by the new daemon. The previous release does not write that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release’s SHA in the database. Its executor continues running and renewing its jobs while the old daemon resumes the same runs without the new in-place coordination. This defeats both the release boundary and worktree exclusion during the explicitly supported rollback path.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator identity and release record whose liveness and version can be verified across rollback, and ensure the previous release cannot resume a worktree until the executor’s processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: A new daemon starts an in-place gate, then deployment rolls back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the release setting unchanged and resumes the run while the new executor continues the gate in the same worktree.

findings.title: Targeted retries and timeout reruns cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial and rebase purposes. A restart during a targeted retry or timeout rerun therefore cancels its still-running in-place job when the stage resumes, and the stage starts work again. The request explicitly requires the targeted retry to use the durable executor and reattach at the same purpose.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough stage progress to resume each retry purpose and reattach its matching job before restarting earlier gate work.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a targeted retry is running. The resumed stage encounters the recorded retry handle, rejects it because its purpose is absent from this list, and cancels or repeats the check.

findings.detail: Executor availability is inferred solely from whether a PID with the recorded birth time exists; the executor table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is consequently treated as available indefinitely. structured.summary: Reviewed the in-place job lifecycle, restart handling, release matching, worktree exclusion and credential redaction. The targeted command `bun test test/gate-inplace-executor.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing the `entities` package; it failed before executing any tests.

findings.title: Executor stores output without the daemon’s registered credentials
findings.detail: The executor runs in a separate process and calls `loadConfig`, which registers configured provider keys, but it does not register credentials acquired dynamically by the daemon, such as the API token, GitHub token or worker tokens. `runLocalGates`, `workers.event` and `workers.complete` therefore cannot redact those values in the executor process before writing check output and results to `gate_jobs`. The daemon’s later redaction cannot undo the persisted disclosure.
findings.suggestion: Provide the executor with the complete current redaction set through a protected mechanism, and redact before any output or result is persisted.
findings.failure_scenario: A gate prints a credential that the daemon registered at runtime, such as a GitHub token appearing in test output. The executor does not recognize it and stores it unredacted in the job events and result.

findings.title: Rollback to the previous release does not stop executor jobs
findings.detail: Release detection depends exclusively on the `executor.daemonRelease` setting written by the new daemon. The previous release does not write that setting, so rolling back leaves the new release’s SHA in the database. Its executor continues running and renewing its jobs while the old daemon resumes the same runs without the new in-place coordination. This defeats both the release boundary and worktree exclusion during the explicitly supported rollback path.
findings.suggestion: Use a coordinator identity and release record whose liveness and version can be verified across rollback, and ensure the previous release cannot resume a worktree until the executor’s processes have stopped.
findings.failure_scenario: A new daemon starts an in-place gate, then deployment rolls back to the base release. The old daemon leaves the release setting unchanged and resumes the run while the new executor continues the gate in the same worktree.

findings.title: Targeted retries and timeout reruns cannot reattach
findings.detail: The resume predicate accepts only baseline, initial and rebase purposes. A restart during a targeted retry or timeout rerun therefore cancels its still-running in-place job when the stage resumes, and the stage starts work again. The request explicitly requires the targeted retry to use the durable executor and reattach at the same purpose.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough stage progress to resume each retry purpose and reattach its matching job before restarting earlier gate work.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon restarts while a targeted retry is running. The resumed stage encounters the recorded retry handle, rejects it because its purpose is absent from this list, and cancels or repeats the check.

findings.title: Executor availability has no heartbeat or freshness check
findings.detail: Executor availability is inferred solely from whether a PID with the recorded birth time exists; the executor table has no heartbeat timestamp. A live but stalled executor is consequently treated as available indefinitely. If it stalls while holding a job, the lease eventually fails, but `waitStopped` keeps waiting for that same live PID and never reaches in-process fallback. If it stalls while idle, new jobs are unnecessarily queued until pickup timeout rather than immediately falling back.
findings.suggestion: Track and check executor heartbeat freshness, and define a safe recovery path that confirms its gate processes are stopped before fallback.
findings.failure_scenario: An executor process remains alive but its event loop stops progressing during a gate. The daemon expires the job lease, then waits indefinitely in `waitStopped` because the executor PID still exists.

Reviewed configuration, identity selection, GitHub callers, polling, and approval handling. The targeted command `bun test test/github-app.test.ts test/doctor.test.ts test/land-queue.test.ts` could not run because the checkout is missing the `entities` package.

Reviewed repository identity selection, token exchange, approval handling, doctor, and key validation. The targeted GitHub App test could not run because the checkout is missing the 'entities' package.

findings.title: Private keys outside the config directory are readable by agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts an absolute private-key path, but the agent read policy only adds the config directory to its denied paths. A key elsewhere is not registered as a denied credential path. Tool-enabled agents can therefore read it when their sandbox otherwise permits that location, exposing the App's signing key.
findings.suggestion: Add the resolved private-key path to the shared read-deny policy for agents and gates, including canonical and symlink spellings, or restrict the key to a protected location.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator configures a mode-0600 key at an absolute path outside the config directory, and a tool-enabled agent reads that path.

findings.title: Startup does not enforce the required key mode or readability
findings.detail: The check accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite the explicit 0600 requirement. It also checks only permission bits, not ownership or actual readability, so a 0600 file owned by another user can pass startup and fail later when a GitHub call tries to read it.
findings.suggestion: Require the specified mode and verify that the key is owned and readable by the factory user during configuration loading.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured key has mode 0700, or has mode 0600 but is owned by another user; startup accepts it instead of refusing with a clear reason.

findings.title: Key validation does not establish the required ownership, readability, or mode
findings.detail: Startup checks only the owner-read bit and the absence of group and other permission bits. It accepts modes such as 0700 and does not check that the file belongs to the daemon user or is actually readable. Consequently startup can accept a key that violates the requested 0600 requirement or cannot be read by the factory; the latter failure appears only on the first App operation.
findings.suggestion: Validate the file's owner and permitted mode, and verify that the daemon can read it during startup. Report a clear configuration error when validation fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A key owned by another user has mode 0600: stat succeeds, configuration loads, but the first configured GitHub call fails when readFileSync cannot read the key. A mode 0700 key is also accepted despite the requested mode.

findings.title: Enforce the required key ownership and mode at startup
findings.detail: The check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world bits. It does not check that the file is owned by the daemon user or that its mode is exactly 0600; the new test explicitly accepts 0400. A file owned by another user with mode 0600 passes startup validation even when the daemon cannot read it, so the configured App fails later on its first GitHub operation instead of refusing startup. Accepting 0400 also contradicts the explicitly required mode.

findings.title: Doctor requires an owner login even when the App is active
findings.detail: Doctor always marks the gh check as failed when `gh auth status` fails, even if every configured repository uses the App and the subsequent App token exchange and installation coverage checks succeed. This reports a working App-only configuration as unhealthy.
findings.suggestion: Make the authentication check reflect the identities needed by the configured repositories, while retaining the owner-login check where it is needed.
findings.failure_scenario: All configured repositories use the App, its installation token works, and no owner gh login is configured; doctor still reports a failure.
