Reviewed the authentication parser, routing, worker fallback, and implementation lifecycle. The targeted test command could not run because the checkout is missing the entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime dependencies.

findings.title: Older workers still count authentication failures as completed rounds
findings.detail: The coordinator recognizes a worker authentication failure only through the new failureClass field. A worker running the previous release does not produce that field: it reports the Claude rejection as an ordinary error, which this branch returns to the engine. During a rolling deployment or while a LAN worker has not yet been updated, the original failure therefore persists: the engine treats the implementation as finished and runs gates and review on unchanged code.
findings.suggestion: Introduce a version-compatible way for the coordinator to identify the structured failure from older workers, or prevent incompatible workers from accepting these jobs until they are updated.
findings.failure_scenario: A new coordinator dispatches an implement job to an older LAN worker whose Claude OAuth token has expired. The worker returns status error without failureClass, so the coordinator accepts the result instead of running locally.

findings.title: New worker reports are rejected by an older coordinator
findings.detail: The previous release validates agent results with a strict Zod object, so adding failureClass to a new worker's report causes the older coordinator to reject that report. The worker then reports a job failure rather than delivering the authentication result. This breaks worker/coordinator compatibility during rollout or rollback precisely when authentication fails.
findings.suggestion: Version or negotiate the worker protocol, or encode the classification in a form accepted by the previous coordinator before sending the new field.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker is updated before the coordinator, or the coordinator is rolled back. A Claude authentication rejection causes the worker to POST a result containing failureClass; the old coordinator's strict AgentResultReport rejects the unknown field.

findings.title: Older workers still report authentication failures as completed rounds
findings.detail: The fallback depends entirely on the new optional failureClass field. A worker running the previous release does not emit that field, so its authentication rejection remains an ordinary error result and is returned to the engine. The engine then records the implement stage as succeeded and proceeds to gates, verify, and review on unchanged code. This is a compatibility gap during coordinator and worker version skew; the added older-worker test explicitly preserves this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Ensure workers capable of structured authentication classification are used before dispatching these jobs, or provide another structured compatibility mechanism for reports from older workers.
findings.failure_scenario: After the coordinator is upgraded, a LAN worker still running the previous release receives an expired Claude token and returns status error without failureClass. The coordinator accepts it as the round result and consumes an implementation round.

findings.title: Authentication errors after successful work are treated as sessions that never ran
findings.detail: The parser classifies every error result with an authentication marker or HTTP 401 as a startup authentication failure, without checking whether the agent already made model calls or used tools. The worker path adopts any resulting commit and then runs the entire session locally; the coordinator path similarly invokes another candidate against the existing worktree. An expired or revoked token during a multi-turn session can therefore repeat work or external tool side effects while the code reports that the first session could not run.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish rejection before the first successful model turn or tool use from authentication failure after a session has begun, and only apply the startup fallback to the former.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude edits files or invokes a tool successfully, then a subsequent API request returns 401. The result is marked authentication; a LAN worker's changes are adopted and the same implementation prompt is run locally again.

structured.summary: Reviewed the authentication parser, routing, worker fallback, and implementation lifecycle. The targeted test command could not run because the checkout is missing the entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime dependencies.

findings.title: Older workers still report authentication failures as completed rounds
findings.detail: The fallback depends entirely on the new optional failureClass field. A worker running the previous release does not emit that field, so its authentication rejection remains an ordinary error result and is returned to the engine. The engine then records the implement stage as succeeded and proceeds to gates, verify, and review on unchanged code. This is a compatibility gap during coordinator and worker version skew; the added older-worker test explicitly preserves this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Ensure workers capable of structured authentication classification are used before dispatching these jobs, or provide another structured compatibility mechanism for reports from older workers.
findings.failure_scenario: After the coordinator is upgraded, a LAN worker still running the previous release receives an expired Claude token and returns status error without failureClass. The coordinator accepts it as the round result and consumes an implementation round.

findings.title: Authentication errors after successful work are treated as sessions that never ran
findings.detail: The parser classifies every error result with an authentication marker or HTTP 401 as a startup authentication failure, without checking whether the agent already made model calls or used tools. The worker path adopts any resulting commit and then runs the entire session locally; the coordinator path similarly invokes another candidate against the existing worktree. An expired or revoked token during a multi-turn session can therefore repeat work or external tool side effects while the code reports that the first session could not run.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish rejection before the first successful model turn or tool use from authentication failure after a session has begun, and only apply the startup fallback to the former.
findings.failure_scenario: Claude edits files or invokes a tool successfully, then a subsequent API request returns 401. The result is marked authentication; a LAN worker's changes are adopted and the same implementation prompt is run locally again.

Reviewed authentication parsing, routing, worker fallback, and restart handling. The targeted test command could not start because the checkout lacks the entities and @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime dependencies.

findings.title: An old worker's authentication failure still counts as a completed round
findings.detail: The fallback depends entirely on the new failureClass field. A worker running the previous release reports the same Claude authentication rejection as status error without that field, so the coordinator returns it as the implementer result and proceeds to gates, verification, and review. In-flight worker jobs can span a coordinator restart and worker update.
findings.suggestion: Provide a mixed-version path that prevents an old worker's unclassified result from being accepted as a completed session, or ensure old-version jobs are safely rerun locally.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator deploys the new release while a previous-release worker is executing a Claude implement job with an expired OAuth token. The worker reports an error without failureClass, and the new coordinator consumes the round.

findings.title: Verification authentication exhaustion can be discarded after review
findings.detail: Authentication exhaustion throws NoCapacityError, but the concurrent review and verification path suppresses verification errors when review requests changes. It then advances to another implementation round instead of stopping in needs_human with the authentication reason. This violates the requirement that the rule apply to verification and that authentication failures never count toward the round limit.
findings.suggestion: Propagate authentication exhaustion through the concurrent-check error handling even when review requests changes.
findings.failure_scenario: In a standard-profile round, review requests changes while every verification candidate rejects authentication. The verification error is logged as ignored, and the pipeline increments the implementation round.

findings.title: Older workers still turn authentication failures into finished rounds
findings.detail: The fallback depends entirely on the new failureClass field. An older worker's Claude harness reports the same structured authentication rejection as status "error" without that field, so the new coordinator returns it as an ordinary implementer result. The engine then commits the unchanged worktree and runs gates and review, reproducing the issue during a mixed-version rollout.
findings.suggestion: Provide a version-compatible way for the coordinator to recognize or avoid dispatching to workers that cannot report structured authentication failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A newly deployed coordinator dispatches an implement round to a worker still running the previous release; that worker has an expired Claude OAuth token and returns an error report without failureClass.

findings.title: Restart during local fallback can strand the round
findings.detail: The completed worker job remains in the durable agentJob checkpoint while the local fallback runs. If the daemon restarts after the local implementer edits files but before implementation-ready is saved, resume reattaches to that completed job and calls adopt again. For an authentication rejection with an unchanged worker SHA, adopt requires a clean coordinator worktree and throws when it sees the interrupted local edits, sending the run to needs_human.
findings.suggestion: Checkpoint the transition to local fallback and resume it without re-adopting the completed worker report, while preserving the existing safety checks for worker publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker rejects authentication, the local implementer starts editing, and the daily daemon restart occurs before the implementation-ready checkpoint.

Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, queue admission, restart handling, and notifier integration. Targeted tests could not run because dependencies including entities and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk were unavailable in the environment.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: Reconciliation skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler is started only when the issue queue has repositories and trusted accounts configured. Consequently, CLI, MCP, label, and comment runs in other repositories receive none of the requested lifecycle labels or comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover every repository with a linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #42` in a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or lifecycle comment is posted.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events disappear before they are checkpointed
findings.detail: Comments are discovered from the current run status rather than durable transition records. A needs_human or failed state that changes before reconciliation reaches it is never recorded or retried. This also occurs when an earlier comment write fails: the loop breaks before marking the later event pending.
findings.suggestion: Persist each lifecycle event and its publication-safe payload when the transition occurs, then reconcile those durable events independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human while the daemon is restarting and is resolved before the next queue poll. The next poll sees resolved, so it never posts the needs-you reason.

findings.title: Repeated needs-human episodes are suppressed
findings.detail: The comment checkpoint is keyed only by run and event name. Once one needs_human comment is marked done, a resumed run that later reaches needs_human again cannot publish the new reason, even though its label is updated.
findings.suggestion: Identify and checkpoint individual status episodes or transitions rather than a single comment per event type.
findings.failure_scenario: A run asks the owner a question, is resumed, and later needs a different decision. The issue gets the needs-you label again but no comment explaining the second decision.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The post-failure check accepts any trusted priority application in the timeline, even when that label is no longer present. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label applied before the failure. Thus a transient priority application does not have to be the current approval that makes the issue eligible.
findings.suggestion: Require a currently applied, trusted priority label whose relevant application event is later than the failure event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains an old trusted priority:2 label, fails, then a trusted user briefly applies and removes priority:1. The old priority:2 makes approved nonempty and the removed priority:1 event satisfies the post-failure check, so the issue can be picked again.

findings.title: Any issue commenter can impersonate a completed lifecycle comment
findings.detail: Recovery treats a marker in any comment body as proof that the factory posted the pending effect, without checking the author or exact body. Issue comments are untrusted data, so a third party can cause a failed or interrupted publication to be marked done without the factory comment being posted.
findings.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the configured GitHub identity and matches the persisted intended body before accepting it as the completed effect.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and its checkpoint remains pending, an issue commenter posts the predictable run/event marker. The next poll marks the effect done and never posts the factory's comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation runs only when the issue queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts, and skips repositories outside that list. Consequently, runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers for other repositories do not receive the requested labels or lifecycle comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover every repository with a linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in githubQueue.repos; no lifecycle label or comment is posted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Events are derived only from the run's current status. An event becomes durable only once reconciliation has observed it and saved a pending comment. If a run reaches needs_human or failed and is resolved or resumed before the next poll, neither its status comment nor its label transition is recorded. The same design also collapses multiple needs_human episodes into one comment because the effect key is reused.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle transition durably when it occurs and reconcile those recorded effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human just after a poll and the owner resolves it before the next poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or reason comment.

findings.title: Existing runs lose their issue status notifications after upgrade
findings.detail: The migration marks every existing run as legacy so lifecycle reconciliation excludes it, but the notifier now suppresses all issue notifications for managed repositories without checking that marker. An in-flight pre-upgrade issue run therefore has neither the old notifier nor the new reconciler posting its later status.
findings.suggestion: Keep the existing notifier responsible for legacy runs while suppressing it for runs managed by the new reconciler.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue-managed repository has an issue-triggered run in progress during deployment; after restart it reaches needs_human, but no issue comment is posted.

findings.title: A newer run can discard an older run's failed label write
findings.detail: Only the latest linked run is allowed to reconcile labels, even when an older run has a pending failed-label write. If GitHub is unavailable when a run fails and another run starts before the write succeeds, the failed label is never applied or retried. This also prevents the failed-label event from enforcing priority re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Durably preserve and reconcile required failure transitions before allowing a later run to supersede them.
findings.failure_scenario: The failed-label API call fails, then a manual run linked to the same issue starts before the next poll. Reconciliation skips the older run's label and leaves the issue without the required failure indication.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation runs only when the issue queue has configured repositories and trusted accounts, and skips repositories outside that list. Consequently, runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers for other repositories do not receive the requested labels or lifecycle comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover every repository with a linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in githubQueue.repos; no lifecycle label or comment is posted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Events are derived only from the run's current status. An event becomes durable only once reconciliation has observed it and saved a pending comment. If a run reaches needs_human or failed and is resolved or resumed before the next poll, neither its status comment nor its label transition is recorded. The same design also collapses multiple needs_human episodes into one comment because the effect key is reused.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle transition durably when it occurs and reconcile those recorded effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human just after a poll and the owner resolves it before the next poll; the issue never receives the needs-you label or reason comment.

findings.title: Existing runs lose their issue status notifications after upgrade
findings.detail: The migration marks every existing run as legacy so lifecycle reconciliation excludes it, but the notifier now suppresses all issue notifications for managed repositories without checking that marker. An in-flight pre-upgrade issue run therefore has neither the old notifier nor the new reconciler posting its later status.
findings.suggestion: Keep the existing notifier responsible for legacy runs while suppressing it for runs managed by the new reconciler.
findings.failure_scenario: A queue-managed repository has an issue-triggered run in progress during deployment; after restart it reaches needs_human, but no issue comment is posted.

findings.title: A newer run can discard an older run's failed label write
findings.detail: Only the latest linked run is allowed to reconcile labels, even when an older run has a pending failed-label write. If GitHub is unavailable when a run fails and another run starts before the write succeeds, the failed label is never applied or retried. This also prevents the failed-label event from enforcing priority re-approval.
findings.suggestion: Durably preserve and reconcile required failure transitions before allowing a later run to supersede them.
findings.failure_scenario: The failed-label API call fails, then a manual run linked to the same issue starts before the next poll. Reconciliation skips the older run's label and leaves the issue without the required failure indication.

findings.title: Status events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human, failed, and cancelled events only from the current run status. It records no pending effect when the transition happens, so a transition that is resolved or retried before the next poll is never published. The single comment key per status also suppresses a later needs-human episode of the same run.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events at the state transition, with a distinct durable identity for each episode, and reconcile those records on polling.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll. No needs-you label or reason comment is ever posted; a subsequent needs-human episode can also be suppressed by an earlier completed comment checkpoint.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a manual issue run to be picked again
findings.detail: A label-write failure is caught and queue selection proceeds in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun check only finds issue source references, while linkedIssues also admits CLI and MCP runs through Closes directives. Consequently, a completed manual run has no local latest-run guard if its failed label has not reached GitHub.
findings.suggestion: Include directive-linked runs in the existing admission evidence so a failed issue remains ineligible while its failure label is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails. GitHub rejects the failed-label write, and issue #12 still has its earlier trusted priority label. The same poll sees no active claim or issue-sourced latest run and starts a queue run without re-approval.

findings.title: Runs created during a rollback receive retroactive comments
findings.detail: The migration marks only runs present when it first executes as legacy. If the daemon rolls back, the older release can create runs without inserting lifecycle markers. When the newer release starts again, it treats those older-release runs as lifecycle-enabled and posts started and terminal comments retroactively.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle eligibility at run creation in the new release, and reconcile only runs explicitly marked eligible.
findings.failure_scenario: Deploy the new release, roll back, create and finish an issue-linked run on the old release, then redeploy the new release. The poller posts lifecycle comments for that pre-feature run.

findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository that has GitHub integration but is not listed in githubQueue.repos; no lifecycle labels or comments are written.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle states can disappear before being recorded
findings.detail: The poller derives events only from the run's current status. A needs_human state that is resolved before the next poll is never recorded, and a comment blocked behind an earlier failed comment is not marked pending before the loop breaks. A later poll cannot reconstruct either event or its reason. The same issue applies to label transitions, which are also derived only from the current status.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions and their publication-safe payloads durably when they occur, then reconcile the recorded effects until completed.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; neither the needs-you label nor the required reason comment is ever posted.

findings.title: Repeated needs-human episodes share one permanent comment checkpoint
findings.detail: The comment checkpoint is keyed only by run and event name. Once one needs_human comment is marked done, subsequent needs_human episodes of the same run are suppressed, even when they have a different reason.
findings.suggestion: Identify each durable needs-human transition separately and checkpoint its comment independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run asks for input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs input for a different reason; the second reason is never posted to the issue.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after the failure, including an event for a label that is no longer applied. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label that was applied before the failure. Together these checks allow an issue to be picked with no currently applied priority label re-approved after failure.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure-label event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure; after failure a trusted user briefly applies and removes priority:5. The issue becomes eligible using the removed priority:5 event and the old priority:2 label.

findings.title: A failed label write can permit a re-pick before failure is visible
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed. If adding failed fails, reconciliation logs the error and queue selection proceeds in the same poll. The existing latest-run check uses the run finish time rather than the failure-label application time, and it does not find CLI or MCP runs linked only through Closes #n. Consequently the issue can be selected without the required post-failure-label approval.
findings.suggestion: Make admission fail closed while the failure label is pending, using the existing single claim/admission check, and account for all linked run paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. The issue still has its old priority label, and the queue starts another run for it during that poll.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-configured repositories
findings.detail: Reconciliation skips every repository outside githubQueue.repos, and the reconciler is not started at all when the issue queue is disabled. Runs started through CLI, MCP, label, or comment triggers in those repositories therefore do not receive the requested lifecycle labels and comments, even though GitHub writes are otherwise configured.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository that has GitHub integration but is not listed in githubQueue.repos; no lifecycle labels or comments are written.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle states can disappear before being recorded
findings.detail: The poller derives events only from the run's current status. A needs_human state that is resolved before the next poll is never recorded, and a comment blocked behind an earlier failed comment is not marked pending before the loop breaks. A later poll cannot reconstruct either event or its reason. The same issue applies to label transitions, which are also derived only from the current status.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions and their publication-safe payloads durably when they occur, then reconcile the recorded effects until completed.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; neither the needs-you label nor the required reason comment is ever posted.

findings.title: Repeated needs-human episodes share one permanent comment checkpoint
findings.detail: The comment checkpoint is keyed only by run and event name. Once one needs_human comment is marked done, subsequent needs_human episodes of the same run are suppressed, even when they have a different reason.
findings.suggestion: Identify each durable needs-human transition separately and checkpoint its comment independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run asks for input, resumes after the owner responds, and later needs input for a different reason; the second reason is never posted to the issue.

findings.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
findings.detail: The re-approval check accepts any trusted priority-label event after the failure, including an event for a label that is no longer applied. The separate approved check can be satisfied by a different priority label that was applied before the failure. Together these checks allow an issue to be picked with no currently applied priority label re-approved after failure.
findings.suggestion: Require the latest trusted application of a currently applied priority label to be later than the failure-label event.
findings.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure; after failure a trusted user briefly applies and removes priority:5. The issue becomes eligible using the removed priority:5 event and the old priority:2 label.

findings.title: A failed label write can permit a re-pick before failure is visible
findings.detail: The transition removes in-progress before adding failed. If adding failed fails, reconciliation logs the error and queue selection proceeds in the same poll. The existing latest-run check uses the run finish time rather than the failure-label application time, and it does not find CLI or MCP runs linked only through Closes #n. Consequently the issue can be selected without the required post-failure-label approval.
findings.suggestion: Make admission fail closed while the failure label is pending, using the existing single claim/admission check, and account for all linked run paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. The issue still has its old priority label, and the queue starts another run for it during that poll.

Reviewed lifecycle reconciliation, eligibility, persistence, and the surrounding delivery paths. The focused command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the checkout is missing `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; it reported 0 passing tests and one module-loading error.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Reconciliation only manages repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts, and it is only started when the queue is enabled. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or issue triggers in another repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, despite the requirement covering any start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from every supported start path.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run containing `Closes #12` targets a repository that is not in githubQueue.repos; it starts and fails without either lifecycle label or comment.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both messages contain only a generic status and UI link. The requested reason is never read from the run, so issue watchers cannot see why the run failed or needs their attention even when the reason is safe to publish.
findings.suggestion: Include the redacted and publication-checked reason, using the fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a non-sensitive gate error; the issue comment says only `failed: see ...` and does not state the error.

findings.title: Publication rejection permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a body, the effect is marked done instead of posting the required fixed fallback. The same happens when a pending body fails its check at delivery. This silently loses the lifecycle notification permanently.
findings.suggestion: Persist and post a checked fixed fallback message when the original text is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL contains a private string, so checking a failure comment throws; the effect is marked done and no failure comment is ever posted.

findings.title: Status transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Comment effects are created only from the run's current status when the poller observes it. A needs-human transition followed by resumption or cancellation before the next poll leaves no durable record for the needs-human comment or label. Restarting the daemon during that interval has the same effect.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when the run state changes, then let polling deliver the recorded effects.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted for that transition.

findings.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failed label is absent, the latest-run check accepts a trusted priority application after finishedAt. If the lifecycle write fails after removing in-progress but before adding failed, that permits another run even though no priority label was applied after the failure label, contrary to the required ordering.
findings.suggestion: Require evidence of the failure label and a later trusted priority application for a failed latest run, including while label delivery is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, removal of in-progress succeeds, addition of failed fails, and an owner reapplies a priority label before the next poll; admission accepts the issue without a failure-label event.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to issue-queue repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only manages repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured, and it runs only through the issue queue. A linked issue in another repository receives none of the requested lifecycle labels or comments, even when a run starts through the CLI, MCP, or a GitHub trigger.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked issues independently of queue admission configuration, while retaining the queue's existing eligibility policy.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #123` in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; the run starts and opens a PR, but issue #123 receives no lifecycle updates.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments never include the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies contain only a generic message and a UI link. The request explicitly requires a comment with the reason for each state, so issue watchers cannot tell what failed or what needs their attention.
findings.suggestion: Include the relevant run reason after redaction and publication checking, with a fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a gate error, or enters needs_human with a specific question; the issue comment says only to see the UI and omits that reason.

findings.title: A blocked publication check permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When publication checking rejects a body, the effect is marked done instead of creating the required fixed fallback comment. The same behavior occurs when rechecking a pending body before delivery, so the comment is never retried or replaced.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a fixed, publication-safe fallback body when the original text is rejected.
findings.failure_scenario: A lifecycle comment contains a configured private string, such as one present in the UI URL; the private-strings check rejects it and the issue receives no comment.

findings.title: Polling can miss a needs-human episode entirely
findings.detail: The reconciler creates a needs-human effect only when the current run status is needs_human. No durable transition record is consulted, so a run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never gets its required label or comment. A restart during that interval has the same result.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably at the state transition and have polling deliver those recorded effects.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and its owner resumes it before the next issue-queue poll; the poll observes only the resumed status and never posts the needs-human update.

findings.title: A blocked publication check permanently drops the comment

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs for repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts configured. Issue-linked runs in other configured repositories receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments, although the request covers every start path and specifies gh as the fallback identity.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue eligibility and include all repositories containing linked runs.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in githubQueue; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments contain only fixed text and a UI link; neither includes the run's reason. The request explicitly requires a comment with the reason for each transition.
findings.suggestion: Include the relevant reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, falling back to fixed text when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with a useful error, or reaches needs_human with an actionable question; issue watchers receive no explanation of what happened or what is needed.

findings.title: Blocked comment bodies are discarded instead of replaced
findings.detail: When the publication check rejects a comment, the effect is recorded as done without posting anything. The required fixed fallback is never attempted, so the checkpoint permanently suppresses that event's comment.
findings.suggestion: Construct and check a fixed safe fallback body, then persist and deliver it through the same retry and deduplication path.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string matches part of a generated lifecycle comment; the issue receives no comment and later polls never retry it.

findings.title: Polling current state loses intermediate lifecycle transitions
findings.detail: Events are created only from the status present when the poll observes a run, and each event has one permanent key per run. A needs_human transition that is resolved before the next poll is never recorded; a later needs_human episode is also suppressed if one was already recorded. Thus the requested durable side effects are not captured at the transition.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events or an outbox at the run-state transition, with a durable identity for each applicable episode, and let polling deliver them.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or comment is ever recorded for that transition.

findings.title: A failed manual run can be picked again when its failure-label write fails
findings.detail: Label reconciliation removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, queue admission continues in the same poll. Its latest-run guard only looks up issue-source references, so a run linked through `Closes #n` is invisible to that guard. The issue then has neither status label nor a recognized latest issue run requiring reapproval.
findings.suggestion: Make admission account for failed linked runs until their failure label is durably applied, and avoid exposing an unprotected gap during label replacement.
findings.failure_scenario: A manual run linked by `Closes #7` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an API error. The queue sees the existing trusted priority label and starts another run without fresh approval.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to issue-queue repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue is enabled and only manages repositories listed in `githubQueue.repos`. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers for another configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the request covers every start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in `githubQueue.repos`; the run progresses without any of the requested issue updates.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments are fixed strings containing only a UI link. They never incorporate the run's failure or needs-human reason, so issue watchers cannot see why the run stopped as required.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and publication checking, using the required fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails because its tests failed, or enters needs-human with a question; the issue comment says only `failed: see ...` or `needs you: see ...`.

findings.title: Publication rejection permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When publication checking rejects a generated comment, the effect is recorded as done without posting anything. The request explicitly requires a fixed safe message when public text is blocked. The same loss occurs if a pending body fails the check during delivery.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a checked fixed fallback message when the intended text fails the publication check.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link, causing `checkPublicationText` to throw; the lifecycle comment is marked done and never appears on the issue.

findings.title: A failed issue can be picked before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failure label is absent, admission falls back to any trusted priority event after the run finished. Lifecycle write errors are logged and polling continues, so this permits admission without the required priority application after the failure label.
findings.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence of the failure label event and a later trusted priority application before allowing another claim, including while the label write is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the failure-label write fails or is delayed, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the label is successfully written. The next queue poll sees the later priority event and starts another run despite there being no approval after the failure label.

findings.title: Polling can miss intermediate lifecycle events
findings.detail: Effects are created only from the run's status at reconciliation time. A needs-human transition that is resolved before the next poll leaves no durable observation, and a later transition to needs-human also reuses the same already-completed effect. Consequently the issue can miss a required needs-human comment and label update.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle transition durably when it occurs and reconcile each recorded episode independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs-human and is resumed before the next issue queue poll, or reaches needs-human a second time after an earlier episode; the corresponding issue update is never posted.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to issue-queue repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue is enabled and only manages repositories listed in `githubQueue.repos`. Runs started through the CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers for another configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the request covers every start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and include linked issues from all applicable repositories.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a repository that is not listed in `githubQueue.repos`; the run progresses without any of the requested issue updates.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments are fixed strings containing only a UI link. They never incorporate the run's failure or needs-human reason, so issue watchers cannot see why the run stopped as required.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and publication checking, using the required fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails because its tests failed, or enters needs-human with a question; the issue comment says only `failed: see ...` or `needs you: see ...`.

findings.title: Publication rejection permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When publication checking rejects a generated comment, the effect is recorded as done without posting anything. The request explicitly requires a fixed safe message when public text is blocked. The same loss occurs if a pending body fails the check during delivery.
findings.suggestion: Persist and deliver a checked fixed fallback message when the intended text fails the publication check.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link, causing `checkPublicationText` to throw; the lifecycle comment is marked done and never appears on the issue.

findings.title: A failed issue can be picked before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failure label is absent, admission falls back to any trusted priority event after the run finished. Lifecycle write errors are logged and polling continues, so this permits admission without the required priority application after the failure label.
findings.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence of the failure label event and a later trusted priority application before allowing another claim, including while the label write is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the failure-label write fails or is delayed, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the label is successfully written. The next queue poll sees the later priority event and starts another run despite there being no approval after the failure label.

findings.title: Polling can miss intermediate lifecycle events
findings.detail: Effects are created only from the run's status at reconciliation time. A needs-human transition that is resolved before the next poll leaves no durable observation, and a later transition to needs-human also reuses the same already-completed effect. Consequently the issue can miss a required needs-human comment and label update.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle transition durably when it occurs and reconcile each recorded episode independently.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs-human and is resumed before the next issue queue poll, or reaches needs-human a second time after an earlier episode; the corresponding issue update is never posted.

findings.title: Older workers can publish ungranted workflow changes
findings.detail: The coordinator sends publication jobs to workers without requiring a version that enforces the new workflow check. A worker running the previous release accepts the job, ignores the new allow field, and pushes its commit before the coordinator receives the result. The coordinator's later check cannot undo a workflow triggered by that push. Jobs already leased to an old worker across a coordinator deploy have the same problem.
findings.suggestion: Require a worker capability or protocol version that guarantees this check before delegating publication, and handle jobs already leased to older workers without allowing them to push.
findings.failure_scenario: After the coordinator is upgraded while a previous-release worker remains connected, an ungranted build job adds .github/workflows/publish.yml. The old worker pushes the commit to the run branch, triggering its push workflow before the coordinator audits it.

findings.title: A resumed old worker job can push an ungranted workflow
findings.detail: The resume check accepts an existing publication job without establishing that its worker runs the new workflow guard. After a coordinator deploy, a job leased to the previous release can remain active and be reattached; that worker's publication code can push its commit before the new coordinator audits it. Release matching prevents new leases to an old worker but does not cancel an already leased job.
findings.suggestion: Fence or cancel publication jobs created under an older release before resuming them, and ensure they cannot push while cancellation is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the coordinator while a previous-release worker is editing a build run. The worker adds .github/workflows/ci.yml and publishes it after restart; the old worker has no workflow check, so the ungranted workflow reaches the remote before the new coordinator can block it.

findings.title: An in-flight old worker can push an ungranted workflow after deployment
findings.detail: The new publication check runs inside the worker, but a worker that leased an agent job before the coordinator upgrade continues executing the old publication code. That code can commit and push a workflow without this check. Release-SHA matching prevents new leases to an old worker; it does not revoke an already leased job. The coordinator only sees the commit after the push, when a push-triggered workflow may already have run.
findings.suggestion: Prevent pre-upgrade worker jobs from publishing under the new coordinator, for example by revoking or fencing existing publication leases before enabling the new policy and requiring a publication capability that old workers cannot satisfy.
findings.failure_scenario: An old worker is editing a GitHub build run when the daemon deploys this release. Its edit adds `.github/workflows/ci.yml` without an allowance, and the old worker pushes its completed commit after the restart.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents the scheduler from resuming an interrupted rollback
findings.detail: The rejection checkpoint is saved with status `needs_human` before rollback. On daemon startup, the scheduler only requeues `running` and `waiting_input` runs, so it never invokes the new rollback resume path for this terminal run. The added restart tests call `executeRun` directly and therefore bypass the scheduler behavior that controls a real restart. A rollback error or shutdown also returns `needs_human` without arranging another attempt.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while keeping the run eligible for scheduler recovery until rollback is complete, then write the terminal status. Exercise the restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon after the rejection save but before `reset`, or immediately after `reset` but before cleanup and the state save. The run remains `needs_human`, but the checkout or persisted head and pending-merge fields remain partially rolled back indefinitely.

findings.detail: The rejection is saved with terminal status needs_human before rollback starts. On daemon restart, Scheduler.start only requeues running and waiting_input runs, and its normal admission path only selects queued runs. Consequently, it never calls rollbackRejectedMerge for this checkpoint. The new restart tests call executeRun directly, bypassing the scheduler and masking this production behavior.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while retaining a recoverable status until rollback has completed, or explicitly recover rejected terminal runs in the scheduler. Exercise the restart through the scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: A deploy restarts the daemon after the rejection is saved but before reset, clean, or the rollback state save completes. The run remains needs_human, while its checkout or persisted head and gate state remain at the rejected merge; no subsequent scheduler run finishes rollback.

findings.title: An initially empty repository loses its first commands
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues stores no boundary. The next poll containing an issue is treated as the first poll, so its comments establish the boundary and are never processed. The existing test explicitly expects this behavior, although the request requires the first successful poll to establish the enable boundary.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue on a repository with no open issues; after its first successful poll, create an issue and post a trusted `/limitless` command before the next poll. The command is skipped permanently.

findings.title: The boundary can predate commands on closed issues
findings.detail: The maximum timestamp among currently open issues can be much older than queue enablement. A comment on a closed issue created after that maximum but before enablement passes the boundary check if the issue is later reopened. This violates the explicit requirement that pre-boundary commands on reopened issues never run.
findings.suggestion: Use GitHub-time evidence that represents the enablement poll rather than only the latest activity among open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: The newest open issue was updated on January 1; a closed issue received a command on January 2; the queue is enabled on January 3 and that issue is reopened on January 4. The January 2 command starts a run.

findings.title: A marker anywhere in a trusted request silently suppresses it
findings.detail: The substring check rejects any command containing `<!-- limitless-`, even when a trusted human authored it and it otherwise meets every command requirement. The request does not exclude commands that quote or discuss factory markers, and skipped comments are never recorded or reported.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments by their author or a narrowly validated factory comment format, without rejecting arbitrary request text.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless investigate <!-- limitless-lifecycle:... -->` to ask about a lifecycle marker. Every poll silently skips the command.

findings.title: An empty first poll causes later commands to be discarded
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues leaves the repository boundary unset. The first later poll containing an issue establishes its boundary from that issue and skips its comments, even though those comments were created after the successful enable poll. They remain at or before the newly stored boundary and never run.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue for a repository with no open issues, then create an issue and post a trusted command before the next poll. The command is permanently skipped.

findings.title: Queue routing suppresses existing pull request comment triggers
findings.detail: GitHub sends pull request conversation comments as `issue_comment` events. This branch intercepts all such events for a queue repository and only requests an issue poll, but the poll queries issues rather than pull requests. Previously an owner’s `/limitless` comment on a pull request reached the webhook request builder. Pull request comments were explicitly out of scope, so enabling the issue queue must not silently disable that behavior.
findings.suggestion: Limit the queue hint routing to issue comments and preserve the existing webhook path for pull request comments.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner posts `/limitless fix this` on a pull request in a configured queue repository. The webhook returns success, but no run is created.

findings.title: Marker text suppresses valid trusted commands
findings.detail: The command definition requires a trusted, unedited comment with a non-empty request. Rejecting any body containing `<!-- limitless-` adds an undocumented exclusion based on arbitrary request text, including text quoted by a user asking the factory to fix its own markers. The author and factory identity should determine whether a comment was posted by the factory.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments without rejecting marker text in trusted users' requests.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless fix parsing of <!-- limitless-status -->` on an open issue. Every poll silently skips the command.

findings.title: Record a rejected timeout rerun as rejected
findings.detail: When a timeout rerun reports success but fails provenance validation, validateRetry restores the failed original result and stores the rejected passing attempt in result.retryAttempt. This branch sees the original timeout and records rerun_failed, losing the fact that the passing rerun was rejected. The requested history includes retry_rejected for provenance rejection.
findings.suggestion: Detect a provenance-rejected timeout rerun from retryAttempt before deriving the timeout-rerun history, and cover it through the real gates stage.
findings.failure_scenario: An initial check times out; its rerun passes after modifying a tracked file. Provenance validation rejects that pass, but the observation is finalized with history rerun_failed instead of retry_rejected.

findings.title: Replay completed in-place results across release changes
findings.detail: The resume path still requires the executor's canResume check for an in-place handle. That check requires the job's releaseSha to equal the current daemon release even when the job is already done and its result is stored. A deploy between result completion and the evidence checkpoint therefore discards the completed job and starts a new execution, losing the first failure observation.
findings.suggestion: Allow a completed in-place job's stored result to replay across release changes, while retaining the compatibility checks needed for jobs that are still running.
findings.failure_scenario: An in-place gate fails and stores its result; the daemon stops before inserting observations; a new release starts and resumes the run. canResume rejects the old release SHA, so the failure is never recorded if the replacement execution passes.

findings.title: Record the timeout rerun when its setup prevents the check from running
findings.detail: Finalization derives history only from a matching final check comparison. If the initial check times out and the timeout rerun fails during setup, compareGates produces a setup failure and a synthetic not_run comparison for that check. This lookup excludes not_run, so observationHistory receives no comparison and records no_retry even though the stage reran and failed. A direct probe, `bun -e 'import { observationHistory } from "./src/gates/failure-class.ts"; console.log(observationHistory(undefined));'`, returned `no_retry`.
findings.suggestion: Carry the stage timeout-rerun outcome into finalization even when the rerun cannot produce a check result, and record rerun_failed for the original timeout.
findings.failure_scenario: A check times out on its initial execution, then a setup command fails on the stage's timeout rerun. The timeout observation is finalized with history no_retry instead of rerun_failed.

findings.title: Replay completed in-place results across a release change
findings.detail: Reattachment depends on `canResume`, which rejects even a completed job when its recorded release SHA, environment or daemon port differs. The completed result is then discarded without recording its failures, and the stage executes again. A deploy between job completion and the evidence checkpoint can therefore erase the failure if the new execution passes.

findings.detail: Real in-place jobs are completed by a separate `WorkerStore` constructed in `runInplaceExecutor`, which never receives the engine's injected `loadSource`. findings.title: A failed daemon replacement can leave the executor running
findings.detail: Installation replaces and health-checks the daemon before reaching the executor unit. If the replacement daemon starts but fails its health check, the error path restores the daemon and exits without shutting down the existing executor. The replacement may already have recorded its release in the database, causing the existing executor to exit and launchd to start another executor from the upgraded release while installation has not confirmed that release healthy. This violates the requirement that a failed install never leave an executor running on an unconfirmed release.
findings.suggestion: Ensure an unsuccessful installation shuts down and disables the installed executor, including failures during daemon replacement, while retaining the existing journal recovery behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: After a packaged upgrade, service install starts the new daemon; it records the new release but fails the health check. Installation restores the daemon unit and exits before processing the executor, leaving launchd free to run the executor from the new package.

The resolver creates a second registration with the default merge policy, and queue runs no longer use the existing repository's settings. Resolution also makes an additional GitHub call that can prevent admission if it fails.

findings.detail: A resumed gates stage receives a new stage ID, but the observation inserted before interruption retains the original stage ID. findings.suggestion: Persist both retry and confirmation outcomes while retaining the specified confirmation classification precedence.

findings.title: Recovered leases are absent from the renewal loop
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated after a directly applied write. Reviewed lifecycle publication, recovery, privacy and command reservation. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Recover uncertain posts before suppressing their bodies
findings.detail: An uncertain POST is marked done without marker recovery if reinspection of its stored body fails. This closes the checkpoint without determining whether GitHub accepted the comment, contrary to the required recovery behavior.
findings.suggestion: Recover the independently generated marker and checkpointed author before closing an uncertain POST; apply body inspection before any subsequent POST.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but its response is lost. Before the next poll, private-string inspection fails or a new private string matches the stored body. The effect becomes done without fetching comments or recording the accepted comment ID.

findings.title: Use fixed diagnostics for publication failures
findings.detail: The comment delivery catch logs the exception text. The subprocess wrapper includes the complete command, including the question or reason body, and stderr in command errors; credential redaction does not remove configured private strings. This also violates the explicit requirement that publication diagnostics contain fixed codes rather than exception output.
findings.suggestion: Log a fixed publication failure code without the exception text or command arguments.
findings.failure_scenario: A comment POST fails and the subprocess error includes its body or server output. If a private string is added while the POST is in flight, or private content appears in the error output, that content is written to the lifecycle diagnostic.

findings.title: Recheck needs-human status before publishing its reason
findings.detail: Eligibility checks the current status only for question effects. A pending needs-human comment remains eligible after the run resumes or is cancelled, including when that transition happens during identity lookup. The stale comment can then tell the issue that the run needs attention and publish an obsolete reason.
findings.suggestion: Include the relevant current run status in eligibility for needs-human publication and recheck it immediately before POST.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and its comment is checkpointed. While posting identity lookup is pending, the user resumes or cancels the run. The lookup returns and the old needs-human comment is posted.

findings.title: Recover an uncertain POST before closing its checkpoint
findings.detail: The pending body is inspected before marker recovery. If inspection now fails, the effect is marked done without looking for the checkpointed author's marker, even when `page` records an uncertain prior POST. This violates the explicit requirement to recover an uncertain prior POST before closing its checkpoint.
findings.suggestion: Perform marker recovery independently of whether the saved body remains publishable, then suppress any new POST if the current publication check fails.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but the response is lost. Before the next poll, private-string configuration becomes unreadable or changes so the saved body fails inspection. The checkpoint is closed without searching GitHub for the accepted comment.

findings.title: Do not include exception output in publication diagnostics
findings.detail: The delivery failure path logs the exception verbatim apart from registered credential redaction. Subprocess errors can contain command arguments and GitHub response output, including configured private strings or other withheld content. The request explicitly requires fixed diagnostic codes and no exception output.
findings.suggestion: Log a fixed delivery failure code without interpolating the exception or subprocess output.
findings.failure_scenario: A GitHub API failure returns an error containing a configured private string. The lifecycle catch passes that error to `logFailure`, which writes the private string to diagnostics.

Reviewed lifecycle checkpoints, publication inspection, recovery, and answer-command reservation. The targeted command `bun test test/issue-queue.test.ts` could not start because the checkout lacks `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/client/index.js`; no test assertions ran.

findings.title: Publication failures log exception output and the comment body
findings.detail: The delivery error path passes the exception to logFailure. A failed gh command includes its arguments and stderr or stdout in the exception, so a failed question or reason POST logs the outgoing body and arbitrary GitHub error output. Credential redaction alone does not enforce the required fixed-code diagnostics or remove configured private strings from exception output.
findings.suggestion: Log a fixed publication failure code without interpolating the exception or command output.
findings.failure_scenario: A question POST fails or times out; the command error includes the body argument, and the lifecycle log records the question text. GitHub error output containing a configured private string can also reach the log.

findings.title: Inspection failure closes an uncertain POST without recovery
findings.detail: The stored body is inspected before marker recovery, and any inspection failure marks the effect done even when its page checkpoint shows that a POST was already issued. This permanently closes an uncertain effect without checking whether GitHub accepted it, contrary to the required recovery behavior. If the POST was not accepted, the question set will never be published after the inspection problem clears.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the uncertain checkpoint and recover its marker before closing it; suppress any subsequent POST if inspection remains unsuccessful.
findings.failure_scenario: A question POST fails before acceptance after page 1 is checkpointed. On the next poll, private-string inspection temporarily fails. The effect is marked done without recovery, and later polls never publish the still-open question set.

findings.title: A superseded, unpublished question set can never be published
findings.detail: An unsent stale effect is marked done, and observation refuses to create another effect whenever that question-set key already exists. If the same unanswered set later becomes eligible again, it remains permanently invisible on GitHub. The same outcome occurs after recovery confirms that a stale uncertain POST was not accepted. The new tests explicitly expect this behavior, but it conflicts with the requirement to publish each unanswered question.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish superseded effects that were never published from completed publications. If the same set becomes eligible again, recover any uncertain POST first, then permit publication when recovery confirms no matching comment exists.
findings.failure_scenario: A run waits with question 42 while identity lookup is deferred; it temporarily leaves waiting status or loses its issue link before the POST, then returns to waiting on the same issue with question 42 still unanswered. The effect is already done, so subsequent polls and restarts never publish the question.
